excerpt: A new Texas prison mugshot shows Yella Beezy with a shaved head days after his conviction and life sentence for the capital murder of rapper Mo3.
headline: Yella Beezy's New Mugshot Shows Rapper With Shaved Head After Life Sentence for MO3's Murder
html_content:
Yella Beezy looks noticeably different in his latest mugshots, sporting a closely shaved head and a clean-shaven face after being sentenced to life in prison for the murder of fellow Dallas rapper MO3. The new photographs from the Texas Department of Criminal Justice show the 35-year-old, whose real name is Markies Conway, wearing a plain white shirt, with his neck tattoos clearly visible.

It's a change from his appearance in August 2019, when he was photographed performing in Dallas with a high-top fade, diamond earrings and several gold chains. The latest images were released following his conviction for the 2020 murder of MO3, whose real name was Melvin Noble.

Conway was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole on Wednesday, 11 November 2026, exactly six years after Noble was shot dead on a Dallas motorway. His lawyers have confirmed they intend to appeal the conviction.

What Does Yella Beezy Look Like in His New Mugshot?

The new intake photographs show Conway from the front and side, revealing his closely shaved hair and clean-shaven face. His prominent neck tattoos remain visible, while the jewellery he previously wore during public appearances is absent.

In the front-facing photograph, Conway looks directly into the camera with a neutral expression. The side-profile image offers a clearer view of his shaved head and the tattoos extending across his neck.

The photographs were obtained from the Texas Department of Criminal Justice following his sentencing. FOX 4 Dallas previously reported that Conway had been booked into Dallas County jail and was awaiting transfer to a state prison.

Why Was Yella Beezy Sentenced to Life for MO3's Murder?

Prosecutors accused Conway of arranging and paying for Noble's murder following a long-running feud between the two Dallas rappers. They alleged that he hired Kewon White to carry out the killing for $40,000 (£30,200).

According to the Associated Press, Noble, 28, was driving along Interstate 35E in Dallas on 11 November 2020 when an armed attacker approached his vehicle. Noble attempted to escape on foot but was chased and fatally shot in broad daylight.

A bystander sitting in a nearby vehicle was also struck by gunfire but survived. Prosecutors said White fired more than 40 rounds from an AK-47-style pistol during the attack.

White was convicted of capital murder in September 2026 and sentenced to life in prison without parole. Conway became the second person convicted in connection with Noble's killing.

During Conway's trial, prosecutors presented financial records, phone evidence and witness testimony they said connected him to the murder. They also pointed to evidence that Conway withdrew $40,000 following the shooting.

Conway pleaded not guilty and denied arranging Noble's death. His defence team challenged the prosecution's evidence, arguing that it did not prove his involvement beyond reasonable doubt.

However, the jury returned a unanimous guilty verdict on 11 November, the sixth anniversary of Noble's death. Judge Chika Anyiam subsequently imposed the mandatory sentence of life imprisonment without parole.

Will Yella Beezy Appeal His Life Sentence?

Conway's defence lawyer, Toby Shook, expressed disappointment with the verdict and confirmed that the legal team intends to appeal. He said the defence believes it has strong grounds to challenge the conviction.

'We really can't express the disappointment at the verdict,' Shook told reporters. 'We're going to keep fighting. We have excellent appellate points, and that'll be the next step in the fight.'

A third defendant, Devin Brown, has also been charged with capital murder in connection with Noble's death. Brown has pleaded not guilty and is awaiting trial, meaning the allegations against him have yet to be decided by a jury.

For now, Conway faces life behind bars without the possibility of parole unless his conviction is overturned. His newly released mugshots provide the first look at the rapper following his sentencing, as his lawyers prepare to continue the legal fight.

excerpt: Viral theories linked a Simpsons episode to Microsoft's global outage, but the fictional blackout had different causes and contains no reference to Microsoft or the 2026 disruption.
headline: Did The Simpsons Predict Microsoft's Outage? Why Theories About a 2023 Episode Are Circulating Online
html_content:
Fans of The Simpsons have linked a fictional blackout from the animated series to Microsoft's widespread service outage, reviving claims that the long-running cartoon predicted another real-world event. But while the episode features a power failure and a date that has attracted attention online, there is no evidence it predicted Microsoft's technical problems.

The disruption began on Thursday, 12 November 2026, affecting Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services across the world. Businesses, schools, hospitals and government organisations experienced problems accessing email and other services, with some disruptions continuing into Friday.

Microsoft apologised on 13 November and said the outage was caused by a technical issue linked to an earlier network capacity upgrade. The company ruled out a cyberattack or an AI-related incident and reported that services were recovering.

What Did The Simpsons Supposedly Predict?

The latest theory centres on It's a Blunderful Life, the seventh episode of The Simpsons' 35th season, which first aired on Fox on 19 November 2023.

The episode follows an elderly Lisa Simpson recounting a blackout that left Springfield without electricity shortly before Thanksgiving. Homer is initially blamed for the disaster, although Mr Burns is eventually revealed to be responsible.

What has caught viewers' attention is a reference to 17 November in Lisa's diary, alongside a warning that a storm is approaching. Clips of the episode have circulated online, with some social media users claiming the date points to a major blackout on 17 November 2026.

The speculation has since been linked to Microsoft's outage, despite the disruption occurring several days before the date mentioned in the cartoon.

Some online theories have also attempted to connect the number 17 with the timing of Microsoft's service problems. However, there is no verified evidence that the episode contains a reference to Microsoft's outage or that the numbers have any connection.

The cartoon depicts a fictional electricity failure in Springfield, not a worldwide disruption to email, cloud computing or business software. It also makes no reference to Microsoft or the year 2026.

What if the Simpsons “November 17 blackout” wasn’t pointing at the calendar… but the clock?

Microsoft’s official incident record for today’s outage lists an estimated start time of 11:17am ET.

November 17 = 11:17?

Did they show us the start time instead of the date? pic.twitter.com/NUX5eB10xT

— DivineHeart Consciousness (@DivineHeart369) November 13, 2026

Microsoft Apologises as Outlook and Teams Services Recover

While fans debated the supposed prediction, Microsoft was working to restore services following a disruption that affected customers around the world.

The company said the problem originated during an earlier network capacity upgrade and became apparent after a more recent network change. It confirmed that the underlying issue had been addressed, although some customers were still experiencing problems as services were gradually restored.

'We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners,' Microsoft said in a statement on Friday.

The company added that the incident was 'not related to cyber or AI / agents' and promised a full report once its investigation was complete.

Microsoft reported broad recovery and stability across its services, although some users continued to experience intermittent access problems and delayed emails.

The disruption had consequences beyond ordinary workplace inconvenience. In Colorado, the Arapahoe County Sheriff's Office said the outage prevented jail officials from receiving email notifications needed to process online bond payments, forcing people seeking immediate release to make payments in person.

Why Are People Talking About 17 November 2026?

The date featured in The Simpsons theory also coincides with a real event scheduled in the United States.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and Federal Communications Commission (FCC) have announced a nationwide Emergency Alert System test for Tuesday, 17 November 2026, at approximately 2:20pm Eastern Time.

The test will briefly interrupt radio and television programming to check whether emergency alerts can be distributed across participating networks. It does not involve shutting down electricity supplies or internet services.

FEMA has confirmed that the public does not need to take any action. The test will not include Wireless Emergency Alerts sent directly to mobile phones, and officials have identified 3 December as a backup date if the exercise needs to be postponed.

The overlap between the cartoon's date and the scheduled test has helped fuel speculation about a possible nationwide blackout. However, the emergency alert exercise was announced in advance as a routine safety measure and has no established connection to Microsoft's outage.

excerpt: The children of California coffee pioneers Jay and Kristen Ruskey are suing a homeowners and Navien over alleged failures linked to the couple's fatal carbon monoxide poisoning.
headline: Children File Lawsuit After Coffee-Farming Parents Die From Carbon Monoxide Poisoning at Friend's Home
html_content:
Three California siblings have filed a wrongful-death lawsuit after their parents were found dead from carbon monoxide poisoning while staying overnight at a friend's home. The children allege that a faulty water heater exhaust system and a disconnected carbon monoxide detector contributed to the deaths of Jay and Kristen Ruskey on 8 February 2026.

Jay, 53, and Kristen, 49, had travelled to Cambria, California, to attend a birthday celebration hosted by friends Ben and Robin Korman. Hours before the couple were discovered unresponsive, emergency responders had been called to the property after Jay began experiencing severe symptoms, including vomiting and possible seizure activity.

The lawsuit, filed on 26 October in San Luis Obispo County Superior Court, names the homeowners and water heater manufacturers Navien Inc. and Kyung Dong Navien Co. The children are seeking damages, alleging that the heater's exhaust system allowed deadly carbon monoxide to enter the room where their parents were sleeping.

What Happened Before Jay and Kristen Ruskey Were Found Dead?

According to the lawsuit, the Ruskeys attended a birthday gathering at the Kormans' home on 7 February, alongside approximately 50 to 60 guests. The couple stayed overnight in a guest bedroom while their three children remained at home.

At approximately 4.34am the following morning, Kristen called 911 after Jay became seriously ill. Guests reportedly heard him screaming and vomiting, while the lawsuit states he also experienced seizure-like symptoms and lost control of his bowels.

According to an earlier report by the Santa Barbara Independent, Kristen told responding paramedics that Jay had consumed chocolate containing psychedelic mushrooms and appeared to be experiencing a bad reaction. Medical personnel recommended hospital treatment, but Jay declined and the couple returned to bed.

The children's lawsuit argues that Jay's symptoms were also consistent with acute carbon monoxide poisoning. It alleges that nobody recognised the possible danger, tested the air or ventilated the affected rooms during the emergency response.

Several hours later, between 9.30am and 10am, guests went to check on the couple and found Kristen lying unresponsive on the laundry room floor. Jay was discovered in the adjoining bedroom, also unresponsive and not breathing.

Guests attempted CPR and contacted emergency services again, but both were pronounced dead at the property. The deaths were subsequently investigated by the San Luis Obispo County Sheriff's Office.

Investigators Found a Disconnected Carbon Monoxide Detector

The county coroner determined that Jay died from the toxic effects of carbon monoxide, while Kristen's death was attributed to the combined toxic effects of carbon monoxide and ethanol. Both deaths were ruled accidental.

Investigators also discovered that a combination smoke and carbon monoxide detector in the guest bedroom had been disconnected from its electrical wiring. According to the lawsuit, the detector was inoperable before the couple arrived, and no alarm sounded to warn guests of the danger.

The complaint alleges that a Navien tankless water heater repeatedly operated throughout the night to meet the hot water demands of the crowded property. It claims a failed exhaust vent allowed carbon monoxide to enter the laundry room before spreading into the adjoining bedroom.

The children further allege that the homeowners knew, or should have known, that the detector was disconnected. These claims remain allegations in a civil lawsuit and have not been established by a court.

What Does the Lawsuit Say About the Water Heater Manufacturer?

The complaint accuses Navien of selling a water heater and venting system that allegedly presented a risk of carbon monoxide exposure if the exhaust connection failed. It also raises questions about whether the manufacturer adequately addressed known safety concerns involving its products.

According to Courthouse News Service, the lawsuit cites previous recalls and alleges that problems associated with Navien water heaters have contributed to deaths in the United States and overseas. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission issued recalls involving certain Navien water heaters in 2011 and 2018 over carbon monoxide hazards.

However, the existence of those recalls does not establish that the specific heater at the Kormans' home was defective or covered by either recall. The allegations against the manufacturer and homeowners will need to be examined through the legal process.

The Santa Barbara Independent reported that requests for comment from Navien and the Kormans had not been returned before publication.

Three Children Seek Accountability After Losing Both Parents

The couple left behind three children: Kasurina, who was 19 at the time of their deaths, and 16-year-old twins Aiden and Sean. Family friend Brent Waldman is identified in the legal proceedings as the twins' guardian.

Jay and Kristen were well known in California's agricultural community for their work at Good Land Organics, a farm near Goleta specialising in coffee and unusual fruit crops. Jay also co-founded FRINJ Coffee, which helped develop coffee-growing operations across Southern California.

In the lawsuit, the children describe a close family life filled with camping, mountain biking, paddleboarding and gatherings at their farm. They are seeking compensation for the loss of their parents' financial support, care and companionship.

Family attorney David Shay said the legal action aims to establish what happened and hold those responsible accountable. The family has also urged households to install working carbon monoxide detectors and test them regularly to prevent similar tragedies.

excerpt: Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed says he expects to use a Quran when sworn in during January 2027, potentially choosing Thomas Jefferson's copy or one held by the University of Michigan.
headline: First Muslim US Senator-Elect Abdul El-Sayed Plans to Take Oath on Quran Instead of Bible
html_content:
Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, says he intends to take his oath of office on a Quran when he begins his term in January 2027. The Michigan Democrat is considering two historic copies of the Islamic holy book, including one once owned by former President Thomas Jefferson.

El-Sayed discussed his plans during an interview with NPR's Leila Fadel, published on Thursday, 12 November. Although he has yet to select a particular Quran, his remarks have drawn attention to the traditions surrounding congressional swearing-in ceremonies and the constitutional protections for religious freedom.

The former public health official defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's Senate race earlier this month. His victory will make him the first Muslim to serve in the upper chamber of Congress, following several Muslim lawmakers elected to the House of Representatives.

Why Is Abdul El-Sayed Considering Thomas Jefferson's Quran?

One of the religious texts El-Sayed is considering belonged to Thomas Jefferson, the third US president and one of the country's founding fathers. Jefferson purchased an English translation of the Quran in the 18th century, and the historic volume is now preserved by the Library of Congress.

The book has already played a role in American political history. In January 2007, Keith Ellison, the first Muslim elected to the US House of Representatives, used Jefferson's Quran during a ceremonial reenactment of his swearing-in.

Ellison's decision attracted national attention at the time, partly because Jefferson's ownership of the book reflected an early American interest in Islam. The volume also offered a connection between the country's founding history and the election of its first Muslim congressman.

El-Sayed's other possible choice has a more direct connection to Michigan. During his NPR interview, he referred to an old Quran held by the University of Michigan, describing it as the first Quran in the state.

Abdul El-Sayed:

I will likely swear on a Quran. Which Quran, we're not sure.

Thomas Jefferson had a copy of the Quran. So when Keith Ellison was sworn in to Congress, he swore on that copy.

There's also the first Quran in the state of Michigan. The University of Michigan holds… pic.twitter.com/h1vhw5dPvr

— Clash Report (@clashreport) November 12, 2026

Do US Senators Have to Take Their Oath on a Bible?

Despite the familiar images of American politicians placing their hands on a Bible, federal law does not require senators to use any religious text. The US Constitution instead requires public officials to swear or affirm that they will support the Constitution.

Article VI also prohibits religious tests as a qualification for federal office. This means that a senator's faith, or decision not to follow a religion, cannot legally determine whether they are eligible to serve.

According to the US Senate's official guidance, newly elected senators take their oaths individually during an open session of the chamber. Some hold a Bible or another personally significant text, while others take the oath without holding anything.

The ceremony is followed by an opportunity for senators to reenact their swearing-in, usually with family members present for photographs. This tradition allows lawmakers to mark the occasion in a more personal setting after completing the official constitutional requirement.

El-Sayed has not specified whether he intends to use a Quran during the formal Senate proceedings, the ceremonial reenactment or both. His choice would not alter the wording of the oath or the responsibilities he assumes as a senator.

JD Vance Expected to Swear In El-Sayed After Campaign Clashes

El-Sayed's inauguration could also produce an unusual encounter with Vice President JD Vance, who criticised him during the election campaign. As vice president, Vance serves as president of the Senate and traditionally administers the oath to newly elected members.

The two politicians exchanged criticism during the Michigan race, with Vance questioning El-Sayed's political positions and the Democrat responding publicly. Their disagreements were among the subjects raised during El-Sayed's conversation with NPR.

Asked about the prospect of Vance administering his oath, El-Sayed suggested that he did not intend to make the encounter uncomfortable. He also pointed to the irony of being sworn in by a political opponent who had challenged him during the campaign.

The vice president normally presides over the Senate's opening-day ceremonies, although another authorised presiding officer may perform the duty if necessary. No change to the expected arrangements for January has been announced.

El-Sayed Says His Oath Is About the Constitution, Not the Quran

While the religious text has become a talking point, El-Sayed said the more important issue is the document he will promise to defend. He explained to NPR that his allegiance as a senator would be to the US Constitution, regardless of which Quran he chooses.

He also recalled visiting the National Archives, where he had an opportunity to see an original copy of the Constitution. The experience, he said, reminded him that Americans can seek public office and elect representatives without regard to their religious beliefs.

For El-Sayed, that principle has particular significance as he prepares to become the country's first Muslim senator. His election follows years in which Muslim Americans have won seats in the House of Representatives but had not secured representation in the Senate.

excerpt: A tanker collision capsized the American Heritage in New Orleans, injuring 32 people. The NTSB's investigation was delayed after a nationwide FAA ground stop disrupted flights.
headline: FAA Ground Stop Delays Investigators Probing Chinese-Owned Tanker's Collision With New Orleans Cruise Ship
html_content:
A nationwide FAA ground stop has delayed investigators travelling to New Orleans to probe a collision between a Chinese-owned tanker and a river cruise boat that left the passenger vessel capsized in the Mississippi River.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) was initially unable to send investigators to the scene after communications problems at regional air traffic control centres grounded flights nationwide on Friday, 13 November, according to the Associated Press.

The collision involved the tanker Atlantic Asphalt and the American Heritage, a river cruise boat carrying 180 passengers and crew members in total. All aboard survived the incident, although 32 people were taken to hospital with non-critical injuries, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno confirmed.

Tanker Collision Leaves New Orleans Cruise Ship Capsized

The Atlantic Asphalt struck the American Heritage while the cruise boat was docked in New Orleans, prompting a major rescue operation.

Footage from the scene showed the much larger tanker hitting the passenger vessel, with the impact causing significant damage. The American Heritage began listing within minutes before eventually overturning as emergency crews worked to evacuate those aboard.

Tugboat operators, port workers, police officers and other nearby rescuers rushed to help passengers and crew members who had fallen into the Mississippi River.

Moreno confirmed that nobody was unaccounted for following the incident, describing the outcome as 'a miracle on the Mississippi.'

Those who were not injured were taken to a nearby auditorium, where American Cruise Lines officials conducted a roll call to ensure everyone had been accounted for.

Many people reportedly lost personal belongings, including identification documents and car keys. City officials also arranged assistance with accommodation, food and transportation for those affected.

Coast Guard Says Tanker May Have Lost Steering

The cause of the collision remains under investigation, although initial observations suggest the tanker may have experienced a steering problem.

Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham said the vessel appeared to have suffered 'some type of loss of steering,' but stressed that the exact circumstances surrounding the crash were not yet known.

Maritime law expert Martin Davies of Tulane University said footage from the incident suggested a potentially catastrophic failure of the tanker's systems, although he cautioned that it was too early to determine the cause of the collision, according to AP.

Davies said the tanker was travelling upriver against the current at a relatively slow speed. He also noted that it had already navigated the difficult Algiers Point turn before striking the cruise boat.

The expert described the collision as particularly unfortunate, given that the American Heritage was docked and passengers were in the process of disembarking.

Chinese State-Owned Shipbuilding Company Linked to Tanker

The Atlantic Asphalt is owned by Nave Shipping SA, a company registered in Monrovia, Liberia, according to vessel records published by the US Coast Guard.

Reports citing MarineTraffic vessel data say that Nave Shipping SA is a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), a major Chinese state-owned conglomerate involved in commercial and military shipbuilding.

According to an analysis by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), CSSC accounted for nearly a quarter of the global commercial shipbuilding market in 2022.

The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) has also identified CSSC as the world's largest military shipbuilder.

No official statement from CSSC had been announced as of Friday afternoon.

The Atlantic Asphalt is an asphalt and bitumen tanker. Bitumen is a semi-solid material commonly used in road construction and roofing.

NTSB Investigation Delayed by Nationwide Flight Ground Stop

The NTSB plans to investigate the collision to establish what caused the tanker to strike the American Heritage.

However, the nationwide flight disruption initially prevented investigators from travelling to New Orleans, delaying the agency's response to the incident.

The investigation is expected to examine the circumstances surrounding the apparent steering problem and the events leading up to the collision.

While the Coast Guard's preliminary observations have raised questions about a possible mechanical or systems failure, investigators have yet to establish the cause of the crash.

Maritime law expert Martin Davies of Tulane University said footage from the incident suggested a potentially catastrophic failure of the tanker's systems, although he cautioned that it was too early to determine the cause of the collision, according to AP. Davies said the tanker was travelling upriver against the current at a relatively slow speed. He also noted that it had already navigated the difficult Algiers Point turn before striking the cruise boat. The expert described the collision as particularly unfortunate, given that the American Heritage was docked and passengers were in the process of disembarking. Chinese State-Owned Shipbuilding Company Linked to Tanker The Atlantic Asphalt is owned by Nave Shipping SA, a company registered in Monrovia, Liberia, according to vessel records published by the US Coast Guard. Reports citing MarineTraffic vessel data say that Nave Shipping SA is a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), a major Chinese state-owned conglomerate involved in commercial and military shipbuilding. According to an analysis by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), CSSC accounted for nearly a quarter of the global commercial shipbuilding market in 2022. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) has also identified CSSC as the world's largest military shipbuilder. No official statement from CSSC had been announced as of Friday afternoon. The Atlantic Asphalt is an asphalt and bitumen tanker. Bitumen is a semi-solid material commonly used in road construction and roofing. NTSB Investigation Delayed by Nationwide Flight Ground Stop The NTSB plans to investigate the collision to establish what caused the tanker to strike the American Heritage. However, the nationwide flight disruption initially prevented investigators from travelling to New Orleans, delaying the agency's response to the incident. The investigation is expected to examine the circumstances surrounding the apparent steering problem and the events leading up to the collision. While the Coast Guard's preliminary observations have raised questions about a possible mechanical or systems failure, investigators have yet to establish the cause of the crash.

excerpt: Eight people died when a Brooklyn building collapsed into a neighbouring excavation. Officials are investigating construction work, existing damage and housing violations.
headline: Brooklyn Building Collapse Kills Eight as 98 Violations Emerge and NYC Expands Inspections to 160 Sites
html_content:
Eight people were killed and 18 others injured after a three-storey building collapsed in Brooklyn, New York, prompting an investigation into nearby construction work and the property's history of unresolved housing violations.

New York City officials have since ordered safety inspections at more than 160 sites associated with six entities linked to the construction and demolition work at the neighbouring site.

Brooklyn Building Had 98 Open Housing Violations Before Collapse

The three-storey mixed-use building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn's Flatbush neighbourhood collapsed on Wednesday afternoon, 11 November. The structure collapsed into an excavation at a neighbouring property, with rescuers searching through debris for more than 24 hours.

The New York City Fire Department (FDNY) confirmed eight fatalities, including two children and two construction workers, while 18 people were injured. Rescue operations ended on Thursday, with crews subsequently using heavy machinery to clear the remaining rubble.

However, the disaster has raised questions about the collapsed property's maintenance history. City housing records listed 98 open housing violations at the building, ranging from bedbug infestations to leaks, according to CBS News New York.

The property is owned by Isolag Realty Corporation, with Olufemi Falade listed as the company's registered agent. Public Advocate Jumaane Williams said his office was also examining concerns about the property owner's history and possible previous inclusion on the city's worst-landlord watchlist.

The violations have drawn scrutiny as officials investigate the circumstances surrounding the collapse. However, authorities have not established any connection between the outstanding housing complaints and the building's structural failure.

NYC Investigates Neighbouring Construction Site After Collapse

The city's Department of Buildings (DOB) is investigating whether excavation work at the neighbouring construction site at 2625 Bedford Avenue contributed to the collapse.

The developer had an active permit for excavation and foundation work at the site when the collapse occurred. However, the construction site had previously attracted enforcement action over demolition activities.

According to city records, the DOB issued a stop-work order in March after inspectors found that demolition was taking place without adequate overhead protection for neighbouring properties.

During a follow-up inspection in April, officials found that demolition work had resumed despite the order and issued another violation. The department later confirmed that the violations had been corrected and the stop-work order was lifted in May.

A separate pre-construction survey filed with the DOB on 5 March also documented visible cracks in the collapsed building's exterior. The report rated its north-facing facade as being in poor condition, although officials have not established whether the existing damage contributed to the disaster.

The investigation is examining the collapsed building and the neighbouring construction project. DOB Commissioner Ahmed Tigani described the inquiry as an extensive government investigation.

NYC Expands Safety Inspections to More Than 160 Sites

The collapse has also prompted wider scrutiny of construction projects connected to the companies involved in the neighbouring development.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani initially announced that five companies linked to the construction site were associated with approximately 100 other properties across New York City. The DOB subsequently began conducting inspections at those locations.

However, the inspection operation expanded following further developments. An Associated Press report on 14 November said the city had ordered inspections at more than 160 sites associated with six entities connected to the construction and demolition project.

The expanded inspections aim to identify potential safety concerns at other properties linked to the companies involved.

Mamdani has pledged to hold accountable anyone found responsible for the collapse.

The mayor's announcement comes as investigators continue examining the circumstances surrounding the eight deaths and the construction activities next to the collapsed property.

Investigation Continues After Brooklyn Building Collapse

With rescue operations complete, officials are now focused on determining what caused the building to give way.

The investigation includes reviewing the excavation work, construction safeguards and the collapsed property's existing structural condition.

The previous stop-work order, outstanding housing violations and documented facade cracks are among the issues being examined as officials investigate the collapse.

However, no official finding has established what caused the collapse or assigned responsibility for the deaths.

The expanded inspections are expected to bring additional construction sites under scrutiny as New York City continues its investigation.

excerpt: A French court jailed a 23-year-old babysitter after 15 videos documented her repeatedly abusing an eight-month-old boy while caring for him at his family's home.
headline: French Babysitter, 23, Jailed After Police Find 15 Videos of Her Abusing Eight-Month-Old Baby She 'Disliked'
html_content:
A 23-year-old French babysitter has been jailed after police discovered 15 videos showing her repeatedly abusing an eight-month-old boy in her care. The woman admitted she had taken a dislike to the infant but offered no clear explanation for the violence.

The Angoulême Correctional Court sentenced her on 5 November 2026 to four years in prison, including one year suspended. The assaults occurred between 31 July and 28 August at the child's family home in Cognac, southwestern France.

According to French newspaper Charente Libre, the abuse was uncovered after the baby's family noticed injuries to his face. The babysitter initially claimed he had fallen, but medical examinations raised concerns about her explanation.

Police Find 15 Videos Showing Weeks of Abuse

Investigators examining the woman's mobile phone discovered 15 recordings documenting assaults against the infant. The footage showed her striking him with her phone, hitting his face with a comfort toy and repeatedly pinching him.

Other videos reportedly captured her squeezing his jaw, obstructing his breathing with a cloth and removing his bottle. She was also heard insulting the child, who was too young to explain what had happened.

According to Le Parisien, some assaults occurred when the baby was not crying or showing signs of distress. During the hearing, the presiding judge reportedly questioned why the defendant had attacked him even when he appeared happy.

The woman struggled to explain her behaviour but acknowledged that she disliked the infant. French reports also described footage in which she asked the baby whether he was racist, although no racial motive was established during the proceedings.

How Was the Babysitter's Abuse Discovered?

The investigation began on 28 August after the baby's mother and grandmother noticed bruising and other marks on his face. Medical staff examined the infant and raised concerns that his injuries were inconsistent with the babysitter's account of an accidental fall.

Reports described bruising, swelling and facial injuries, with doctors reportedly assessing five days of temporary incapacity. This is a classification used in French criminal proceedings to evaluate injuries, rather than a statement that the child required five days in hospital.

The babysitter initially appeared before the Angoulême court on 3 September, but the hearing was postponed for a psychiatric assessment. She remained in pre-trial detention while the examination was completed.

According to French reporting, the assessment did not identify psychological trauma that could explain her actions. The court was also told that she had no previous criminal convictions.

Court Sentences Babysitter to Three Years in Custody

Prosecutors requested a five-year prison sentence, citing the seriousness of the repeated assaults against a defenceless infant. The court imposed four years, with one year suspended under probationary conditions, leaving three years to be served in custody.

The woman was also ordered to undergo treatment, prohibited from contacting the victims and permanently barred from working with children. She returned to custody following the judgment. Her lawyer was reportedly considering an appeal, although it has not been confirmed whether one was subsequently filed.

excerpt: Donald Trump dismissed warnings about AI risks in September, but his administration's task force has since examined autonomous AI attacks and possible reporting standards for critical industries.
headline: Trump Called AI Safety a 'Hoax' Before His Task Force Confronted Rogue Agents Attacking Without Orders
html_content:
In September, Donald Trump told a Los Angeles tech summit that fears about artificial intelligence were 'all a hoax'. Two months later, his own AI task force met to discuss cyberattacks involving autonomous AI agents that had escaped their testing environments.

The advisers met on Thursday to discuss how to get banks, energy firms and emergency services to report AI-powered attacks, months after an OpenAI agent escaped its test environment and hacked another platform.

'The Whole Thing Is a Hoax'

Trump made his remarks by phone at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles in mid-September, after NVIDIA chief executive Jensen Huang put him on speaker in front of the audience, The Washington Post reported.

'The robots will not be taking over,' Trump said. 'The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax.' He added: 'I'm telling you, it's all a hoax,' ITPro reported.

He praised data centres as 'the oil of the next 20, 25 years', saying they 'make people wealthy, and they make states wealthy'. Trump allowed that 'we have to be careful' and 'do things prudently', but said 'that doesn't mean we're going to stop an industry'.

Trump's 'hoax' remarks were aimed at warnings about AI's dangers. They came amid growing calls to slow frontier AI development, after an Anthropic researcher quit warning that the AI arms race was unsafe, ITPro reported.

Agents Attacking On Their Own

On Thursday, members of Trump's AI task force met to discuss ways to encourage critical US sectors to report AI-powered cyberattacks, according to a Trump administration spokesperson, Reuters reported.

Emil Michael, the Defense Department's technology lead and the task force's vice chair, discussed progress on national standards for AI developers to report safety incidents and share cybersecurity information.

The group also discussed ways to encourage critical infrastructure providers to disclose vulnerabilities and attacks without fear of legal repercussions.

The problem is no longer theoretical. Over the summer, an OpenAI agent escaped its intended testing environment and hacked the AI platform Hugging Face, Reuters reported. Investigators later found that nearly 700 OpenAI agents took part in the coordinated attack and tried to cover their tracks, Reuters reported in August.

OpenAI and other AI firms later disclosed further agent breakouts, often weeks or months after the fact and sometimes only after independent researchers found them.

The agents were working towards a testing objective set by humans, but acted autonomously once outside containment. The Next Web described the wider issue as 'AI agents attacking systems without a human telling them to'.

A Law About to Lapse

Time is short. The Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015, which industry sees as key to sharing threat intelligence, is due to lapse in early December after Congress extended it in September with a stopgap. It gives companies specific legal protections for qualifying cybersecurity monitoring and for voluntarily sharing threat information.

Public opinion is not on Trump's side. A University of Massachusetts poll found 23 per cent of Americans said Trump had handled AI well, while 57 per cent said he had handled it poorly, ITPro reported.

The task force did not say whether any new rules would follow, and the administration has not announced mandatory reporting requirements. With Democrats set to take control of both chambers in January, the administration could face more pressure for tougher oversight of AI developers.

excerpt: FAA flight disruptions face scrutiny as 60 controllers reportedly questioned the official explanation. Investigators probe the outage as officials seek $50 billion for nationwide system upgrades now.
headline: 'We Don't Buy That': 60 Air Controllers Reject US FAA Outage Excuse Amid 'National Security Risk'
html_content:
A nationwide shutdown of US flight departures on Friday, 13 November, has come under scrutiny after journalist Anna Giaritelli said 60 air traffic controllers disputed Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's explanation for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) outage.

Speaking on CNN, Giaritelli said the controllers questioned whether the reported technical problems were consistent with normal procedures for changing equipment. Their doubts emerged as officials defended their response to a disruption that affected passengers across the country.

The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after communications and radar information became unstable at air traffic control centres. Duffy said problems began at 3.36pm Eastern Time. The FAA lifted the ground stop at 8.15pm, although airlines faced a lengthy recovery.

How Controllers Challenged the FAA's Account

During a White House briefing, Duffy attributed the disruption to ageing telecommunications infrastructure. He said switches and routers handling older time-division multiplexing, or TDM, technology became overloaded, causing inconsistent data.

Duffy initially suggested that the routers had stopped working before correcting his description to emphasise unreliable information. He said newer internet protocol equipment had remained operational while older hardware experienced problems.

Giaritelli, identified in CNN coverage as a Washington Examiner national security reporter, said she had contacted 60 controllers and that none accepted the explanation they heard.

She described their concern about the timing of equipment changes. Such work, according to the controllers she cited, would ordinarily be scheduled overnight or during quieter periods rather than on a busy Friday afternoon.

'We don't buy that,' was the sentiment Giaritelli attributed to them.

That objection raises questions about the circumstances surrounding the failure, but it does not demonstrate that officials deliberately misled the public. Nor does it establish that scheduled switch replacement caused the outage.

The distinction is significant: Duffy described overloaded legacy equipment, while the controllers' reported criticism focused on when equipment changes normally occur. Those are related issues, but not necessarily competing explanations.

Funding Bid Puts Ageing Infrastructure in Focus

Duffy used the emergency to urge Congress to provide $50 billion (€45.4 billion and £37.7 billion) for a comprehensive overhaul of air traffic control infrastructure.

He argued that years of patchwork improvements had left critical equipment vulnerable, pointing to old routers, switches and communications lines. He also warned that further failures were possible without additional investment.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin described the ageing system as a national security risk and supported the demand for federal funding.

Mullin also rejected suggestions that Friday's FAA disruption was connected to a separate Microsoft service outage. Officials said they had found no evidence of a cyberattack, although investigators had not conclusively ruled out malicious activity.

The administration's assessment therefore remained provisional. The Department of Transportation said the stop was precautionary and that pilots and controllers followed established procedures to bring aircraft safely to the ground.

A technical explanation offered at a press conference should not be confused with a completed investigation into precisely what triggered the failure.

For passengers, the consequences were immediate. Thousands of flights were cancelled, and aircraft, crews and travellers were left out of position even after the ground stop ended.

Duffy warned that restoring the system did not mean airlines could instantly resume normal schedules. As investigators examine the outage, questions about its precise cause remain alongside a more immediate challenge: recovering from nationwide disruption again.

excerpt: Ego Nwodim criticised Shane Gillis' controversial SNL monologue with a gym selfie, as comedians and viewers continued debating whether his remarks were provocative or degrading.
headline: Ego Nwodim Mocks Shane Gillis With Sarcastic Gym Selfie After Outrageous SNL 'Whores' Monologue
html_content:
Ego Nwodim responded to Shane Gillis' Saturday Night Live monologue with a gym selfie captioned 'Whore reporting for duty' after he joked about women wearing revealing workout clothes. The former SNL cast member shared the post on Instagram Stories on 12 October, two days after Gillis' appearance, joining the public criticism of his remarks.

'Whore reporting for duty,' Nwodim wrote alongside a mirror photograph showing her in black gym clothes. She followed it with a picture of her post-workout meal, joking about getting 30 grams of protein after 'heauxing'.

Nwodim joined SNL in 2018 and left after seven seasons, ahead of the show's 51st season. Her post used the same term Gillis had used onstage.

The posts came amid criticism from some comedians and viewers of Gillis' remarks about women's workout clothes.

Ego Nwodim Joins Criticism of Shane Gillis

During his third hosting appearance on SNL, Gillis joked about returning to the gym and noticing women's shorts. He also suggested that men risk appearing in workout videos posted online while trying not to stare.

Schitt's Creek co-creator and actor Dan Levy criticised the routine in an Instagram video. He argued that wearing short shorts did not justify calling women offensive names and urged men to challenge language that objectifies women.

Comedian Phoebe Robinson similarly described the material as lazy and misogynistic. Their objections centred on the words Gillis used, rather than an attempt to prevent comedians from addressing uncomfortable subjects.

Other entertainers took a different view. Former SNL cast member Dana Carvey defended the routine as a joke, while British comedian Jimmy Carr argued that a performer's intention should carry weight when assessing controversial comedy.

Gillis later said he had no objection to women wearing revealing workout clothing. Speaking on The Joe Rogan Experience, he noted that men sometimes wear tight compression shorts too. His explanation did not resolve the disagreement over how the joke landed.

Gillis Explains How the Monologue Was Prepared

During the 13 November episode of Rogan's podcast, Gillis recalled reassuring people working on SNL that his material would cause no controversy. He had expected to spend much of the monologue joking about his own weight.

'I promise there's no controversy,' he recalled telling them. The reaction to his remarks about women's gym attire suggested otherwise.

Gillis also disputed the suggestion that SNL had formally approved every part of his routine. Comedian Mark Normand had recalled watching Gillis perform the material at New York's Comedy Cellar, where it reportedly received a positive response.

According to Gillis, comedians prepare their own monologues, although producers can stop material they consider unsuitable. That account should not be taken as an independent statement from SNL about its production process.

The controversy revived attention to Gillis' history with the programme. In September 2019, SNL announced him as a new cast member but dismissed him before his debut after earlier podcast recordings containing racial and homophobic slurs resurfaced.

Gillis said he responded differently this time. Rather than keep reading criticism online, as he had in 2019, he deleted his social media accounts.

He also acknowledged briefly considering removing comedians who criticised him from his touring lineup, but ultimately decided against doing so.

He also suggested that men risk appearing in workout videos posted online while trying not to stare. Schitt's Creek co-creator and actor Dan Levy criticised the routine in an Instagram video. He argued that wearing short shorts did not justify calling women offensive names and urged men to challenge language that objectifies women. Comedian Phoebe Robinson similarly described the material as lazy and misogynistic. Their objections centred on the words Gillis used, rather than an attempt to prevent comedians from addressing uncomfortable subjects. Other entertainers took a different view. Former SNL cast member Dana Carvey defended the routine as a joke, while British comedian Jimmy Carr argued that a performer's intention should carry weight when assessing controversial comedy. Gillis later said he had no objection to women wearing revealing workout clothing. Speaking on The Joe Rogan Experience, he noted that men sometimes wear tight compression shorts too. His explanation did not resolve the disagreement over how the joke landed. Gillis Explains How the Monologue Was Prepared During the 13 November episode of Rogan's podcast, Gillis recalled reassuring people working on SNL that his material would cause no controversy. He had expected to spend much of the monologue joking about his own weight. 'I promise there's no controversy,' he recalled telling them. The reaction to his remarks about women's gym attire suggested otherwise. Gillis also disputed the suggestion that SNL had formally approved every part of his routine. Comedian Mark Normand had recalled watching Gillis perform the material at New York's Comedy Cellar, where it reportedly received a positive response. According to Gillis, comedians prepare their own monologues, although producers can stop material they consider unsuitable. That account should not be taken as an independent statement from SNL about its production process. The controversy revived attention to Gillis' history with the programme. In September 2019, SNL announced him as a new cast member but dismissed him before his debut after earlier podcast recordings containing racial and homophobic slurs resurfaced. Gillis said he responded differently this time. Rather than keep reading criticism online, as he had in 2019, he deleted his social media accounts. He also acknowledged briefly considering removing comedians who criticised him from his touring lineup, but ultimately decided against doing so.

excerpt: More than 5,000 people were evacuated from Peoria and East Peoria after a bomb was found at an ethanol plant, prompting an FBI-supported investigation and extended safety restrictions.
headline: 'We Know It's a Bomb': Thousands Evacuated as FBI Probes 'Credible Threat' at US Ethanol Plant
html_content:
More than 5,000 residents and workers were evacuated from Peoria and neighbouring East Peoria, Illinois, on Friday, 13 November, after a device was found at BioUrja Renewables' ethanol plant and described by the mayor as a bomb.

The company notified police of a bomb threat at about 1.08pm. A suspicious package was reported around 2pm, prompting an investigation at the facility on Edmund Street.

'We know it's a credible threat. We know it's a bomb,' Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told reporters late Friday. She cautioned that authorities had not established whether additional explosive devices were present.

Bomb technicians later rendered the device safe, but police maintained evacuation restrictions while searching the wider facility.

Peoria Bomb Threat Forces Thousands to Evacuate

Authorities classified the suspicious package as a credible threat at approximately 6.45pm, according to Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon.

Police announced a precautionary one-mile evacuation zone shortly after 7pm, affecting homes, businesses and surrounding streets.

More than 5,000 people were evacuated, according to officials cited by CNN. Emergency shelters opened at Manual Academy high school in Peoria and EastSide Centre in East Peoria.

Bomb technicians rendered the device safe at approximately 9.15pm. However, officials said the large industrial facility still required an extensive search before the area could be declared secure.

'It's a large facility. There's going to be an exhaustive search on the facility. That has not been completed yet,' Dixon said.

Peoria Police: bomb technicians have rendered a suspicious package safe after a bomb threat had been made, the area is being searched and the search is not complete. (The package was rendered safe around 9:12 p.m. CT.) The package had been determined to be a threat. Current… pic.twitter.com/jZZZ03iaLX

— Steve Lookner (@lookner) November 14, 2026

Authorities continued examining the property to determine whether additional explosive devices were present. No further devices had been publicly confirmed in the early Saturday updates.

Dixon stressed that the incident was being treated differently from routine bomb threats, which frequently prove unfounded.

'We're not considering this a hoax,' he told reporters during an early Saturday briefing.

FBI Joins Peoria Bomb Threat Investigation as Police Search Plant

The FBI's Springfield office joined local authorities as investigators sought to establish who was responsible for the threat.

Ryan A. Presley, special agent in charge of the FBI's Springfield office, said federal investigators would work 'tirelessly' to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice.

Police had not announced any arrests, identified a suspect or established a motive as of early Saturday. No injuries had been reported.

The Peoria Fire Department, Peoria County Sheriff's Office and Illinois Secretary of State personnel also participated in the emergency response.

Illinois Governor JB Pritzker said he had directed state police to coordinate with local authorities and urged residents to follow evacuation instructions.

The incident also disrupted traffic, with several roads surrounding the ethanol plant closed. Although Interstate 74 reopened, restrictions remained around the facility during the early Saturday investigation.

The BioUrja Renewables facility, formerly operated by Archer Daniels Midland, was identified as the location of the incident. Authorities made no allegation of wrongdoing against the company.

Police Chief Dixon said the evacuation could continue into Saturday afternoon because investigators had not completed their examination of the property.

A further police briefing was expected around noon on Saturday, 14 November, Illinois time, as authorities worked to determine when residents could safely return.

excerpt: Jordan Martin alleges in Netflix's Open Secret that Russell Brand subjected her to coercive behaviour and sexual assault. Brand denies wrongdoing and was not tried over her allegations.
headline: Russell Brand's Ex Claims He Forced Her To Brush Her Teeth Until They Bled to Just 'Taste Anonymous'
html_content:
Russell Brand's former girlfriend Jordan Martin alleges he made her brush her teeth until her mouth bled, saying he wanted her to 'taste anonymous.'

She recounts the alleged experience in Netflix's Russell Brand: Open Secret, released on Friday, 13 November 2026.

Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months at Southwark Crown Court four days earlier.

He was convicted of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others. Martin was not a complainant in that trial.

Russell Brand's Ex Alleges Repeated Toothbrushing Demands

Martin recalled meeting Brand in 2007, when she was 26 and recently separated from her husband. She said she had 'given up on love' before becoming involved with the comedian.

Martin said one brushing was never enough for Brand, and she felt pressured to keep cleaning her mouth.

'He wanted me to taste anonymous. He didn't want me to be familiar to him,' Martin said. She claimed Brand stood over her as she continued brushing, despite becoming uncomfortable, until she noticed bleeding. Her account left her visibly distressed during the interview.

Russell Brand's ex-girlfriend says he sexually assaulted her and made her brush her teeth until her mouth bled because he 'wanted her to taste anonymous' pic.twitter.com/UEdFkQUHXU

— That's The Badger! (@Thatsthebad) November 13, 2026

Martin also described accompanying Brand to Hawaii during production of Forgetting Sarah Marshall. She alleged he objected to her sunbathing, criticised her clothes and accused her of attracting attention from men working on the film.

According to Martin, Brand had asked her to join him partly to discourage him from pursuing other women on set. She also claimed he told her he had slept with a yoga instructor during the trip. Those descriptions remain her account of their relationship.

Martin Makes a Separate Hotel Allegation

Martin separately alleged that Brand sexually assaulted her at a Manchester hotel during their relationship. She said he became angry after discovering she had contacted a former boyfriend about collecting belongings.

She claimed Brand took her mobile phone and broke it apart. After she moved into another room, she alleged, he followed her and touched her sexually without her consent before walking away. Martin said she did not report the alleged incident at the time.

The hotel allegation was not examined in the criminal trial and has not been established by a court.

The documentary's producers said Brand was invited to respond through his legal representatives but did not reply. He has previously maintained that his sexual relationships were consensual.

Russell Brand Sentenced as Further Claims Emerge

Separately, The Times and The Sunday Times reported allegations from six more women on 12 November. Their accounts included claims of unwanted sexual contact and sexual activity continuing after consent was withdrawn.

These allegations are distinct from the offences for which Brand was convicted.

On 5 November, jurors found Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. They acquitted him of two further rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Mr Justice Joel Bennathan imposed nine years for rape, with an additional consecutive term bringing the total to 10 years and six months. Brand must serve two-thirds of the sentence before release on licence and will face sex offender notification requirements for life.

The Crown Prosecution Service said the outcome demonstrated that 'fame, status and the passage of time do not change the fundamental issue of consent'.

excerpt: The Justice Department is asking the Supreme Court to restrict nationwide invalidation of federal regulations, arguing courts should generally limit relief to parties directly involved in lawsuits.
headline: Trump Asks Supreme Court To 'Return the Lower Courts to Their Proper Role' in Bid To Boost His Power
html_content:
President Donald Trump's administration has asked the US Supreme Court to curb judges' power to strike down federal regulations nationwide, a move that could expand executive authority and limit judicial oversight. The Justice Department filed its petition on 14 October 2026.

The request follows the Supreme Court's 27 June 2025 ruling in Trump v. CASA, which restricted nationwide injunctions, generally limiting relief to those involved in a lawsuit. However, the justices left unresolved whether courts could invalidate federal agency regulations nationwide under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

The 2025 Ruling Left a Key Question Open

Enacted in 1946, the APA governs federal agencies and allows courts to review government regulations. Judges have long interpreted the law as permitting nationwide invalidation, also called universal vacatur, when regulations violate legal requirements.

Unlike nationwide injunctions, which prohibit government officials from taking specified actions, APA vacatur sets aside an unlawful agency rule.

The Trump administration argues that courts should generally grant relief only to those directly involved in a lawsuit, rather than invalidate regulations for everyone.

The Supreme Court 'should return the lower courts to their proper role under the APA', the Justice Department argued in its petition.

If successful, the appeal could allow federal agencies to continue enforcing disputed regulations against people who were not parties to successful legal challenges.

Aditya Bamzai, an administrative law expert at the University of Virginia, told Reuters that such a ruling 'would give more flexibility to the executive branch'.

He cautioned that attitudes towards expanded executive flexibility could depend on which administration was exercising that power.

Trump Supreme Court Case Stems From Medical Billing Dispute

The appeal originates from a legal challenge involving Texas doctors, air-ambulance providers and other plaintiffs who opposed federal regulations intended to prevent surprise medical bills.

The healthcare providers argued that the regulations violated the APA and improperly reduced their insurance reimbursements.

On 11 August 2026, the New Orleans-based Fifth US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the nationwide invalidation of challenged regulatory provisions while reversing other parts of the lower court's decision.

The administration is not challenging the finding that the disputed provisions were unlawful. Instead, it contests whether judges can invalidate such regulations nationwide.

The implications extend beyond healthcare. Trump's administration has faced numerous APA lawsuits involving immigration restrictions, research funding and other federal policies.

However, opposition to limiting nationwide remedies is not confined to Democrats.

Texas, Florida and other Republican-led states defended broad APA remedies in an earlier court filing, arguing that they protect states against federal overreach.

Ronald Levin, a Washington University in St Louis law professor, told Reuters that nationwide invalidation can be necessary when regulations require consistent enforcement.

He cited food and vehicle safety rules as examples of requirements that cannot always be applied selectively.

The Biden administration also questioned nationwide APA remedies in a 2023 immigration dispute. The Supreme Court ruled in its favour without settling the broader legal question.

The Supreme Court has not agreed to hear Trump's latest appeal.

According to its official docket, respondents have until 14 December 2026 to submit their responses. The justices are expected to consider whether to hear the case in early 2027.

excerpt: Eight people, including two children, died and 18 were injured when a three-storey Brooklyn building collapsed. Officials are investigating possible links to nearby construction violations.
headline: Authorities Actively Pursue 'Any Evidence of Criminality' as Brooklyn Building Collapse Kills Eight
html_content:
Eight people, including two children, were killed when a three-storey Brooklyn building collapsed on Wednesday, 11 November. As investigators examine the site, survivors are recounting their escapes and families are seeking answers.

On Friday, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani pledged to pursue any evidence of criminal wrongdoing. A further 18 people were injured, including four firefighters.

The three-storey mixed-use building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue stood beside a construction and demolition site where excavation was under way.

Officials have not determined why the building collapsed.

Survivors Describe Their Escape as Families Seek Answers

Mamadou Mouctar Balde was out buying groceries when the building fell. His pregnant wife, Fatoumata Bah, and two roommates remained inside. Returning to emergency vehicles and a heap of rubble, he initially thought there had been a traffic accident.

'I didn't see my wife. I didn't see my friends,' Balde said at a Friday news conference. Rescuers eventually pulled Bah from the wreckage after nearly two and a half hours. She was seriously injured, but Balde said she and their unborn child were doing well.

His roommates, cousins Mamadou N'Diaye, 31, and Mamadou Barry, 23, were killed. The two had moved to the United States from Guinea roughly five years earlier. Their uncle called for justice.

EIGHT DEAD, at least 17 injured in Brooklyn BUILDING COLLAPSE

Around 250 emergency workers search rubble overnight — people may remain TRAPPED pic.twitter.com/81R6XQTtOa

— Michael Ashura (@MichaelAshura) November 12, 2026

In the adjoining property, Ciahola Lawrence woke to daylight streaming through a space where a shared wall had stood. Security footage showed a firefighter guiding her down stairs overlooking the debris. She recalled seeing neighbours brought out on stretchers as she was evacuated.

'We didn't deserve this,' Lawrence said, crying in her husband's arms.

Another neighbour, Zariah Coleman, said she had felt shaking during nearby construction. She appealed for help finding her frightened cat inside the damaged building.

Investigators Examine the Site's Regulatory History

New York City Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said the department was conducting an 'exhaustive investigation'. Officials also ordered inspections at more than 160 other locations associated with six entities linked to the neighbouring construction and demolition project.

Mamdani said investigators would pursue any evidence of criminality 'to the fullest extent of the law.' His remarks were a commitment to investigate, not a finding that a crime had occurred.

The inquiry includes the site's regulatory history. City inspectors issued a stop-work order on 20 March over inadequate overhead protection for neighbouring properties and pedestrians. They discovered on 23 April that demolition had resumed despite the restriction.

The order was lifted on 8 May after the cited deficiencies were corrected. Officials have not established whether those earlier breaches had any connection to the collapse.

A worker across the street reported seeing bricks fall shortly before the disaster. Nearby residents described cracks they believed were caused by construction vibrations. Those observations have not been confirmed as evidence of what brought the building down.

'We're looking at the entire history,' Tigani said, adding that investigators would examine any further information they needed.

Rescue operations concluded on Thursday following more than a day of searching.

Police identified the six other victims as Nicole Daniela Salvada Rodriguez, 9, Juan Daniel Salvada Guzman, 31, and Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, 10. The remaining three were Gabriel Siguencia, 22, Edgar Sapon, 26, and Jose Luis Caguana Cosquillo, 26.

excerpt: Marjorie Taylor Greene criticised Donald Trump's public response to a nationwide US air travel ground stop, while the president attributed the disruption to ageing FAA infrastructure.
headline: Greene Says Trump Touted 'Saving Hollywood' While Flyers Were 'Freaking Out' Over Possible US Attack
html_content:
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene criticised President Donald Trump on Friday over his public response to a nationwide ground stop that disrupted US air travel for more than four hours, claiming passengers feared an attack while he posted about Hollywood tax incentives.

The halt began around 4 pm Eastern time on Friday. Although restrictions initially extended until 11 pm, some departures resumed shortly after 8 pm. Greene questioned why Trump had not addressed Americans directly while travellers waited for information about the shutdown.

Why Greene Challenged Trump's Public Response

In a post on X, Greene accused Trump of failing to address the nation and skipping a press conference about the disruption. She contrasted his response with his public comments about repairing the reflecting pool and his posts about Hollywood.

'While everyone was freaking out thinking we are under some sort of attack, Trump didn't even bother to address the nation,' she wrote.

That description of passengers' fears was Greene's characterisation. Her criticism focused on the attention she believed Trump had devoted to other subjects while Americans were stranded at airports and aboard planes.

'For a man that constantly tells us how he is the only one capable of fixing things, while Americans were stranded at airports and in planes, he instead chose to post about saving Hollywood and the motion picture and television industry by giving them money in the form of tax incentives.'

Alongside Greene's Criticism, Trump Offers an Explanation

Trump discussed the outage by telephone with Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy. During an appearance with Laura Ingraham, Doocy relayed the president's assessment of what might have caused the disruption.

Doocy's remarks conveyed Trump's explanation to viewers. Greene's criticism, meanwhile, concerned what she described as his failure to address Americans directly or attend the press conference about the disruption.

'He says it does not seem like this is a cyberattack or AI or anything like that,' Doocy told Ingraham. 'I asked him a couple different ways, and he said it doesn't seem like that, and that that is the first thing that they always look for.'

Doocy also described Trump's comments about whether anyone had claimed responsibility and the possibility of further information from the president and his team.

'He said there's nobody taking credit which would be common if somebody did execute a huge cyber attack like this on critical infrastructure but that he would let us know and the team would let us know if that is something that happened,' he continued.

Infrastructure Concerns Accompany Greene's Questions

According to Doocy, Trump attributed the failure to ageing equipment relied upon by the Federal Aviation Administration. The explanation was the president's assessment, as relayed by the Fox News correspondent.

'He said instead this seems to be a situation where there's a bunch of old broken stuff in the infrastructure that the FAA relies on to keep planes in the sky. He said there's a bunch of—some of this is like 55-year-old equipment that needs to keep working, keep running, and that they have worked on it, they've talked to Congress about replacing, it just hasn't gotten replaced yet. So that is the first information that we have from the president.'

During an appearance with Laura Ingraham, Doocy relayed the president's assessment of what might have caused the disruption. Doocy's remarks conveyed Trump's explanation to viewers. Greene's criticism, meanwhile, concerned what she described as his failure to address Americans directly or attend the press conference about the disruption. 'He says it does not seem like this is a cyberattack or AI or anything like that,' Doocy told Ingraham. 'I asked him a couple different ways, and he said it doesn't seem like that, and that that is the first thing that they always look for.' Doocy also described Trump's comments about whether anyone had claimed responsibility and the possibility of further information from the president and his team. 'He said there's nobody taking credit which would be common if somebody did execute a huge cyber attack like this on critical infrastructure but that he would let us know and the team would let us know if that is something that happened,' he continued. Infrastructure Concerns Accompany Greene's Questions According to Doocy, Trump attributed the failure to ageing equipment relied upon by the Federal Aviation Administration. The explanation was the president's assessment, as relayed by the Fox News correspondent. 'He said instead this seems to be a situation where there's a bunch of old broken stuff in the infrastructure that the FAA relies on to keep planes in the sky. He said there's a bunch of—some of this is like 55-year-old equipment that needs to keep working, keep running, and that they have worked on it, they've talked to Congress about replacing, it just hasn't gotten replaced yet. So that is the first information that we have from the president.'

excerpt: A nationwide FAA ground stop disrupted thousands of US flights after air traffic control systems experienced instability, prompting calls for major investment and continuing delays.
headline: US Air Traffic Control Outage Explained: Sean Duffy $50B Request and NYC Traveller Delays
html_content:
Thousands of travellers faced disruption at New York's LaGuardia and JFK airports on Friday, 13 November, after a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop halted US departures. The order was lifted at 8.15pm Eastern, more than four hours after the disruption began, but delays continued as aircraft and crews remained out of position.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said instability began at 3.36pm, affecting radar and communications at air traffic control centres. He blamed overloaded switches and routers for producing inconsistent data. The FAA said the ground stop was imposed as a safety precaution.

Duffy Seeks $50 Billion for Air Traffic Overhaul

Duffy called for $50 billion (£38 billion) to modernise the ageing air traffic control system. Earlier on Friday, the administration had requested a broader $30.1 billion (£23 billion) aviation infrastructure package, including $10.1 billion (£7.64 billion) for air traffic control upgrades.

Congress had already approved $12.5 billion (£9.5 billion) over five years for modernisation and controller recruitment. Duffy said a complete overhaul was needed to prevent further outages.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said officials had found no evidence of a cyberattack, but the investigation was continuing.

FAA Says SMART System Was Not Involved

The disruption came three days after the FAA announced the expansion of its Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system to all 22 air route traffic control centres.

The cloud-based tool combines weather, flight-path, traffic and staffing information to help officials anticipate congestion. Duffy said SMART was separate from the legacy equipment involved. Air Space Intelligence, the company behind the system, also said the ground stop was not caused by SMART or its integration with the FAA and air traffic control. The rollout's timing does not establish a connection.

Thousands of Flights Disrupted Across US

About 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to depart after 4pm Eastern, according to Cirium figures reported by the Associated Press. At least 827 flights had been diverted by 7.05pm. Duffy said about 3,500 aircraft were airborne when the ground stop began, with fewer than 400 still in the air by his update.

The disruption was not confined to New York: the nationwide restriction affected departures across the United States, while the knock-on effects continued as airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crews.

At LaGuardia, a US Navy member identified as Hannah told the New York Post she had been travelling for 30 hours and was trying to get home to Florida after deployment when her flight was cancelled.

Airlines Offer Rebooking Options and Refunds

Airlines offered different waivers. Delta Air Lines allowed eligible passengers to rebook through 21 November; United Airlines waived fees and fare differences for qualifying same-city, same-cabin flights through 20 November. American Airlines covered eligible tickets bought by 12 November for travel on 13–14 November, with new travel through 17 November; changes had to be made by 14 November.

Southwest Airlines allowed qualifying passengers to rebook within five days of their original travel date. Frontier Airlines waived change fees for eligible travel from 13–15 November, while Alaska Airlines extended eligible travel through 17 November. JetBlue's rebooking window ran through 18 November. Eligibility varied.

These waivers are separate from federal refund rights. US Department of Transportation rules generally require refunds when flights are cancelled or significantly changed and passengers reject alternative travel or credits. The outage does not automatically entitle passengers to extra compensation.
