excerpt: Israeli authorities are examining claims Netanyahu's office tipped off police before the election-day arrests of three Ra'am activists; his office denies wrongdoing.
headline: Netanyahu's Office Accused of Orchestrating Arrests of Arab Activists Ahead of Israeli Election
html_content:
Israeli authorities are examining allegations that officials in Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office deliberately provided police with information that may have led to the arrests of three southern Bedouin men affiliated with the Arab political party Ra'am, according to an investigative report broadcast by Israeli broadcaster Channel 12.

The men were arrested on 27 October, election day, after Netanyahu's chief of staff, Ido Norden, reportedly contacted senior police officials about them the previous day.

Election Eve Tip Sparks Dawn Raids

Channel 12's investigative programme Uvda reported that Norden contacted the office of Police Commissioner Daniel Levy on 26 October, alleging that activists from the Arab Ra'am party were paying voters to increase turnout. He reportedly referred police to another source, identified as a former Prime Minister's Office employee, who was contacted by investigators before the arrests.

According to the outlet, 14 police officers searched the homes of three men in southern Israel without obtaining search warrants. The police issued a statement claiming they discovered envelopes containing tens of thousands of shekels during the raids.

However, officers reportedly found no evidence of vote-buying at Rahat resident Dr. Saef Abu Reash's home. Abu Reash spent six days in detention before the Beersheba Magistrate's Court ordered his release without conditions.

Two other men, Hussein al-Masoudin and Ibrahim al-Garibi, were also released without charges or restrictions. Both denied wrongdoing, maintaining that money discovered during the searches was intended for charity.

Abu Reash Denounces 'Political Persecution'

Footage obtained by the outlet captured Abu Reash's pregnant wife questioning officers during the raid. 'Are you taking him?' she asked. 'Why? I'm just asking because I'm about to give birth, and I'll be home alone.'

Following his release, Abu Reash described his arrest as 'pure political persecution', calling his detention 'one of the most humiliating moments of my life.' According to the outlet, Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara and the police's Investigations and Intelligence Division are examining whether the operation formed part of a pre-planned effort to undermine the election's legitimacy.

Shin Bet Chief Faces Separate Allegations

Separately, Channel 12 reported that Shin Bet chief David Zini sought permission on election day to wiretap five Arab lawmakers over suspicions of foreign interference in the vote. According to the outlet, the Attorney General's Office reportedly rejected the request. The Shin Bet chief met with Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main political challenger, two days after the election, according to the outlet.

During the meeting at Zini's office, the outlet reported that Zini presented a large binder containing intelligence material and claimed that 'since 2018, the Arabs have been stealing the election in Israel. All the Shin Bet heads have ignored it. I came and turned over this stone.'

Netanyahu's Office Rejects Claims

Netanyahu's office rejected the allegations, saying Norden had merely connected an individual who provided information about suspected wrongdoing with police. 'He fulfilled his duty, as expected of every law-abiding citizen,' the statement said. The office rejected suggestions of further involvement, warning that such allegations could constitute grounds for defamation proceedings.

Meanwhile, Yashar chair Gadi Eisenkot pledged to establish a commission of inquiry into what he described as 'the interference of the Prime Minister's Office on election day and the behaviour of the security agencies around it.'

Authorities are continuing to examine the allegations. No finding has established that Netanyahu's office deliberately planted false information or orchestrated the arrests.

excerpt: Jensen Huang quit NVIDIA on 11 November and backers now want him reinstated before results on 17 November; learn who decides and who else could lead the chipmaker.
headline: Jensen Huang Allies Push NVIDIA Comeback as Board Sounds Out Cambridge's Arm Boss Rene Haas: Report
html_content:
Jensen Huang's allies are lobbying NVIDIA's board to bring him back as chief executive, the Financial Times (FT) reported on Sunday 15 November. Huang resigned on 11 November. On Friday 13 November, the FT reported that the board had approached Rene Haas, who runs Cambridge-based chip designer Arm, as a possible successor.

NVIDIA's board, which hires and fires its boss, makes the choice. That choice matters well beyond the company, because NVIDIA is the main supplier of chips for artificial intelligence (AI). Its shares fell 4.3 per cent on the day it announced Huang's exit, and it reports quarterly results on Tuesday 17 November.

Why Huang Left and Who Wants Him Back

NVIDIA's filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the US markets regulator, shows the board accepted Huang's resignation on 11 November and named finance chief Colette Kress interim chief executive. The filing gives no reason. Days earlier, Huang told staff he had had an affair. Reports had linked him to Alice Huang, a businesswoman US officials reportedly suspect of spying for China. Beijing rejected that accusation. The two are not related.

Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management, two NVIDIA shareholders, wrote to the board on Friday 13 November. They urged it to keep 'all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.' An open letter with more than 150,000 signatories, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, makes the same demand. Gerstner posted the shareholders' letter on X, and the post appears below.

This letter was sent to the Nvidia Board today which we believe outlines the minimum acceptable standards the Board owes shareholders as it manages this difficult situation. Onward. 🫡 pic.twitter.com/fIsyXVQ5tR

— Brad Gerstner (@altcap) November 13, 2026

A Former NVIDIA Manager on the Shortlist

Haas once worked at NVIDIA. He spent seven years there, rising to lead its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013, and became Arm's chief executive in 2022. He took Arm public on the Nasdaq exchange in 2023. Arm designs processor architectures and licenses them to other chip companies. The FT said Haas is one of several candidates, with no guarantee of an offer or an acceptance. Arm declined to comment.

The board said in a statement that it was still choosing a firm to run the search and had not formally engaged any potential candidates. The statement added: 'Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature.' Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the US finance secretary, has said the next chief executive should come from outside NVIDIA. Until the board appoints someone, Kress runs NVIDIA while keeping her finance role, according to Nvidia's filing.

What Comes Next for NVIDIA

Kress presents her first results as interim chief executive after US markets close on Tuesday. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, told Agence France-Presse (AFP) the board had done what it needed: to 'rip off the band-aid and take NVIDIA into its next chapter without him.'

Spokespeople for NVIDIA and Jensen Huang declined to comment on the FT's comeback report, which cites unnamed sources. Any return would need approval from the directors who accepted his resignation. Their independent investigation into reports that he was a foreign intelligence target, launched on Sunday 8 November, has found nothing.

excerpt: TSA officers at Ontario International Airport found two live snakes, including a rattlesnake, concealed in a green pillowcase inside a passenger's checked bag during an October inspection.
headline: Passenger Packs Venomous Rattlesnake in a Pillowcase and Tells TSA He Has Flown With His 'Pets' Before
html_content:
TSA officers at a Southern California airport discovered two live snakes, including a rattlesnake, concealed inside a green pillowcase in a passenger's checked luggage.

According to an account published by the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) on 13 November, the discovery occurred during a routine inspection of checked baggage at Ontario International Airport in October.

Airport police took possession of the bag and brought it to the airline ticketing area, where the passenger removed the snakes and handed them to a family member who was not travelling. According to the Los Angeles TSA Coordination Center, the passenger said the reptiles were his pets and that he had previously travelled with them on another airline.

TSA temporarily paused screening operations in the immediate area while airport police and airline representatives were notified and officers coordinated a safe response.

Discovery in Checked Baggage

View this post on Instagram

TSA Officer Benjamin Andrade-Carillo noticed the pillowcase while inspecting a checked bag and realised the item was alive, according to the TSA. X-ray images initially showed what appeared to be a rope, but the item turned out to be two live snakes concealed in the pillowcase, TSA said.

'When I realized the item in my hand was alive, I told myself, "I need to escalate this immediately,"' Andrade-Carillo said in a TSA statement. Supervisory TSA Officer Suggey Flores examined the bag and confirmed something inside was moving.

'I felt it tense up and start moving,' Flores said. 'I have held snakes before, so I wasn't too spooked. I was more impressed because it's not something you see every day.'

Screening Paused as Police Respond

Screening operations in the immediate area were paused due to safety concerns while airport police and the passenger's airline were notified, TSA said. 'Safety was a concern because we didn't know what kind of snakes they were,' Flores said.

'TSA officers should not be handling live snakes for safety reasons,' TSA Manager Francisco 'Frank' Calderon said. 'Our priority was ensuring the safety of our officers and everyone in the area while making the proper notifications and coordinating a safe resolution.'

Airport police took the bag to the airline ticketing area, where the passenger removed the snakes and handed them to a relative who was not travelling, according to TSA. No injuries or bites were reported, and airport-wide screening operations were not disrupted, the agency said.

'I am very happy with the way our team handled the situation, stopped screening when they needed to and made the proper notifications,' Calderon said. 'No injuries or bites were reported, thank goodness.'

Passenger's Prior Travel Claim

The passenger told the Los Angeles TSA Coordination Center that the snakes were pets and that he had travelled with them on another airline, TSA said. The agency said travellers should contact their airline before arriving at the airport to understand requirements for travelling with pets, including reptiles.

After the snakes were removed, TSA rescreened the checked bag and cleared it, and the airline allowed the passenger to continue his trip without the snakes.

Andrade-Carillo said: 'In my two years of service, I had not found anything like this. In San Diego, I experienced a gentleman trying to bring live lobsters as a carry-on.'

excerpt: Australian agencies shared Centrelink, bank, and tax records with the ACIC fraud task force, which uses Palantir tools, prompting scrutiny of data oversight.
headline: Australian Government Agencies Shared Citizens' Bank, Welfare, and Tax Data With a System Using Palantir Software
html_content:
Australian government agencies have shared sensitive information, including Centrelink claims, bank account details, and taxpayer records, with a fraud task force whose intelligence operation uses Palantir software. The arrangement raises questions about how much control departments retain over personal information once it enters a wider government intelligence network.

The information is shared with the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC), which hosts the intelligence operation supporting the Fraud Fusion Taskforce. Palantir is one of several analytical tools used by the commission, but documents do not establish that every dataset supplied by partner agencies is entered into its software.

Centrelink and Financial Records Enter a Wider Network

Established in November 2022, the Fraud Fusion Taskforce is co-led by the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) and Services Australia. It targets suspected fraud involving government payments, including welfare, childcare, and disability support.

At least 10 federal agencies have shared information with the ACIC. They include the Department of Education, the Australian Taxation Office (ATO), the Australian Federal Police, and the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission.

Services Australia authorised the ACIC to obtain names, dates of birth, addresses, telephone numbers, identity documents, Centrelink claims and reviews, income and asset details, employer information, bank account details, and surveillance material.

ATO records show 758 disclosures between November 2022 and July 2026. Of these, 376 went to the NDIA and 42 to the ACIC. The documents do not detail the full scope of information disclosed, while tax file numbers cannot legally be shared.

Services Australia said disclosures were assessed individually. It recorded 47 in 2024-25, 21 in 2025-26 and two in the financial year to date.

Agencies Cannot Confirm How Their Data Is Used

The ACIC said Palantir forms part of a suite of analytical tools used in specific cases to help partner agencies disrupt serious organised crime networks. It did not clarify whether departments were notified when information they supplied was entered into the software.

Neither the ATO nor Centrelink knew whether their data had been used in Palantir, according to the released documents. The ATO said information was disclosed only where legally permitted under its agreements and relevant legislation.

Palantir maintains that it does not have access to data customers enter into its software. The company has defended its government work as software provision supporting efforts to tackle financial crime.

The evidence establishes information-sharing with the ACIC, not that Palantir independently collected citizens' records or received every dataset. The unresolved issue is whether agencies have sufficient visibility over how their disclosures are subsequently analysed.

Oversight Arrangements Face Further Scrutiny

A 2024 memorandum of understanding between task force agencies envisaged an ethics and human oversight framework, with risks assessed and recorded in a register.

Correspondence from September 2025 indicates the framework was considered too difficult to implement and was replaced by an ethics guide the following month.

Independent researcher Gabrielle Josling told the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) that the revised approach removed requirements for defined assessments and reviews. She also said a framework for evaluating the taskforce's performance had not been developed.

A privacy impact assessment noted that the ACIC is not subject to the Privacy Act. Its protocols state that it follows the Australian Privacy Principles wherever reasonably consistent with its statutory functions.

excerpt: Sydney Sweeney has denied undergoing plastic surgery, saying she fears needles and asking fans not to compare childhood photographs with professionally styled images of her as an adult.
headline: Sydney Sweeney Plastic Surgery Rumours: Star Calls Social Media 'Insane' for Comparing Her to Her Preteen Self
html_content:
Sydney Sweeney made headlines for shutting down allegations of plastic surgery she faced last year, speaking out in December 2025 as she revealed whether or not she had been under the knife. The White Lotus star often faces allegations of being cosmetically enhanced, but her clap-back offered more than just a simple denial.

Speaking to Allure alongside The Housemaid co-star Amanda Seyfried, Sydney said she was 'so scared of needles', also reminding fans that professional make-up and lighting can do wonders for one's appearance.

Sydney Sweeney Addresses Plastic Surgery Rumours and Asks To Stop Comparing Her to When She Was 12

'Let's debunk them all. I mean, I have never gotten work done,' Sydney said. 'I am so scared of needles, you have no idea.' When Amanda hinted at being a fan of getting a few tweaks, saying, 'But it's really effective once you get older, I'm telling you right now,' Sweeney didn't appear convinced.

'I am too scared of needles,' the SYRN founder responded. She has also spoken about having a size DD chest by the time she was in sixth grade.

Noting that people change as they grow older, Sydney Sweeney continued: 'You cannot compare a photo of me from when I was 12 to a photo of me at 26 with professional make-up and lighting! Of course I'm going to look different. Everybody on social media is insane.'

Sweeney usually delivers hyper-polished, extravagant social media photos, many of which come with a full hair and make-up team, plus top-of-the-range stylists and photographers. The actress is now signed to an array of brands, including Armani Beauty, Laneige Beauty and Miu Miu.

Sydney Sweeney Reveals What She Would Do if She Got Cosmetic Surgery

The Hollywood star may be saying 'no' to plastic surgery for the time being, but it didn't stop her from speaking in hypotheticals.

'If I did [have cosmetic surgery], you guys, my face would be even...' she told Amanda, also saying that she feels her eyes are 'uneven'.

'When I was younger, I had a wakeboarding accident right here, and I got 19 stitches. So I feel like it pulls like my eye just a little differently than the other,' Sydney explained. The A-lister joins the list of stars suspected of having cosmetic surgery. While stars including mogul Kylie Jenner and rapper Iggy Azalea have admitted to undergoing surgery, others are still in the rumour stage.

Sydney Sweeney Recently Went Under Fire for Sexualised Novig Ad

This is far from the first time that Sydney Sweeney has faced scrutiny for her looks. The actress starred in an ad for sports betting market Novig in September, in which she pretended to play sports while almost entirely naked.

The ad drew major criticism from onlookers and Olympic athletes, including swimmer Ariarne Titmus. 'I can't describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this,' the Olympic gold medallist shared on Instagram.

'Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity ...'

'How do we live in a world where monetising a woman's body and sexualising women's sport is still a thing?'

Meanwhile, Sweeney had previously lost more than 30 pounds after gaining weight and muscle for her 2025 boxing biopic Christy. As fans continue to comment on her appearance, it seems that the Hollywood star will continue to use her beauty as a conversation starter.

excerpt: An unofficial Bruce Springsteen fan group with more than 18,000 members is closing after political disagreements escalated into personal attacks, bullying and hostile rhetoric.
headline: Bruce Springsteen 'Spring-Nuts' Fan Club Shuts Down After Reaching 'Breaking Point' Over El-Sayed Backing
html_content:
Bruce Springsteen's unofficial Spring-Nuts fan group is closing after political arguments divided a Facebook community of more than 18,000 members.

Founders Julie and Howie Chaz said the singer's endorsement of Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed was the breaking point after years of mounting tensions.

The decision brings an end to an 11-year online gathering place devoted to Springsteen's music, friendships and charity events.

Members were originally expected to avoid politics and respect differing views. The founders said those rules became increasingly difficult to enforce as arguments turned personal.

In a farewell statement reported by the Asbury Park Press, the couple said disagreements had deteriorated into 'personal attacks, bullying, insults' and hateful rhetoric. Their account describes disputes within a private group, not independently established misconduct by particular members.

How Bruce Springsteen's Politics Tested the Spring-Nuts Community

Howie Chaz said Springsteen's increasingly outspoken criticism of President Donald Trump created a dilemma for administrators. They respected the musician's right to express political opinions but struggled to keep those views out of discussions.

After all, Chaz asked, how could members ignore statements from 'the very artist who brought us all together'?

The political message was unmistakable during Springsteen's 20-date Land of Hope and Dreams American Tour, which opened in Minneapolis on 31 March.

Official merchandise carried 'No Kings' artwork, while Springsteen described the concerts as a defence of American democracy and freedom. He also said fans were welcome regardless of their political beliefs.

Bruce Springsteen Endorsed Democrat El-Sayed

On 2 November, Springsteen endorsed Democrat El-Sayed in Michigan's US Senate contest. He called him 'a fighter for our American Constitution' and declared, 'That's why I'm in his corner 100%'. El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in the election the next day.

The Chazes called the endorsement 'deeply disappointing to us, given our concerns as proud Jews'. Howie cited El-Sayed's appearances with political streamer Hasan Piker and the candidate's comments following an attack on Temple Israel synagogue in Michigan in March.

Those objections need important context. El-Sayed explicitly condemned the synagogue attack, saying there was no justification for targeting innocent people. He later apologised for comments about the attack that critics considered insensitive. He also rejected Piker's past assertion that America deserved the 11 September attacks.

The founders said they did not believe Springsteen intended to make anybody feel unwelcome. Instead, they criticised fans they felt had appointed themselves judges of who belonged in the E Street community. Reddit discussions also questioned the closure and the proposed replacement group, although those comments do not represent all fans.

What Happens Next for Bruce Springsteen's Former Fan Group?

Closing the Facebook group will not end the activities organised around it. Spring-Nuts members previously supported WhyHunger and gathered at events celebrating Springsteen's music.

At the Stone Pony in Asbury Park, New Jersey, Springsteen virtually greeted the group's 2022 Seaside Serenade. He thanked those gathered for supporting WhyHunger, a charity that had become part of the community's identity.

Howie told the Asbury Park Press that the Seaside Serenades and Spring-Nuts podcasts would continue under different names. The podcasts have often featured members of the E Street Band. Organisers also intend to support the Asbury Park music scene and charities including TeachRock and Light of Day.

The proposed replacement community will focus more broadly on music while retaining Springsteen and the E Street Band as part of its activities.

excerpt: The Trump assassination attempt case against Cole Tomas Allen now includes a D.C. terrorism charge, with prosecutors detailing 100 rounds allegedly brought from California
headline: Prosecutors Say Man Brought 100 Rounds From California in Alleged Plot To Kill Trump at D.C. Dinner
html_content:
Federal prosecutors in Washington have added an armed terrorism charge against 31-year-old Cole Tomas Allen over an alleged attempt to assassinate President Donald Trump at the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner.

Filed on Thursday, 12 November 2026, and unsealed the following day in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, the three-page superseding indictment adds a count of committing an act of terrorism while armed under local criminal statutes alongside four existing federal charges.

Prosecutors allege that the Torrance, California resident transported approximately 100 rounds of ammunition, a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun, a .38-calibre semi-automatic pistol, and six knives and daggers across the country before rushing a Secret Service security checkpoint at the Washington Hilton on Saturday, 25 April 2026.

According to the Justice Department, Allen sought to influence executive branch policy through intimidation and coercion whilst intimidating a significant portion of the civilian population.

Trump Assassination Attempt: What the Terrorism Charge Alleges

Prosecutors allege Allen intended to influence the president's office and federal agencies through intimidation and coercion. They also accuse him of seeking to intimidate a significant portion of the civilian population. Those are allegations about his intended purpose, not conclusions reached by a court.

The filing retains four charges from the original indictment issued on 5 May. They concern the alleged assassination attempt, assault on a federal officer, interstate weapons transport and discharging a firearm during a violent crime.

The defence has also challenged the prosecution team. Allen sought to remove US Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro and then-Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche from the case. Both attended the dinner, and the defence raised concerns about potential conflicts of interest.

In a 22 June ruling, US District Judge Trevor McFadden rejected the motion. He found their attendance, subsequent statements and Pirro's friendship with Trump did not establish disqualifying conflicts.

Trump Assassination Attempt: Prosecutors Detail Around 100 Rounds

The indictment says Allen brought a Mossberg Maverick 88 12-gauge pump-action shotgun and a Rock Island Armoury 1911 .38-calibre semi-automatic pistol from California to Washington. Prosecutors place the journey between 21 and 25 April.

They allege he transported approximately 45 shotgun rounds and 55 handgun rounds, about 100 in total. The weapons and ammunition were allegedly intended for crimes including an assassination attempt and assault on a federal officer.

According to the Justice Department, Allen rushed through a Secret Service screening checkpoint shortly after 8.30pm. He ran towards stairs leading to the ballroom where Trump was attending the dinner, but never reached it.

Prosecutors say Allen fired his shotgun, striking a Secret Service officer once in the chest. The officer returned fire five times. Allen fell, was restrained and arrested, sustaining a minor knee injury but no gunshot wound.

Investigators reported recovering two knives, four daggers, sheaths, holsters, needle-nose pliers and wire cutters. The new charge references knives and other sharpened instruments alongside firearms.

An assault count identifies the officer as V.G. Another accuses Allen of using, carrying, brandishing and discharging a firearm during a crime of violence. Neither allegation amounts to a finding of guilt.

Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, condemned political violence after the original charges. The Justice Department says its National Security Section is prosecuting the case, while the FBI's Washington Field Office investigates.

Allen previously entered pleas of not guilty to the original four charges, and as of Friday, 13 November, had not yet entered a plea to the newly unsealed terrorism count.

Jury selection for the trial is scheduled to begin on 7 September 2027 after Judge McFadden granted defence attorneys additional time to prepare their case.

excerpt: England and Wales will automatically pardon women convicted of abortion offences linked to their own pregnancies and delete qualifying police and court records.
headline: UK Automatically Pardons Women Prosecuted for Abortions, Erases Criminal Records Without Requiring Applications
html_content:
Women previously convicted or cautioned for abortion offences relating to their own pregnancies are receiving automatic pardons under a new law taking effect in England and Wales. Police and court authorities must also remove relevant details of arrests and investigations, including cases that never resulted in prosecution.

The changes came into force on 16 November under section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026. No application is needed: authorities must search records they are aware of and delete qualifying information where reasonably practicable. The reform is intended to prevent historical cases from affecting employment checks and other aspects of women's lives.

Who Qualifies for a Pardon and Record Deletion

The law distinguishes between a pardon and the removal of records. Women, living or deceased, who were convicted, or cautioned for a qualifying abortion offence while acting in relation to their own pregnancy are automatically pardoned.

Separate record-deletion rules cover convictions, cautions, arrests, and investigations. A woman investigated but never charged may therefore have relevant details removed, although she is not receiving a formal pardon. The provisions cover offences under sections 58 and 59 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 and section 1 of the Infant Life (Preservation) Act 1929.

The rules do not apply to people prosecuted for an abortion offence relating to another woman's pregnancy. They also cover trans men who were acting in relation to their own pregnancies.

What Happens to Police and Court Records

The Ministry of Justice says police and court officials must delete relevant details they identify through reasonable searches, where they are aware of the information and removal is reasonably practicable. Court records cannot be completely erased because they are public records. Instead, relevant entries must be annotated and treated as if they had been deleted.

Authorities aim to update identified records within one month of the law taking effect, although older paper files may take longer. The department says affected people do not need to contact officials and will not be proactively notified, to avoid revealing a sensitive past event to others.

Once qualifying details are deleted, they should not appear in criminal record checks, including enhanced Disclosure and Barring Service checks. People who want confirmation can contact the Ministry of Justice's dedicated team.

The Wider Abortion Law Remains in Place

The pardons follow section 241 of the Act, which came into force at Royal Assent on 29 April 2026. It removed criminal liability for a woman acting in relation to her own pregnancy.

However, the change did not abolish the wider regulation of abortion services. The Abortion Act 1967 continues to govern access in England and Wales, including the general 24-week limit and requirements for authorised medical practitioners. Later abortions remain permitted in specified circumstances.

Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who campaigned for the reform, said she expected more than 100 women to benefit, including through posthumous pardons. The Ministry of Justice has not confirmed the total number.

The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists welcomed the change. Its president, Dr Alison Wright, said the pardons recognised the injustice of historical convictions. The British Pregnancy Advisory Service also described the reform as a meaningful step towards justice, while acknowledging that legal recognition cannot undo the distress women experienced.

excerpt: Donald Trump used Truth Social charts to defend Republican midterm losses, but the comparisons omit important electoral context as Democrats prepare to control Congress.
headline: Donald Trump Floods Truth Social With Self-Praise and Past Election Comparisons as His Approval Rating Slumps
html_content:
President Donald Trump shared two charts on Truth Social on Sunday, 15 November, comparing Republican midterm election losses with those under previous US presidents.

The findings came after Democrats won control of both chambers in the 3 November elections, leaving Trump's approval one point above its career low.

Democrats won enough seats to take control of the House of Representatives and Senate when the new Congress begins on 3 January 2027.

The result followed a campaign in which Trump backed Republican candidates, although some races remained undecided when he posted the charts.

Trump's Charts Leave Out Important Context

The first graphic listed 63 House seats lost under Barack Obama, 54 under Bill Clinton and 48 under Trump. A second graphic compared Senate losses, showing nine under Obama and eight each under Ronald Reagan, Clinton and Trump.

The figures placed Republican losses alongside setbacks suffered by earlier administrations. However, the graphics omitted which elections were being compared, making it difficult to assess whether they provided a like-for-like account of the results.

Obama's 63 House-seat losses occurred in 2010, but the nine Senate seats attributed to his administration were lost in 2014. Clinton's figures came from the 1994 midterms, while Reagan's eight Senate-seat losses occurred in 1986.

The charts also left out how many seats the parties held before each election. Democrats entered the 1994 and 2010 midterms with larger House majorities than Republicans held before the 2026 vote, an important distinction when comparing the scale of losses.

Trump's figures of 48 House seats and eight Senate seats came from his graphics, not certified totals. Several races were still unresolved on 15 November, and seat-change calculations can shift as results are confirmed.

Whatever the final margins, Democrats' congressional victories will change the political balance in Washington. From January, the party will have greater power to set committee priorities, conduct oversight hearings and challenge the administration's legislative plans.

Trump had already defended his political standing on election night. In a 3 November Truth Social post attacking Fox News polling, he declared, 'My numbers are better than they have ever been.'

Hours later, he wrote, 'I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!' The statement describes a hypothetical outcome, rather than an election result that can be independently tested.

Poll Shows Approval Near Career Low

An Ipsos survey conducted from 6 to 9 November found that 32 per cent of American adults approved of Trump's job performance, while 65 per cent disapproved.

The survey questioned 1,705 adults and had a margin of error of 2.4 percentage points. His overall approval was unchanged from two previous Reuters/Ipsos polls, remaining one point above the 31 per cent career low recorded in October.

Economic concerns produced weak figures. Just 21 per cent approved of Trump's handling of living costs and 72 per cent disapproved. His management of the economy received 25 per cent approval, while inflation received 19 per cent.

Immigration fared comparatively better at 38 per cent approval, although 55 per cent disapproved. His handling of Iran received 26 per cent approval.

On 8 November, Trump promised his administration would return 'BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE'. His latest comparisons offer another public defence of the election outcome, while the polling indicates that dissatisfaction with his performance remains widespread.

excerpt: Alabama's fetal-protection laws face scrutiny as pregnant women in Houston County face drug charges, while ex-officer Robert Maddox receives probation.
headline: Alabama Jailed Pregnant Women for Drug Use but Gave Cop Probation After He Was Accused of Causing His Wife's Miscarriage
html_content:
Pregnant women in Alabama's Houston County have faced felony prosecutions after drug tests during childbirth, while a former police officer accused of assaulting his pregnant wife received probation after pleading guilty to domestic violence. The contrast raises questions about how the state's fetal-protection laws are enforced.

Former Headland police officer Robert Maddox Jr was arrested in February 2022 after investigators examined his wife Brittany's miscarriage and allegations of assault. He was initially charged with murder, but a grand jury declined to indict him on that charge and returned a manslaughter indictment.

In May 2026, the manslaughter charge was dismissed under a plea agreement. Maddox pleaded guilty to domestic violence and received five years' probation, a fine of about $3,000 (£2,270.10) and an order to attend anger management classes. Released on bond about five weeks after his arrest, he did not return to jail or prison.

How Alabama's Chemical Endangerment Law Is Used

Alabama enacted its chemical endangerment law in 2006 to protect children from controlled substances, including exposure in homes where methamphetamine was produced. Prosecutors later applied it to pregnancies. In 2013, the Alabama Supreme Court ruled in Ex parte Ankrom that 'child' under the law included an unborn child.

The ruling allowed prosecutors to charge women over prenatal drug exposure, including when babies were born healthy. ProPublica identified more than 40 pregnant women arrested in Houston County since 2009 after testing positive for drugs. The county had one of the state's highest rates of chemical endangerment prosecutions, although court data did not identify pregnancy-related cases.

Women Faced Jail After Treatment and Probation Problems

Courtney Haney's case illustrates how prosecution can continue beyond childbirth. Her daughter was born healthy, but Haney was later arrested and offered a plea deal involving a lesser charge and just over a year of probation. She did not complete court-ordered drug treatment and repeatedly failed to report to her probation officer. Those violations resulted in four months in jail.

District Attorney Russ Goodman said his office sought treatment-based sentences, although some defendants were imprisoned after breaching probation or failing to complete treatment. He said straight prison sentences were rare during his tenure unless other circumstances, such as prior criminal history, applied.

Houston County does not offer a drug court programme, which can provide treatment instead of conventional prosecution and imprisonment. A former nurse arrested after testing positive for drugs while in labour in 2018 spent nearly 10 months in prison.

Manslaughter Case Ended Without a Conviction

Goodman said the evidence against Maddox was inconclusive and questioned the earlier decision to seek an indictment. He said prosecutors could not establish a causal link between the alleged assault and the miscarriage, and no expert could provide one.

Maddox declined an interview but said in an email: 'I was made out to be someone I wasn't.' Brittany Maddox alleged that her husband struck and choked her, and provided investigators with photographs and messages. She said she was devastated when the manslaughter charge was dropped after years of preparing for trial.

The cases involved different offences and evidential questions. Their contrasting outcomes have intensified scrutiny of Alabama's fetal-personhood approach: women can face felony charges over prenatal drug exposure, while proving that violence caused a pregnancy loss can present a substantial evidential hurdle.

excerpt: A former model told the BBC that Jeffrey Epstein used promises of a US visa, modelling introductions and immigration dependence to draw her into years of alleged abuse.
headline: Former Model Says Epstein Used Promises of US Visas and Agency Introductions To Keep Women Under Control
html_content:
Speaking in a BBC Eye documentary released on 10 November 2026, 'Anka' described how a career opportunity in Paris became a system of control.

The investigation, The Model Trap: Exposing Jeffrey Epstein's Network, examines fashion industry links that continued after Epstein pleaded guilty in 2008 to felony solicitation of prostitution and procuring a minor for prostitution.

Epstein's Visa Promise Left Model Dependent on His Network

Anka was in her early twenties and already represented by a Paris agency when scout Daniel Siad suggested she meet a wealthy American with influential fashion contacts. Siad arranged an interview at Epstein's apartment on Avenue Foch, she told the BBC.

Epstein offered to help secure her US visa and meetings with leading agencies. Anka believed the introductions could advance her career. 'I was just one of many young women who he played,' she recalled.

Epstein later arranged for her to travel to America, where she signed with MC2 Miami. But she said the agency produced no modelling jobs. Instead, Epstein offered her an assistant role, which she alleged exposed her to repeated sexual abuse.

Anka said MC2 sponsored her modelling visa, although she worked for Epstein rather than the agency. She alleged that visa renewals depended on his discussions with agency figures, making her immigration status another source of uncertainty.

'There was no escape for a woman like myself,' she said, describing dependence on Epstein for housing, finances and immigration arrangements.

She said that, at one stage, she was among seven assistants pressured to introduce more young women. She alleged that Epstein intensified physical and emotional abuse when they failed to recruit anyone.

Survivor lawyer Sigrid McCawley said assistants were themselves being abused and faced threats to their livelihoods.

Siad died in France in July 2026 while under investigation over trafficking allegations. He had denied wrongdoing and said his dealings with Epstein were professional.

Modelling Agency Ties Raise Questions About Accountability

Jeff Fuller previously denied knowing that Roza Gilles had visited Epstein's Florida home or experienced abuse. Faith Kates' lawyers said Epstein misled her and denied that she recommended plastic surgery to a model.

The BBC reported that Epstein provided $1 million (approximately €908,790 and £758,000) to MC2 Model Management in 2005. The agency was co-founded by French agent Jean-Luc Brunel, and records showed models continued communicating with Epstein after his conviction.

Former Uzbek model Roza Gilles said MC2 sent her to two photoshoots at Epstein's Florida home when she was 18. She alleged he later employed and sexually abused her. An expense record examined by the BBC suggested US agency president Jeff Fuller booked her return flight. Fuller previously denied knowing she visited Epstein's home or experienced abuse.

Another model, 'Simona', alleged Epstein raped her more than 200 times. She described meeting Faith Kates, who left her senior executive role at Next Management in December 2025 but remained listed as a director. Kates' lawyers said Epstein misled her and denied she recommended plastic surgery to a model.

New York senator Zellnor Myrie's bill S9960B, targeting those who benefit from trafficking ventures, passed the state Senate on 2 June 2026 but remained before the Assembly. It has not become law.

Epstein died in federal custody in August 2019 while awaiting trial on sex-trafficking charges.

excerpt: Harvard's Avi Loeb suggests 1998 KY26 could be lost Soviet probe Phobos 1, but orbital similarities and physical clues do not prove its identity
headline: Harvard's Avi Loeb Says 'Dark Comet' 1998 KY26 Could Be Lost Soviet Phobos 1 Probe, but Proof Is Still Lacking
html_content:
Avi Loeb, Harvard's Frank B. Baird Jr. Professor of Science, has suggested that near-Earth object 1998 KY26 could be the lost Soviet spacecraft Phobos 1.

His hypothesis, outlined in a June 2026 arXiv preprint, cited similarities in the objects' calculated orbits, size and brightness. However, the evidence does not establish that they are connected.

Loeb discussed 1998 KY26 during an interview with FOX Weather meteorologists Melanie Black and Michael Estime.

He described it as a 'dark comet', a term for small Solar System bodies showing non-gravitational acceleration without a visible coma or tail.

Why Avi Loeb Thinks 1998 KY26 Could Be Phobos 1

Phobos 1 launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome on 7 July 1988. NASA records show that it shut down on 2 September after receiving a faulty command sequence from Earth.

In their preprint, Loeb and co-authors Adam Hibberd, Adam Crowl and Carlos Gómez de Olea Ballester compare the spacecraft's calculated orbit with that of 1998 KY26. They describe similarities but acknowledge differences in orbital positions and elements. The paper does not claim the objects followed an identical path.

The researchers model two hypothetical changes in Phobos 1's velocity, with a combined change of about 1.9 kilometres per second. One is placed shortly after the spacecraft was lost in 1988, and the other in May 1996, before 1998 KY26 was discovered. These are elements of a mathematical reconstruction, not documented manoeuvres.

A 2025 study in Nature Communications estimated 1998 KY26's diameter at 11 ± 2 metres, or about 36 feet. It measured a geometric albedo of 0.52 ± 0.08, indicating unusually high brightness. That figure does not mean the asteroid reflects 52 per cent of all sunlight striking it.

What Avi Loeb Says About 1998 KY26 as a Dark Comet

Researchers introduced the dark-comet category in 2023 for small Solar System objects showing unexplained acceleration without detected cometary activity.

The category includes 1998 KY26. Faint outgassing remains one possible explanation, even when telescopes detect no gas or dust.

Loeb offered his explanation during the interview. 'Well, comet experts argue that it's a dark comet because there is a non-gravitational force acting on it, something that is not gravity that is pushing it, and they don't see any gas or dust coming off it. So they say it's a comet, but we can't see any signs of a comet, so it's a dark comet,' he said.

Loeb has also proposed that sunlight pressure acting on a spacecraft could explain the object's acceleration.

He connected the discussion to interstellar object 1I/'Oumuamua, discovered in 2017. 'The reason the dark comet concept was invented is another visit by an object from outside the solar system, called Oumuamua, that was discovered in 2017 and again showed non-gravitational acceleration without any outgassing, no gas or dust around it,' Loeb said.

Researchers formalised the category in 2023, but NASA says 'Oumuamua itself is not classified as a dark comet.

A 2025 study measured 1998 KY26's rotation period at 5.3516 ± 0.0001 minutes. The European Space Agency lists its orbital period as 497.6 days and its next close approach to Earth as 24 May 2039, at about 10.1 million miles. ESA does not list the asteroid as a risk.

Japan's Hayabusa2 spacecraft, operated by JAXA, is scheduled to rendezvous with 1998 KY26 in 2031 as part of its extended mission. The encounter is intended to study the object, not test Loeb's Phobos 1 hypothesis.

Loeb has separately suggested that 'Oumuamua could have an artificial origin. That remains speculative and provides no independent evidence that 1998 KY26 is the missing Phobos 1 probe.

excerpt: A nationwide FAA ground stop delayed and cancelled thousands of US flights. Trump blamed Biden-era spending as Sean Duffy sought $50 billion for upgrades.
headline: Trump Points Finger at Biden Administration After Nationwide FAA Ground Stop Sparks Travel Chaos
html_content:
US President Donald Trump has accused the Biden administration of worsening America's ageing air traffic control system after a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop disrupted flights on Friday. In his first public remarks on Sunday, Trump accused his predecessor's administration of mismanaging aviation infrastructure spending while urging Congress to release additional funding for upgrades.

Trump Calls Biden-Era FAA Spending a 'Disaster', Demands Fresh Funding

'The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster,' Trump wrote on Truth Social. 'Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began.' The president also said his administration had 'the knowledge and plan for the Flight Control Systems,' but stressed that 'we need Congress to give the money, FAST!'

'Our FAA is doing a great job and is ready to go,' the president added. The Trump administration has also pointed to problems involving the replacement of ageing copper communication lines.

CNBC reported that Congress approved $12.5 billion for the FAA last year through a major tax and spending package. However, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has warned that modernising the country's ageing aviation infrastructure would require further investment.

Four-Hour Shutdown Throws Flights Into Chaos

Friday's nationwide ground stop lasted more than four hours, halting nearly all departing flights and disrupting air travel across the United States. Thousands of flights were delayed or cancelled, stranding passengers and leaving airlines scrambling to restore normal operations.

The FAA said its equipment became unstable after unusually high volumes of data overwhelmed its network. The agency identified contractor work at one site as a possible contributing factor but stressed that the root cause remains under investigation. Nationwide ground stops are exceptionally rare, with major previous disruptions occurring after the 11 September attacks and during an FAA outage in January 2023.

Duffy Rejects Resignation Calls Amid Backlash

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said on Saturday that air travel was expected to return to normal by Sunday evening, following widespread disruption that left millions of passengers facing delays and cancellations.

However, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned on Sunday that disruptions could persist as airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crews following Friday's nationwide ground stop. Speaking to ABC News, Duffy said flight operations were expected to return fully to normal by Monday. 'We had airplanes and crews out of position because of Friday, so it takes a little bit of time to do that,' he explained.

Duffy also rejected calls to resign over the widespread travel disruption and defended his department's handling of the crisis. He pointed to longstanding problems with ageing aviation infrastructure, including radar equipment dating back to the 1960s. 'So when we do work and things go wrong, of course I'm the secretary. But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me,' he told CNN.

As per ABC News, Duffy has called for $50 billion to modernise the country's ageing air traffic control system, urging Congress to 'meet this moment' by approving the necessary funding. The disruption has renewed debate over federal aviation spending and the urgency of replacing ageing technology, with investigators still working to determine precisely what caused the nationwide failure.

excerpt: Cynthia Diekema, 61, was killed by an alligator in Florida after the canoe she shared with her husband struck the animal in Tiger Creek.
headline: 'About To Go Right Over Top of One': Chilling Final Words of Grandmother Killed by Alligator Resurface
html_content:
Eighteen months after 61-year-old Michigan grandmother Cynthia Diekema was killed by an 11-foot, 4-inch alligator during a holiday in central Florida, the harrowing police record of her final moments continues to serve as a stark safety warning as autumn tourism peaks across the state's waterways.

According to her husband David's formal police statement and investigative details attributed to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, the fatal encounter unfolded on 6 May 2025 after the couple launched an 11-foot plastic canoe from Lake Kissimmee State Park.

Moments before their hull struck the reptile resting motionless on the bed of Tiger Creek in Polk County, Cynthia warned her husband that they were about to pass directly over an alligator. Cynthia had said they were 'about to go right over top of one.'

Startled by the impact around 4pm, the massive predator thrashed violently and capsized the vessel, throwing both paddlers into the shallow water before clamping onto Cynthia's torso and executing a fatal death roll despite David's desperate struggle to pry her free.

With cooler November 2026 weather drawing thousands of seasonal visitors back to Florida's scenic creeks and marshes, wildlife educators often cite the documented Tiger Creek tragedy to underscore the hidden risks beneath shallow subtropical waters.

Alligator Encounter Overturns Canoe

In his statement to police, David described standing up in the water and seeing his wife's torso in the alligator's mouth. He tried to pull her free for several minutes but could not release her from its grip.

During the struggle, Cynthia initially appeared alert, David stated. He then noticed a 'puzzled look on her face' as she lost the ability to speak.

The alligator struck David with its tail, knocking him down. It briefly released Cynthia before biting her again on the shoulder.

After being knocked down by the tail strike, David managed to stand back up in the water and tried once more to save his wife. The animal then performed a 'death roll' and swam away with her, according to his statement.

The manoeuvre involves an alligator twisting its entire body while biting its prey, a movement that can disable, kill and dismember it.

Search Follows Fatal Alligator Attack

David had lost his phone when the canoe overturned, leaving him unable to call 911. To seek assistance, he scooped water out of the canoe and paddled north towards Lake Kissimmee, where an airboater rescued him.

Wildlife officers searched the area after the attack and located Cynthia's body about 20 minutes later. Paramedics pronounced her dead at the scene.

A medical examiner determined that she died from blunt force injuries caused by the alligator. Those injuries included the loss of her right arm below the shoulder, and her death was ruled an accident.

Trappers captured and put down the alligator at around 7:30pm that day. Officers returned to the creek the following day to check for other dangerous alligators and removed another animal from the area.

Cynthia was from Paw Paw, Michigan, and is survived by David, her two children and two grandchildren. Her obituary described her love for her family and the experiences they shared.

'She radiated her inner and outer beauty in all she did and had unconditional love for everyone,' the obituary stated. 'She cherished her family and every moment and adventure they spent together.'

Eighteen months after the incident, the documented sequence of events remains a vital reminder for paddlers navigating narrow Florida creeks to maintain safe distances from wildlife and stay alert to submerged hazards.

excerpt: Elon Musk rated SNL's latest impersonation of him five out of 10 and criticised the show's political comedy after a sketch mocked technology executives.
headline: 'They Need To Try Harder': Elon Musk Gives His SNL Impersonation a Lukewarm Rating After Tech CEO Skit
html_content:
Elon Musk gave Saturday Night Live's latest impersonation of him just five out of 10, then told the programme to 'try harder' after its 14 November sketch made the Tesla and SpaceX boss part of a joke about technology executives.

The opening sketch featured John Mulaney as a CIA official teaching technology executives how to recognise attempts to obtain confidential information. Jeremy Culhane portrayed Musk, alongside fictional versions of Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman and Dario Amodei.

Elon Musk Rates SNL Impersonation Five Out of 10

Musk delivered his verdict beneath an X post comparing the comedians' impressions with their real-life counterparts.

'I'd give them maybe 5/10 for me,' he wrote, before adding: 'They need to try harder.'

His criticism went beyond the impersonation. After SNL promoted the sketch on X, Musk replied with a Venn diagram suggesting that the programme and humour had little in common, adding 'Lol'.

He also shared footage from his 2021 SNL hosting appearance, captioning it 'fwiw', meaning 'for what it's worth'.

fwiwhttps://t.co/d4vZZ4usfx

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 16, 2026

In another exchange, an X user criticised the programme's political comedy, arguing that personal insults were not funny. Musk agreed, replying: 'Exactly'.

The sketch had received nearly four million YouTube views when The Daily Beast reported on Musk's reactions on Monday, 16 November. Some viewers praised the opening sequence, while others focused on a recurring joke involving a spray bottle.

How SNL's Tech CEO Sketch Made Elon Musk the Punchline

The sketch followed an announcement on 12 November that Jensen Huang had resigned as chief executive of NVIDIA. The company appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while it searched for a permanent replacement.

Huang's reported departure provided the backdrop for the fictional CIA briefing, which centred on technology executives potentially revealing sensitive information through romantic relationships. Mulaney's character warned them that strangers expressing romantic interest might actually be seeking industry secrets.

Culhane's Musk repeatedly interrupted the briefing with jokes, prompting the fictional CIA official to spray him with water.

Former cast member Bowen Yang made a surprise appearance as Huang, wearing the technology executive's signature leather jacket. Culhane's Musk suggested their jackets gave them something in common and that they could form a biker gang riding Harley-Davidsons.

Yang's character sprayed him again and shouted: 'Bad Elon!'

The exchange prompted reactions on YouTube. One commenter suggested interviewers should keep a spray bottle beside them when speaking to Musk, while another called for merchandise featuring the joke.

A Second Musk Impression Earlier in November

The 14 November sketch followed Culhane's earlier impersonation of Musk during SNL's Weekend Update segment on 7 November.

In that appearance, Culhane's fictional Musk asked a scripted version of his AI chatbot Grok to deliver an insulting assessment of its creator. The fictional chatbot's responses included jokes about Musk's South African background and family relationships.

The two November appearances used different comic devices: in Weekend Update, the fictional Grok supplied remarks about its creator; in the later opening sketch, Culhane's Musk took part in a group briefing.

Musk hosted Saturday Night Live in May 2021. His latest criticism was therefore directed at a programme on which he had previously appeared as a guest host.

excerpt: Russell Brand reportedly objected after prison staff confiscated his hair-loss medication at HMP Wandsworth, while he also requested specialist shampoo, according to an unverified report.
headline: Russell Brand 'Blowing Up' Over Hair-Loss Pills and Shampoo After Prison Refuses Request, Source Claims
html_content:
Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months for rape and sexual assault before reportedly complaining that prison staff had confiscated his hair-loss tablets and requesting specialist shampoo, according to a report published on Sunday, 15 November. The allegations emerged days after his conviction.

Brand, 51, was sentenced at Southwark Crown Court on 9 November. A jury convicted him on 5 November of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others in offences committed between 2004 and 2009.

Russell Brand Hair-Loss Pills Reportedly Confiscated at Wandsworth

An unnamed source told The Sun that Brand wanted to continue taking Propecia, a prescription treatment for male pattern baldness. He also reportedly sought permission to use Alpecin caffeine shampoo, which is marketed as a hair-loss product.

'He was kicking off because he's worried he's going to lose his hair,' the source alleged. 'He takes Propecia pills for his hair, but he had them confiscated inside.'

The insider claimed the tablets were considered non-essential because they were being used for cosmetic reasons. Brand reportedly asked for specialist shampoo, too, but the report did not establish whether prison officials formally refused the request.

The claims are based on an anonymous source and have not been independently verified. The Ministry of Justice declined to comment when approached by The Sun. IBTimes UK said it could not independently verify the allegations.

Prisoners undergo healthcare assessments when they enter custody, including reviews of existing prescriptions. Medication must be authorised by prison healthcare professionals; prisoners cannot simply bring it directly into their cells.

According to the NHS, Propecia contains finasteride, a medication used to treat male pattern baldness. When prescribed for hair loss, finasteride is available only on private prescription.

The Sun reported that Propecia can cost up to £60 a month, while Alpecin shampoo sells for about £6.49 a bottle. The newspaper also noted that Brand was photographed carrying Propecia tablets in 2010. The report did not say whether he had a current prescription or provide details of the medication's assessment by prison healthcare staff.

Russell Brand Reportedly Transferred to HMP Littlehey

Brand was reportedly transferred to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire on Friday, 13 November. The Category C prison houses men convicted of sexual offences, although prison authorities have not independently confirmed the move.

According to The Sun, Brand had been held separately at Wandsworth over concerns for his safety. He was reportedly assessed for HMP Wakefield before prison officials selected Littlehey. The report did not provide further details about the assessment or explain how the decision was reached.

It remains unclear whether Brand regained access to his medication following the reported transfer. There is also no official confirmation about the outcome of his shampoo request.

The reported transfer drew criticism from retired prison governor Vanessa Frake, who told The Sun she was 'absolutely flabbergasted' by the decision. She argued that a Category B prison might have been more appropriate given Brand's lengthy sentence.

Mr Justice Joel Bennathan said Brand would serve two-thirds of his prison sentence, equivalent to seven years, before being released on licence. He could be recalled to custody if he breaches its conditions.

The Metropolitan Police confirmed that Brand will remain on the sex offenders' register for life.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy addressed the outcome following sentencing. 'Today's sentence marks a significant milestone in our investigation and means Russell Brand has been held accountable for his crimes.'

excerpt: Ray Dalio warns US debt and rising interest costs could trigger a financial crisis as the federal deficit grows, while turning to gold as a portfolio diversifier.
headline: 'It's Like Plaque': Ray Dalio Warns of a US Economic 'Heart Attack' While Touting Gold as an 'Effective Diversifier'
html_content:
Billionaire investor Ray Dalio has warned that America's mounting federal debt and persistent budget deficits are putting the US economy at risk of a financial crisis, comparing years of excessive borrowing to plaque accumulating in arteries. He believes the country could face an economic 'heart attack' unless policymakers rein in government spending and bring the budget deficit under control.

'We are very exposed to a heart attack,' Dalio said in a recent interview with Money Rehab. The Bridgewater Associates founder argued that growing debt-servicing costs are gradually squeezing the resources available for other economic priorities, leaving the country increasingly vulnerable.

'It's like plaque,' he said, explaining how rising interest payments consume money that could otherwise support government services, investment, and economic growth. Dalio believes the US needs to reduce its budget deficit to 3% of gross domestic product, compared with approximately 6.5% under current conditions.

Dalio's Views Coincide With Shocking Official Figures

According to the Government Accountability Office's (GAO) latest report, total federal debt reached $40.2 trillion in fiscal 2026, which is a 105% increase from $19.6 trillion a decade earlier.

Federal debt increased by $2.5 trillion during fiscal 2026 alone, including a $2.1 trillion increase in debt held by the public. The government recorded a $2 trillion budget deficit, up from approximately $1.8 trillion in fiscal 2025, as spending continued to exceed tax revenues.

Growing debt levels are also making government borrowing increasingly expensive. Interest costs on publicly held federal debt nearly tripled over five fiscal years, rising from approximately $392 billion in 2021 to $1.1 trillion in 2026.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) painted a similarly concerning picture in its 9th November Monthly Budget Review. The federal deficit reached 6.2% of GDP in fiscal 2026, considerably above the 50-year average of 3.8%. The agency's February 2026 outlook projected that debt held by the public would climb to 120% of GDP by 2036, while annual net interest costs would more than double from $1 trillion in 2026 to $2.1 trillion in 2036.

Why Dalio Is Turning to Gold

Dalio warned that the government has limited options if investors become increasingly reluctant to finance America's borrowing.

'Either interest rates have to go up and constrict the demand...or the Federal Reserve has to come in and print money and buy all this debt, which is inflationary,' he said.

Both scenarios could undermine Americans' purchasing power, either through higher borrowing costs across the economy or inflation eroding the value of savings. 'You don't increase wealth by printing money. You just lessen the value of money,' Dalio added.

Against this backdrop, he sees gold as an important portfolio diversifier, particularly during periods of excessive borrowing, currency uncertainty, and financial instability.

'When there's too much debt, and there are big problems, gold is an effective diversifier,' he said, adding that investors should consider holding the precious metal as part of a diversified portfolio.

Dalio suggested that investors with traditional portfolios could consider allocating approximately 10% to 15% to gold to help diversify against adverse economic conditions.

Remember, investments are subject to market risks, and past performance does not guarantee future returns.

excerpt: Royal expert Ingrid Seward said Catherine would not be troubled by publicity tensions surrounding Prince Harry's Ukraine visit as she and Prince William began their India tour.
headline: Kate Middleton Not 'Interested in Ridiculous Games' Over Prince Harry's Ukraine Visit, Royal Expert Says
html_content:
Prince Harry's Ukraine visit ended before Prince William and Catherine arrived in India for their first joint official overseas tour in four years.

Royal expert Ingrid Seward said Catherine was unlikely to be troubled by the timing as the Princess of Wales arrived in Mumbai with William on Monday, 16 November. The couple are in India for the sixth Earthshot Prize.

Primce William and Catherine last undertook an official overseas tour together in Boston in December 2022. Catherine later missed three Earthshot Prize ceremonies. Her absence in 2023 came before the public disclosure of her cancer diagnosis in 2024.

The Waleses are visiting India for the awards ceremony, which takes place on Tuesday, 17 November. William founded the environmental initiative in 2020.

Prince Harry's Ukraine Visit Raises Questions Over Royal Schedule

Prince Harry spent Saturday and Sunday, 14 and 15 November, in Lviv, Ukraine, meeting wounded veterans and visiting the Superhumans Center rehabilitation clinic. He also addressed a conference on war-related injuries and watched wheelchair rugby players prepare for the 2027 Invictus Games in Birmingham.

Reuters reported that the trip was Harry's fourth visit to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, and his second visit to the country this year.

The timing drew attention because Harry's engagements took place immediately before William and Catherine arrived in Mumbai. Royal commentator Robert Jobson told The Sun that the visits were 'competing for the same headlines'.

Jobson suggested that Harry and Meghan Markle pursued their own agenda without necessarily considering the Waleses' activities. Sources close to Harry, however, pointed out that his Ukraine engagements had ended before William and Catherine arrived in Mumbai.

The reports provide no evidence that Harry deliberately scheduled his visit to divert attention from his brother's tour.

Ingrid Seward Says Kate Middleton Is Unlikely To Be Troubled

Seward, editor-in-chief of Majesty magazine, also questioned the timing of Harry's Ukraine visit. Speaking to The Sun, she described the scheduling as unfortunate and suggested Harry wanted the attention surrounding his engagements for himself.

She argued that Catherine would be unlikely to worry about the situation, describing her as above such publicity disputes. Seward also doubted Harry could overshadow the Waleses' first joint official overseas tour in four years, although she suggested his visit could still 'put a pin in the balloon'.

These are Seward's interpretations of the royal family's dynamics, rather than confirmed accounts of Catherine's private feelings. Neither Catherine nor Harry was quoted addressing the alleged publicity rivalry in the reports reviewed.

A spokesman for the Princess told The Sun that Catherine was 'enormously proud' of William's Earthshot initiative.

The couple's three-day India programme includes engagements focused on environmental innovation, sustainability and youth leadership. Catherine's attendance puts her alongside William at an Earthshot event for the first time since the 2022 ceremony in Boston.

The programme is due to conclude in New Delhi, where the couple are scheduled to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi, according to the UK government. In Mumbai, the Earthshot Prize will recognise five environmental solutions, with each winner receiving £1 million to support its work.

excerpt: Intel faces a proposed shareholder lawsuit alleging executives misled investors about weakening PC demand and other issues before a $23 billion share offering.
headline: Intel Hit With Shareholder Lawsuit After 29% Stock Plunge as Investors Allege Company Hid a PC Sales Problem
html_content:
Intel is facing a proposed shareholder class-action lawsuit accusing the chipmaker of concealing worsening PC sales, excess inventory, and manufacturing constraints before raising $23 billion from investors — weeks before its shares suffered their biggest one-day decline in decades, wiping approximately $140 billion off its market value.

The lawsuit, filed on 13th November in federal court in San Jose, California, alleged that Intel and two senior executives misled investors about the severity of the company's business problems between 23rd July and 29th October.

The plaintiffs argued that mounting weakness in the PC market was already damaging revenue and margins, while management continued to promote the company's growth prospects amid the artificial intelligence boom.

Led by the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System, a Michigan pension fund, the proposed class action names Intel Chief Executive Lip-Bu Tan and Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner as defendants. It seeks unspecified damages for investors who purchased Intel shares during the alleged class period.

Understating Faltering PC Demand

At the centre of the lawsuit is the allegation that Intel understated the damage caused by weakening PC demand and an accumulation of unsold computers at original equipment manufacturers and distribution partners.

According to the complaint, rising PC component prices made computers more expensive, leaving Intel's partners struggling to sell existing inventory to consumers. That, in turn, reduced demand for Intel's processors and weakened its ability to offset lower sales volumes through higher prices.

The plaintiffs also allege that Intel's Client Computing and Physical AI Group suffered a substantially greater deterioration than investors were told, with revenue falling by hundreds of millions of dollars sequentially and margins coming under pressure.

The complaint further argues that growth associated with AI infrastructure and data centre construction was insufficient to offset the damage from the PC slowdown. Manufacturing constraints involving semiconductor substrates also allegedly prevented Intel from ramping up server processor production to capitalise fully on stronger demand. However, note that these claims have not been proven in court.

The $23B Share Sale Under Scrutiny

The timing of Intel's August fundraising is another central element of the proposed lawsuit.

On 12th August, Intel completed a public share offering at $95 per share, issuing approximately 242 million shares and generating $23 billion in gross proceeds. The company reported receiving $22.6 billion after offering expenses and underwriting costs, according to its regulatory filings.

The plaintiffs argued that Intel had an incentive to downplay deteriorating business conditions while seeking fresh capital, particularly because the offering took place during the third quarter, which they described as disastrous.

Intel said the proceeds would support general corporate purposes, including investment and working capital. Investors must understand that the lawsuit does not establish that the share offering was unlawful or that Intel knowingly misrepresented its financial position.

Intel's Earnings Exposed the Scale of the Slowdown

Intel's 29th October earnings announcement provided the immediate financial context for the allegations.

The company reported Q3 revenue of $16.5 billion, up 21% year over year. However, its client computing business generated $8.1 billion, down 5% from the same period a year earlier. By comparison, its Data Center and AI division recorded $7.3 billion in revenue, representing 78% annual growth.

CFO Zinsner acknowledged that the PC slowdown could continue through at least H1 2027. While CEO Tan separately cited manufacturing supply shortages and an unprecedented memory crunch, saying the company needed to address the challenges urgently.

The following day, 30th October, Intel shares plunged 28.6%, erasing approximately $140 billion in market value. The decline followed the disappointing outlook and concerns about the company's ability to meet demand for its processors.

excerpt: Amazon MGM Studios has named Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, with Denis Villeneuve directing and Steven Knight writing, although production details remain undisclosed.
headline: Robert Pattinson Named Next James Bond After Aaron Taylor-Johnson and Henry Cavill Rumours: Why Was He Chosen?
html_content:
Robert Pattinson has been named the next James Bond, giving the 007 franchise a new leading man after Daniel Craig's departure. Amazon MGM Studios announced the 40-year-old British actor's appointment on Monday, 16 November 2026. Denis Villeneuve will direct, with a screenplay by Steven Knight.

The announcement ends months of speculation about Craig's successor. Pattinson is also committed to another major franchise: Matt Reeves's The Batman Part II, which has resumed production.

The official 007 Instagram account marked the news with a short teaser captioned 'Identity Confirmed', followed by a first-look image of Pattinson in a tuxedo.

View this post on Instagram

The casting marks the first new Bond lead under Amazon MGM's creative control. The studio secured that control through a 2025 joint venture with longtime franchise producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, who remain co-owners of the franchise's intellectual property. Craig's final appearance was in No Time to Die, released in 2021, ending his five-film run as the secret agent.

Amazon MGM announced no release date, filming schedule or additional cast members. Its statement confirmed the creative team but offered no plot details.

Why Amazon MGM Chose Robert Pattinson

The studio's explanation focused on Pattinson's acting range and screen presence. Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, praised his 'remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity'. Villeneuve said Pattinson had 'the timeless soul of 007' while bringing 'a spirit that is completely new'.

Producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman praised his 'fearlessness as an actor' and 'self-deprecating wit', calling him 'the perfect Bond for our times'. Variety reported on 9 November that Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult had screen-tested. Its report also named Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor and Jack Lowden among the rumoured contenders.

Pattinson's recent work spans studio franchises and independent projects. He appeared as Antinous in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, played Chris Hansen in A24's Primetime and starred opposite Zendaya in The Drama. His other film credits include Tenet, The Lighthouse and Mickey 17.

Pattinson has also worked with Villeneuve on Dune: Part Three, playing Scytale, a shapeshifting Face Dancer assassin. The film is scheduled for release later this year.

What Bond Means for the Batman Part II

Pattinson's appointment raises a scheduling question. He is returning as Bruce Wayne in The Batman Part II, the sequel to Reeves's 2022 film. Warner Bros. has scheduled the follow-up for 18 February 2028, following several delays.

Production was temporarily paused in October while Reeves dealt with a family matter. However, Pattinson confirmed on 26 October that filming had resumed and that he was expected to return to set within days. Amazon MGM has not announced a shooting schedule for Bond, so it is not yet clear whether the two films will overlap.

Henry Cavill's absence may revive discussion of his long association with Bond. He auditioned for Casino Royale in 2005 but lost the part to Craig. In a March 2026 Heat interview, Cavill said he might be 'a bit old to start now' at 42, but would consider playing a villain.

Aaron Taylor-Johnson has also been linked to Bond for years. There is no report that he made the final shortlist alongside Pattinson.

The studio has yet to reveal the film's title, release date, supporting cast or story. For now, fans will have to wait to see how Pattinson plays 007.
