A Superior Court jury found Randall Bird, 49, guilty of four counts of crimes against the dead on 12 November 2026. Bird worked at Banner – University Medical Center Phoenix, where his duties included transporting deceased patients to the morgue and placing their bodies inside the freezer. He was taken into custody after the verdict and is scheduled for sentencing on 18 December 2026. Four Guilty Verdicts Follow Hospital Investigation A jury found Bird guilty of four counts of crimes against the dead, according to court records. The indictment had accused him of 'having sexual intercourse with a dead human body' and sexual contact with the woman's breasts. The four offences are Class 4 felonies, each carrying a potential prison term of between 12 and 45 months. The circumstances surrounding the discovery and the subsequent police investigation were detailed in reports following the incident, although the evidence presented during Bird's trial and the arguments made in court have not been publicly detailed. Colleagues Find Woman's Body Bag Open The woman's body arrived at the hospital on 22 October 2023, and Phoenix police received the initial report on 24 October. Two security guards described encountering Bird inside the morgue freezer at around 5.30am, with his uniform dishevelled and his duty belt resting on the woman's gurney. Their account to investigators described the body bag as completely unzipped and the woman lying face down, with her gown rolled above her belly button and her lower body exposed. They said Bird tried to cover her by pulling down the gown when they entered the freezer. Bird Claimed He Suffered a Medical Episode Bird told colleagues that he had suffered a medical episode and fainted, grabbing the body bag as he fell and accidentally tearing it open and breaking the zipper. Witnesses disputed his explanation when speaking to a supervisor, saying neither the bag nor its zipper was broken. He subsequently maintained that he had fainted but said he could not remember what happened afterwards during police inquiries into the incident. Bird gave that explanation during the 2023 police investigation, but it remains unclear whether he presented the same account as part of his defence at trial. DNA Findings Formed Part of Police Inquiries Investigators found Bird's DNA on the woman's body, while an examination also identified rib fractures sustained after her death. The circumstances surrounding the findings have not been publicly established. Bird was initially booked on five counts in November 2023. The subsequent verdict resulted in four guilty findings, although the available reporting does not explain the outcome of the fifth count. His trial was later delayed in part because he underwent quadruple bypass surgery in May 2026 at a separate medical centre in Chandler. Banner Health Confirmed Dismissal Before Arrest Banner Health told Becker's Hospital Review that Bird's employment was terminated on 24 October 2023, two days after the woman's body arrived at the hospital and more than a month before his arrest. The organisation also said he had undergone a thorough pre-employment background check, as required for all hospital employees. 'We are saddened and appalled by the alleged actions of an individual at Banner University Medical Center Phoenix that resulted in his arrest on November 28, 2023,' the hospital said. That statement was issued following his arrest, rather than the November 2026 conviction.

excerpt: Thousands report US banking problems, but Chase says the disruption was a software bug, not a cyberattack.
headline: Chase Outage Sparks Cyberattack Fears as Thousands Report US Banking Problems
html_content:
Thousands of customers reported problems accessing online banking services across the United States on Monday, 16 November.

Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, US Bank and Truist were among the institutions flagged in user reports on Downdetector, although the reports did not establish that all five banks had experienced independent service disruptions.

The disruption prompted speculation about a possible cyberattack, with customers questioning whether their money and personal banking information were safe.

The reports emerged amid several technology disruptions affecting major services in recent days. Customers had already experienced a Microsoft outage that affected Outlook, Teams and Copilot. The latest banking problems added to concerns about the reliability of essential digital services.

Major Bank Disruptions in the US

According to outage-tracking website Downdetector, users reported problems with several major banks on Monday. However, the reports did not establish that every named institution had suffered an independent system failure.

Chase appeared to be at the centre of the disruption. Some customers encountered messages stating, 'Some services aren't available. We're working on them. Please try back later.'

Bank of America, Wells Fargo and another banks...

Was there a cyberattack? https://t.co/7TElCLEUUh

— Ufi (@ufiturkey) November 16, 2026

The problems also affected transactions involving Chase, potentially causing delays for customers banking elsewhere.

The uncertainty quickly spilled onto social media. Some X users questioned whether Bank of America, Wells Fargo and other banks were experiencing a cyberattack. Others described the situation as a possible coordinated attack targeting the aforementioned banks.

'Bank of America, Wells Fargo and another banks...Was there a cyberattack?' one asked. Another added, 'Possible bank cyberattack underway targeting Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, Truist, and more'.

NEW: Possible bank cyberattack underway targeting Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, Truist, and more

Downdetector is reporting thousands of user reported outages within the last hour pic.twitter.com/Xe1qmxr89c

— Eric Spracklen 🇺🇸 (@EricSpracklen) November 16, 2026

A separate post questioned how a bank outage could leave customers unable to access their money, declaring, 'That's a cyberattack.' These were individual online claims, not independently verified evidence of a cyberattack.

Another user claimed Chase customers had been turned away while trying to access their funds. However, this claim was not independently verified, and Chase maintained that customers could still access their accounts and money.

BREAKING: Chase Bank customers now reporting they were turned away and unable to access their money from banks during possible cyberattack targeting the bank’s computer system https://t.co/zkMfOfrCNj

— Eric Spracklen 🇺🇸 (@EricSpracklen) November 16, 2026

Chase Responds to US Bank Cyberattack Fears

Chase rejected suggestions that its disruption was connected to a cyberattack, identifying a software problem instead.

'JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence it is cyber-related. It is taking longer than usual to service some customers,' a spokesperson for the bank said.

The spokesperson also stressed that the incident was not a systemic banking problem. Other institutions might have experienced slower transactions only when processing payments involving Chase.

The bank said customers could still access their accounts and funds and that it was working to resolve the issue. The explanation offered an important distinction between a bank experiencing technical difficulties and a wider security breach. There was no confirmed evidence in the available reports that hackers had accessed customers' accounts or stolen banking information.

Bank of America and Wells Fargo did not immediately comment on the reported problems. However, Downdetector recorded user reports of problems involving both institutions, although these reports did not independently confirm that their banking systems were experiencing outages.

US Bank clarified that its systems were not directly affected. However, a spokesperson warned that customers sending or receiving Zelle payments involving another financial institution could experience delays.

Zelle's operator, Early Warning Services, similarly said its payment network was operating normally. It acknowledged that problems at participating financial institutions could affect some customers' transactions.

excerpt: JD Vance said the United States would not remain committed to the Iran war for two years, but gave no timetable, exit conditions or strategy for ending the wider conflict.
headline: JD Vance Promises Trump Will End Iran War by 2028 as Fears Grow Over Another US 'Forever War'
html_content:
Vice President JD Vance said on Fox News on Monday, 16 November, that the Iran war would not become a 'forever war'. He said: 'We are not going to allow this to become a 10- or 15-year commitment, or frankly even a two-year commitment.' Vance also said President Donald Trump would get the country out of the conflict with 'great results'.

His remarks suggest that Vance does not expect the US commitment to last two years. However, he did not give a specific end date or say whether all hostilities would cease when US involvement ends.

Iran War Began With US and Israeli Strikes in February

The conflict began on 28 February 2026, when US and Israeli forces launched strikes on Iran. The Congressional Research Service says Iranian attacks subsequently hit targets in several countries.

Israeli strikes killed Iran's then-Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, while US and Israeli operations significantly degraded Iran's military capabilities, according to the service.

Early Iranian threats and attacks on commercial shipping largely halted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

Some shipping has since resumed, but tanker movements have continued to face disruption and require security arrangements, including US and Gulf partner escorts. Attacks have also continued, the Associated Press reported on 12 November.

That leaves no clearly established endpoint. Trump has described the war as effectively over in military terms.

However, he has also threatened renewed strikes if mediation fails, the Associated Press reported on 12 November.

JD Vance's Iran War Assurances Follow Political Fallout

Vance was a lead US negotiator in efforts to pause the fighting. The United States and Iran signed a 14-point memorandum of understanding on 17 June.

It established a 60-day period for negotiations. The Congressional Research Service says the agreement collapsed amid renewed fighting and formally expired in August without a broader settlement.

The vice president's role became politically sensitive after the 3 November midterm elections.

Vance blamed the Iran war for Republican losses. He wrote on X: 'The reason we lost is the war.' Trump largely agreed that the conflict had affected the result, although he continued to defend the military action.

An AP Voter Poll found about six in 10 voters considered the US decision to take military action against Iran wrong. Only about one-third said the war was crucial to their congressional vote. Cost of living and government corruption ranked higher in the survey.

On 12 November, Trump directed Vance to shift his attention away from Iran. He told the vice president to focus instead on an anti-fraud campaign, the Associated Press reported.

The instruction came days before Vance's latest defence of the administration's approach.

Vance's comments offer reassurance about the expected duration of US involvement, not an exit strategy for the wider conflict.

He did not set conditions for ending military operations or explain what would count as success. Nor did he say how Washington would respond if diplomacy failed.

Trump and Vance's current terms do not end in 2028. Under the 20th Amendment, presidential and vice-presidential terms end at noon on 20 January. Their current terms are scheduled to end on 20 January 2029.

excerpt: A widespread United Airlines technology outage delayed hundreds of flights after pilots lost access to essential take-off performance data, leaving passengers waiting on aircraft and at gates.
headline: United Airlines Outage Disrupts Departing Flights Just Days After FAA Failure Grounded Thousands Nationwide
html_content:
United Airlines passengers faced flight delays on Monday, 16 November, after a widespread system outage prevented departing aircraft from accessing essential take-off performance data. The disruption left passengers waiting on aircraft and caused some flights to be held at their gates, raising fresh concerns about the reliability of critical aviation technology.

The incident came just days after a separate Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) disruption affected thousands of flights across the United States. Although the two incidents involved different systems, their proximity has drawn attention to the vulnerability of essential travel infrastructure.

United Airlines Outage Leaves Passengers Stuck on the Tarmac

Passengers reported delays after United Airlines experienced a company-wide technology problem affecting departing flights.

Pilots reportedly experienced difficulties obtaining the weight-and-balance information and performance calculations needed to confirm that aircraft could safely take off. NBC News reported that air traffic control audio captured United pilots describing problems receiving the necessary take-off data from dispatch.

One passenger described being 'stuck on tarmac.' The passenger said the airline had an IT issue and could not clear planes for take-off because they could not connect to the weight system.

Currently stuck on tarmac from nationwide @united IT issue as they can’t clear planes for take off as can’t connect to the weight system. 😤

— Craig Gruen (@craiggruen) November 16, 2026

Other travellers shared similar experiences on X, formerly Twitter. One passenger said the pilot had announced that United Airlines was experiencing a system-wide IT issue and that the aircraft could not obtain the performance data needed for take-off.

flight unable to take off today!

Pilot just announced ALL of United Airlines has a company wide IT issue “unable to get performance data for takeoff”

we’re going back to the gate 👍 https://t.co/UY7hnhdjth pic.twitter.com/ArTNF4CB82

— Halina.eth 💎 (@halina_eth) November 16, 2026

Another traveller reported waiting on the runway before the pilot announced that the airline's computer outage meant the aircraft could not depart.

Some passengers were subsequently told their aircraft would return to the gate, while others faced uncertainty over departure times as crews waited for the technical problem to be resolved.

Waiting to take off, on the runway, and the pilot just said we can’t take off because United is experiencing a system-wide computer outage.

— zooko🛡🦓🦓🦓 ⓩ (@zooko) November 16, 2026

United Airlines Addresses the System-Wide Technology Failure

United Airlines acknowledged the disruption in a post on X, apologising to affected customers and confirming that its teams were working to restore normal operations.

'We're aware of the widespread system outage,' the airline wrote. It asked passengers to monitor their flight status through the United app or its website while technicians investigated the problem.

We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible. We appreciate your patience while we work through this. Please check back with us for updates, and keep… https://t.co/Y6hG6u2Kjj

— United Airlines (@united) November 16, 2026

In a subsequent update, United clarified that the 'technology issue' affected departing flights only.

'There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,' the company said.

We are troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights. There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.

— United Airlines (@united) November 16, 2026

The airline did not initially provide a detailed explanation of what caused the failure. However, a spokesperson said there was no indication that the outage was related to cybersecurity.

United later confirmed that the technology problem had been resolved. Flight-tracking website FlightAware reported 418 delayed United flights late on Monday afternoon, illustrating the immediate operational impact of the disruption.

United Airlines Outage Follows Nationwide FAA Ground Stop

The latest disruption followed a difficult week for American aviation. On Friday, 13 November, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after a technical failure affecting air traffic control communications disrupted operations.

The ground stop halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours, from approximately 3.30pm to 8.15pm ET. Reuters reported that airlines cancelled approximately 9,200 flights and delayed another 7,500 on Friday. Further cancellations and delays continued over the weekend as carriers struggled to restore normal schedules.

The FAA's preliminary investigation found that excessive data traffic had destabilised its legacy telecommunications equipment, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds.

Investigators identified two potential sources of the excessive data traffic: a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where the FAA's network service provider, L3Harris, had been installing a new router. The agency said it was continuing to investigate the incident alongside the contractor.

Officials ordered the ground stop as a precaution to protect flight safety.

The FAA subsequently said the system had stabilised and that it was continuing to investigate the incident alongside its network service provider, L3Harris.

The United Airlines outage also came amid other major technology disruptions.

1) Microsoft
2) FAA system outage
3) Major Bank Outage today
4) United Airlines systems outage

Am I alone - or does this no longer feel like a coincidence. https://t.co/hs7xpLfWui

— CALL TO ACTIVISM (@CalltoActivism) November 16, 2026

On Monday, customers reported difficulties accessing online accounts at several major US banks, including Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America. Chase confirmed that it was experiencing a technical issue affecting some transactions, but said customers could still access their accounts and funds.

Microsoft had also experienced a major outage beginning on Thursday, 12 November, affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot. The disruption continued into Friday, with the company confirming that its services had been fully restored by Saturday.

These incidents prompted questions on social media about the cybersecurity of essential American infrastructure. However, the outages should not automatically be treated as evidence of a coordinated attack.

IT OUTAGES / DISRUPTIONS REPORTED OVER THE LAST 7 DAYS:

- November 11: Microsoft
- November 13: FAA Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs)
- November 15: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
- November 16: Chase, U.S. Bank, Wells Fargo, USAA and other financial institutions
- November… https://t.co/ZAffObNH8V

— GeoInsider (@InsiderGeo) November 16, 2026

United said there was no indication that its outage was cybersecurity-related. Chase also attributed its problems to a technical issue rather than a cyberattack. Microsoft said its disruption was caused by technical problems and that it had found no indication of malicious activity, while the FAA's preliminary investigation pointed to telecommunications and equipment-related issues.

There is currently no confirmed evidence linking these incidents or establishing that the United Airlines outage resulted from a security breach. For passengers, however, the immediate concern was simpler: their flights were not going anywhere.

excerpt: Looksmaxxing influencer Clavicular faced criticism after presenting his girlfriend's shaved head as support for his skincare routine, while she defended the decision as her own choice
headline: Clavicular's Girlfriend Shaves Her Head to Help His Looksmaxxing Journey as He Calls Her Sacrifice the 'Bare Minimum'
html_content:
Looksmaxxing influencer Clavicular has attracted widespread attention after his girlfriend, Lillian 'Lily' Snyder, shaved off her long blonde hair in a video that he initially presented as a sacrifice to support his physical appearance goals.

The 20-year-old content creator, whose real name is Braden Peters, shared footage on X (formerly known as Twitter) showing Snyder giving herself a buzz cut at home. He claimed the decision would help prevent acne caused by contact with hair products while they slept.

Clavicular praised the gesture as an act of love but described it as the 'bare minimum', prompting criticism from social media users who questioned his expectations of his girlfriend.

Clavicular Links Girlfriend's Haircut to His Looksmaxxing Journey

In his post on X, Clavicular suggested that contact with a woman's hair during sleep could expose his skin to pore-clogging hair-product residue and contribute to acne.

'Nocturnal facial contact with a woman's hair may expose skin to comedogenic hair-product residue, causing acne,' he wrote.

He then explained that Snyder had shaved her head to accommodate his appearance-focused routine.

'My girlfriend in an attempt to aid me in my looksmaxing journey shaved all of her hair off. Very loving gesture, bare minimum IOI,' he added.

According to Zach Margolius of PerthNow, who reported on the incident on 16 November 2026, the influencer's comments prompted followers to question his reasoning and suggest he had taken his looksmaxxing ideology too far.

The report also highlighted criticism from users who challenged his explanation, arguing that hair-product residue could still transfer through pillows and bedding.

Nocturnal facial contact with a woman's hair may expose skin to comedogenic hair-product residue, causing acne.

My girlfriend in an attempt to aid me in my looksmaxing journey shaved all of her hair off. Very loving gesture, bare minimum lOI. pic.twitter.com/zJBdXrpCXp

— Clavicular (@clavicular) November 16, 2026

Social Media Users Criticise His 'Bare Minimum' Remark

Clavicular's description of Snyder's haircut as the 'bare minimum' became a major talking point, with viewers questioning whether such a dramatic personal change should be considered an ordinary expectation in a relationship.

Another suggested that the incident could become the subject of a future documentary.

The Mirror also covered the controversy, reporting on the criticism directed at Clavicular after he presented his girlfriend's shaved head as a loving gesture supporting his looksmaxxing routine.

Snyder Defends Her Decision to Shave Her Head

Snyder offered her own explanation for the haircut, saying she intended to donate her hair to someone close to her.

In a post on X, she shared a photograph of her long hair inside a zip-lock bag, accompanied by the caption: 'Donating my hair to a loved one.'

She also defended herself against suggestions that she was unwell or had been manipulated into shaving her head.

'Stop saying I'm unwell because I chose to be stylish and hot and shave my head like Sinéad O'Connor and Britney Spears. My body, my choice,' she wrote.

She further questioned why people could not accept that she genuinely liked her new appearance.

'Do you think I would shave my head if I didn't know I would look stylish bald?' she added.

The controversy took another turn after Clavicular removed the video following the negative reactions.

According to Khaled S. of Al Bawaba, in a report published on 16 November 2026, the influencer said Snyder had asked him to take down the footage.

He subsequently described the post as 'the best bait in Twitter history', adding that looksmaxxing already had a negative reputation.

Al Bawaba also reported that Clavicular later claimed Snyder had shaved her head to donate her hair to a family member suffering from cancer. However, Snyder's own post only said she was donating her hair to a loved one, and the cancer-related explanation was not independently confirmed.

The incident has drawn renewed attention to looksmaxxing, an internet trend focused on improving physical attractiveness through skincare, grooming, fitness and other appearance-related practices.

excerpt: A wounded US Army major says a counter-drone system promised for a Kuwait command post never arrived before an Iranian drone strike killed six soldiers and wounded dozens.
headline: Trump's Claims of Effective Defences Contrasted With Whistleblower's Account of Vulnerable Kuwait Base
html_content:
President Donald Trump says only two Iranian attack drones got through US defences and caused American fatalities during the war. But a wounded Army major has questioned whether troops at a US military command post in Kuwait had adequate protection before a drone strike killed six soldiers.

An Iranian drone struck the operations centre of the US Army Reserve's 103rd Expeditionary Sustainment Command at Port Shuaiba, a seaport in Kuwait. The attack came during Operation Epic Fury, the US-led campaign against Iran that began on 28 February. Trump's figures concern fatalities across the campaign. Maj Stephen Ramsbottom's account focuses on protection at one site.

Trump Says Two Drones Caused US Fatalities

In a Truth Social post on 16 November, Trump said Iran had launched between 8,000 and 9,000 one-way attack drones since the campaign began. 'Only 2 of them got through, resulting in U.S. fatalities, both on the first day, hitting Kuwait and Saudi Arabia,' he wrote.

The two locations Trump cited were Port Shuaiba in Kuwait, where six soldiers were killed, and Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, where another US soldier later died from injuries sustained in an Iranian attack on 1 March.

He also said Iran had fired about 2,000 ballistic missiles, with one getting through and causing US fatalities in Jordan. Trump described US Central Command's defensive measures as 'historically effective' and said 99.99% of Iranian missiles and drones had been shot down or had not caused US deaths.

His percentage is not an interception rate: it combines weapons reportedly intercepted with those that did not cause US deaths. Trump criticised CBS's 60 Minutes report for omitting his figures. The programme examined the Kuwait strike and Ramsbottom's allegations about the command post's protection.

Major Says Port Shuaiba Had No Dedicated Drone Protection

Ramsbottom, deputy chief of operations for the 103rd Expeditionary Sustainment Command, told CBS the command post lacked a dedicated system designed to protect it from aerial attacks.

'There was nothing there designed to protect from an aerial attack,' he said.

The operations centre was housed in trailers surrounded by concrete T-walls. Ramsbottom said the barriers were intended to protect against ground-level threats, including car bombs, rather than drones approaching from above.

He said a command sergeant major told troops a counter-drone system would be sent, but it never arrived. The account does not establish whether the system was formally ordered or requested.

Soldiers also spotted five quadcopters circling the site the night before the attack and suspected they were conducting surveillance, Ramsbottom said. On the morning of 1 March, troops received the all-clear. About 30 minutes later, an Iranian drone struck the central trailer, killing six soldiers and wounding dozens.

Whistleblower Says Warnings Were Dismissed

In a complaint submitted to congressional Armed Services committees, Ramsbottom alleged military leaders dismissed concerns about the command post's vulnerability. He said intelligence assessments had identified Port Shuaiba as a potential Iranian target before the war.

'I feel this is a tactical failure by the Army, our leadership, and myself,' Ramsbottom told CBS. 'We just did not plan this well, and this needs to be a lesson that we learn.'

His account differs from Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's public description of the tactical operations centre as fortified. Hegseth referred to the attacking drone as a 'squirter' on 2 March, saying it had penetrated air defences and hit a fortified tactical operations centre. Ramsbottom's complaint questions whether the site had adequate protection against aerial threats.

The allegations have not been independently substantiated. They raise questions about whether warnings were acted on and whether the command post had adequate equipment to defend against the threat.

Army Findings Have Not Been Released

The Army completed its investigation into the strike in June 2026, but its findings have not been publicly released, Stars and Stripes reported.

Ramsbottom has also filed a complaint with the Pentagon inspector general seeking an independent investigation, Stars and Stripes reported. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, the ranking member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has separately requested a classified briefing and Port Shuaiba's force-protection assessments from Hegseth.

The Pentagon declined to comment to CBS on Ramsbottom's allegations or whether adequate force protection had been in place.

excerpt: Representative Robert Garcia said Melania Trump could be sought as a witness in congressional investigations into Jeffrey Epstein, while acknowledging that any subpoena and testimony remain uncertain
headline: Melania Trump Could Face Epstein Subpoena as Robert Garcia Calls Her an 'Important Witness'
html_content:
Melania Trump could face a congressional subpoena over the Jeffrey Epstein investigation after Representative Robert Garcia said he wanted the first lady to testify, describing her as an 'important witness.'

Speaking to Don Lemon in an interview publicised on 16 November, Garcia discussed the possibility of seeking her testimony as Democrats prepare further investigations. His comments outlined a potential step, rather than announcing that a subpoena had been issued.

The proposal brings renewed scrutiny to the first lady's past encounters with Epstein and correspondence with Ghislaine Maxwell. Melania has denied knowing about Epstein's abuse, participating in his activities or having a friendship with him. Her previous public statement also urged Congress to give survivors an opportunity to testify.

Garcia Wants Answers From the First Lady

Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, said he wanted to hear what Melania might know about Epstein.

'I think she'd be an important witness in the investigation,' he said.

Asked whether Melania knew something about Epstein, Garcia said: 'I would imagine she does, I don't know for a fact, but I imagine that she knew, she's met Jeffrey Epstein.' He added that investigators would want to hear from her if she had relevant information.

That distinction matters: describing someone as a potential witness does not establish that they witnessed criminal conduct. Garcia's remarks did not identify new evidence showing that Melania knew about Epstein's abuse.

The interview forms part of a broader discussion about congressional oversight, including access to Epstein-related documents and potential investigations involving the Trump administration. Lemon's programme identified Epstein, Trump family finances, immigration enforcement and corporate corruption as Garcia's four investigative priorities.

Melania Has Denied Knowledge of Epstein's Crimes

In a statement released by the White House on 9 April, Melania said she first encountered Epstein in 2000 at an event she attended with Donald Trump.

She said the couple sometimes attended the same social gatherings as Epstein, but rejected the suggestion that this amounted to friendship. She also denied that Epstein introduced her to her husband, saying she met Trump at a New York party in 1998.

'I have never had any knowledge of Epstein's abuse of his victims,' she stated.

Melania further denied travelling on Epstein's plane or visiting his private island. Addressing her email exchange with Maxwell, she characterised it as casual correspondence rather than evidence of a relationship.

Her Earlier Call for Survivor Hearings

Melania's April statement also asked Congress to organise a public hearing centred on Epstein's survivors. She advocated allowing women who wished to participate to give sworn testimony and have their accounts entered into the congressional record.

Garcia publicly supported that request at the time. In an official committee statement, he encouraged Oversight Chairman James Comer to arrange a hearing immediately. That earlier agreement concerned providing survivors with a platform; Garcia's latest remarks additionally raise the prospect of questioning the first lady herself.

Hearings Proposed for Next Year

Garcia said four major investigations would begin rolling out in January, with most hearings likely to follow around February. He presented public Epstein hearings as part of that programme. These were his stated plans, rather than a published schedule for Melania to appear.

For now, the development is Garcia's expressed intention to seek answers. Whether that becomes a formal subpoena, and whether the first lady provides testimony, remains unresolved.

excerpt: Lizbeth Vargas Andrade says ICE agents pepper-sprayed and restrained her while she filmed an arrest outside a California jail. She was released without charges.
headline: Pregnant US Citizen Says ICE Agents Pepper-Sprayed Her and Threw Her Face-Down While She Filmed an Arrest
html_content:
A pregnant US citizen says she was pepper-sprayed and forced face-down onto the ground by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents while filming an arrest outside a California jail, in an encounter that has raised questions about the treatment of bystanders during federal immigration operations.

Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23, was detained outside the Stanislaus County jail in Modesto on 15 November as agents attempted to remove a man from a vehicle. She was released later that evening without criminal charges or immigration allegations, according to her lawyer, Patrick Kolasinski.

Footage recorded by her husband shows agents restraining Andrade as he warns them that she is pregnant. The incident has drawn attention to the safeguards governing the use of force against pregnant people in federal custody.

View this post on Instagram

Video Captures the Confrontation Outside the Jail

Andrade said she was livestreaming the attempted arrest on TikTok when an agent grabbed her arm. The footage shows another agent deploying pepper spray before two officers take her to the ground and handcuff her face-down. Her husband can be heard telling the agents: 'She's pregnant with child.' Andrade later said she struck her abdomen when she was forced down.

She also described being accused of assaulting an agent, an allegation she denied. 'We kind of bumped into each other, and then he was like, "She hit me,"' she said after her release.

Andrade was taken to an ICE field office in Stockton. She said her sister called an ambulance, which transported her to hospital while two agents remained with her. Andrade, who has diabetes, also said she was initially denied access to a lawyer.

She was released that evening without being charged. Subsequent reporting said an ultrasound found no concerns with her pregnancy.

ICE Rules Set Limits on Restraining Pregnant Detainees

The incident raises questions about ICE's own rules for handling pregnant people in its custody. Directive 11032.4, introduced in July 2021, says the agency should generally avoid detaining people known to be pregnant for administrative immigration violations unless release is prohibited by law or exceptional circumstances exist.

The directive also says restraints should not normally be used on pregnant people in ICE custody. Exceptions include situations involving an immediate and serious threat to others or a credible risk of escape that cannot reasonably be reduced by other means.

It further prohibits placing a pregnant detainee face-down when four-point restraints are used. The footage of Andrade shows her handcuffed while face-down, but does not establish that four-point restraints were applied. It is therefore not possible to determine from the available material whether that specific restriction was breached.

ICE has not publicly explained the legal basis for Andrade's detention, whether officers knew she was pregnant before restraining her, or whether the use of force is being reviewed.

Sheriff's Office Says Deputies Were Not Involved

The confrontation happened in the parking area of the Stanislaus County jail, where community members had gathered as federal agents attempted to detain someone leaving custody. Sheriff's Office spokesperson Erich Layton said county deputies had no involvement in Andrade's arrest and referred questions about the incident to ICE.

Andrade said she belongs to a network of residents who monitor immigration enforcement in the Central Valley. She said the incident would not stop her from documenting federal operations or supporting immigrant communities.

Her detention has put renewed focus on the risks faced by people recording immigration enforcement, particularly when officers use physical force. Whether the agents followed ICE's procedures remains unclear, with the agency yet to provide a public account of the encounter.

excerpt: John Summit called the Grammys 'a joke' after a 2027 dance snub, but his own fans turned on him, telling the DJ to be humble as Madonna landed three nominations.
headline: Who Is John Summit? Even His Own Fans Tell the DJ To 'Shut Up' and 'Be Humble' Over His Grammy Boycott
html_content:
American DJ John Summit torched the Grammys as 'a f****** joke' on Monday after the Recording Academy snubbed him across all three dance categories, and the backlash came fast when fans told him to 'be humble'.

The 2027 nominations landed on 16 November, and Summit's name was nowhere in them. His team had submitted three entries: his second album 'CTRL Escape', the single 'Lights Go Out', and 'Don't Believe It', according to Billboard. All three missed.

Summit, 32, is the former certified public accountant turned house phenomenon behind 'Where You Are' and 'Shiver', with more than 11.5 million monthly Spotify listeners. One of the biggest touring DJs in the US, he did not hide his frustration.

'Zero Respect' and a Vow To Walk

He went to X. 'Never submitting to the grammys again unless shit changes, it's all a f****** joke,' he wrote, before widening the attack.

never submitting to the grammys again unless shit changes, it’s all a fucking joke. i’m not just talking about myself either there’s zero respect for real electronic dance music & dj’s. the whole dance category is just music industry fueled pop stars

— John Summit (@johnsummit) November 16, 2026

Summit said the problem ran bigger than his own snub, posting that the awards show 'zero respect for real electronic dance music' and dismissing the nominees as 'just music industry fueled pop stars'. In a follow-up, he claimed no DJ plays the nominated songs in clubs.

The Fans Who Told Him To Sit Down

Normally a snub rant rallies the base. This one split it. Summit wrote that he was getting 'attacked hard on here' before signing off to 'continue my sold out arena tour for my real fans'.

Under that post, one reply from a dance fan told him to 'shut up' and called his comments embarrassing, then reminded him that Madonna had shaped dance music long before he arrived. It ended with five words, 'be humble and move on'.

@johnsummit Girl shut up. This is embarrassing, speaking as fan. Madonna is a legend and more dance than you ever could be. Be humble and move on

— . (@HausOfSlayyyter) November 16, 2026

Summit later clarified that he did not intend to attack nominees and wanted another category for dance DJs and producers.

logging back on as i realized i didn’t do a good job of making my point earlier. my intent was not to drag other artists down and i seriously congratulate everyone who was nominated they fully deserve the recognition. i just think there should be an extra category for more dance music djs & producers much love everyone. signing off from twitter now for a while

— John Summit (@johnsummit) November 16, 2026

Madonna, Slayyyter and the Pop Problem

The nominees Summit wrote off tell their own story. Madonna, Slayyyter, and Tame Impala landed in the dance recording field, while Madonna, Robyn, and Skrillex made the album list.

Madonna is no bandwagon pop act in this lane, having won Best Electronic/Dance Album in 2007 for 'Confessions on a Dance Floor'.

Fans seized on the contradiction of a DJ calling the category fake while a dance pioneer sits on the ballot he wanted. The dance pop field lined up Zara Larsson, RAYE, and Tinashe, none of them the club-first producers Summit says the awards ignore.

Summit Is Not the First To Walk

Boycotting the Grammys over a snub has history. The Weeknd pledged a boycott in 2021 after his 'After Hours' drew zero nominations, blaming the Academy's then-secret committees, which the Grammys later scrapped. Summit now joins a 2027 season with acts like BTS choosing not to submit at all.

Whether his threat holds is another question, because a boycott means pulling future submissions, not a ban. For a former accountant who bet everything on dance music, the irony is hard to miss.

His North American arena run ends on 12 December at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, his biggest headlining show yet, and Billboard had received no Academy comment at press time.

'Never submitting to the grammys again unless shit changes, it's all a f****** joke,' he wrote, before widening the attack. never submitting to the grammys again unless shit changes, it’s all a fucking joke. i’m not just talking about myself either there’s zero respect for real electronic dance music & dj’s. the whole dance category is just music industry fueled pop stars — John Summit (@johnsummit) November 16, 2026 Summit said the problem ran bigger than his own snub, posting that the awards show 'zero respect for real electronic dance music' and dismissing the nominees as 'just music industry fueled pop stars'. In a follow-up, he claimed no DJ plays the nominated songs in clubs. The Fans Who Told Him To Sit Down Normally a snub rant rallies the base. This one split it. Summit wrote that he was getting 'attacked hard on here' before signing off to 'continue my sold out arena tour for my real fans'. Under that post, one reply from a dance fan told him to 'shut up' and called his comments embarrassing, then reminded him that Madonna had shaped dance music long before he arrived. It ended with five words, 'be humble and move on'. @johnsummit Girl shut up. This is embarrassing, speaking as fan. Madonna is a legend and more dance than you ever could be. Be humble and move on — . (@HausOfSlayyyter) November 16, 2026 Summit later clarified that he did not intend to attack nominees and wanted another category for dance DJs and producers. logging back on as i realized i didn’t do a good job of making my point earlier. my intent was not to drag other artists down and i seriously congratulate everyone who was nominated they fully deserve the recognition. i just think there should be an extra category for more dance music djs & producers much love everyone. signing off from twitter now for a while — John Summit (@johnsummit) November 16, 2026 Madonna, Slayyyter and the Pop Problem The nominees Summit wrote off tell their own story. Madonna, Slayyyter, and Tame Impala landed in the dance recording field, while Madonna, Robyn, and Skrillex made the album list. Madonna is no bandwagon pop act in this lane, having won Best Electronic/Dance Album in 2007 for 'Confessions on a Dance Floor'. Fans seized on the contradiction of a DJ calling the category fake while a dance pioneer sits on the ballot he wanted. The dance pop field lined up Zara Larsson, RAYE, and Tinashe, none of them the club-first producers Summit says the awards ignore. Summit Is Not the First To Walk Boycotting the Grammys over a snub has history. The Weeknd pledged a boycott in 2021 after his 'After Hours' drew zero nominations, blaming the Academy's then-secret committees, which the Grammys later scrapped. Summit now joins a 2027 season with acts like BTS choosing not to submit at all. Whether his threat holds is another question, because a boycott means pulling future submissions, not a ban. For a former accountant who bet everything on dance music, the irony is hard to miss. His North American arena run ends on 12 December at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, his biggest headlining show yet, and Billboard had received no Academy comment at press time.

excerpt: Robert Pattinson, 40, has been announced as the seventh official James Bond, joining Sean Connery, Roger Moore, Daniel Craig and three other actors who previously played 007.
headline: All Seven James Bond Actors From Sean Connery to Robert Pattinson and Their Ages at Their 007 Debuts
html_content:
Robert Pattinson has been announced as the seventh actor to play James Bond in the official film series, joining a line-up that includes Sean Connery, Roger Moore and Daniel Craig. Amazon MGM Studios confirmed the casting on 16 November 2026, with Pattinson, 40, set to lead the 26th Bond film.

The announcement also renews interest in how old previous actors were when they first played 007, particularly as the franchise prepares for its next chapter under director Denis Villeneuve.

1. Sean Connery — 32

Sean Connery’s introduction in DR. NO (1962) became one of cinema’s most iconic moments. Director tweaked the timing of Connery’s lighter flick, letting the smoke clear before the line landed. A small adjustment that helped create movie history. https://t.co/pb9TovJAU7

— cinesthetic. (@TheCinesthetic) October 26, 2026

Connery established the character's screen identity with his confident portrayal of the British secret agent. Born on 25 August 1930, the Scottish actor was 32 when Dr No premiered, beginning a run that defined the franchise's early years.

2. George Lazenby — 30

Australian actor Lazenby became the youngest Bond debutant at 30. His only appearance as 007 in On Her Majesty's Secret Service (1969) introduced a more emotionally vulnerable interpretation of the character, although he left the franchise after one film.

3. Roger Moore — 45

Bringing style, wit and charisma to the role of Bond. Remembering Sir Roger Moore on what would have been his 99th birthday. https://t.co/OA3w9O769L

— James Bond (@007) October 14, 2026

Moore was 45 when he made his debut in Live and Let Die (1973), making him the oldest actor to begin playing Bond. His lighter, more humorous approach helped distinguish his seven-film tenure from Connery's portrayal.

4. Timothy Dalton — 41

Dalton introduced a more serious, hard-edged Bond at 41 in The Living Daylights (1987). His interpretation, which continued in Licence to Kill (1989), placed greater emphasis on the character's dangerous profession.

5. Pierce Brosnan — 42

Halle Berry says Pierce Brosnan “restored” her faith in men during the making of their James Bond movie. “He will always be my Bond, always. I’m a Pierce Brosnan fan. There couldn’t be a human who is more of a gentleman than Pierce Brosnan.” https://t.co/r25lz6r0uT

— Emir Han (@RealEmirHan) June 14, 2026

Brosnan was 42 when GoldenEye (1995) arrived in cinemas. His Bond combined the character's traditional charm with a more contemporary action style, helping revive the franchise after a six-year absence.

6. Daniel Craig — 38

Craig began playing Bond at 38 with Casino Royale (2006), bringing a more physically demanding and emotionally complex interpretation to the role. His five-film tenure concluded with No Time to Die in 2021.

7. Robert Pattinson — 40 at casting

Born on 13 May 1986, Pattinson is 40 following the announcement. If the next film arrives in 2028, he will be 41 or 42 at its release, depending on the date. His actual debut age therefore remains unconfirmed.

How Pattinson's Age Compares With Previous 007s

Pattinson's appointment at 40 places him within the franchise's established age range. However, unlike his predecessors, his debut age cannot yet be calculated because his film has no confirmed release date.

Pattinson's casting followed months of speculation over who would succeed Daniel Craig as the next James Bond. Several British actors, including Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O'Connor, had been linked to the role, while Nicholas Hoult also reportedly emerged as a contender. However, Amazon MGM Studios ultimately selected Pattinson to lead the franchise's next chapter.

Amazon MGM Studios confirmed that Denis Villeneuve will direct the next instalment from a screenplay by Steven Knight, with Amy Pascal and David Heyman producing. The project marks a new chapter following the transfer of creative control from long-time Bond custodians Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Pattinson called the appointment 'the honour of a lifetime', while Villeneuve praised his ability to bring something new to the character.

With production expected to begin in 2027 according to multiple media reports, Pattinson's first appearance as 007 will also test whether an established Hollywood star can bring a fresh identity to a role previously reinvented by six very different actors.

excerpt: Dekendrick Crawford faces a third murder charge after investigators found partly buried skeletal remains in Tuscaloosa. He denies involvement, while police work to identify the victim and establish a motive.
headline: Alabama Man Accused of Killing Dog Sitter and Student Faces Third Charge After Partly Buried Remains Found
html_content:
Alabama man De'Kendrick Crawford faces a third murder charge after investigators recovered a man's partly buried skeletal remains from a wooded area in Tuscaloosa on Thursday, 12 November, the Tuscaloosa Police Department stated.

The 24-year-old was already facing capital murder charges over the shooting deaths of dog sitter Jose Felix Alvarez-Duenas, 31, and University of Alabama student Jazmine Alexis Bates, 22, at a Brookwood home in July.

Crawford denied involvement in the newly investigated death when interviewed by police. Investigators believe the unidentified man was killed before Alvarez-Duenas and Bates.

Alabama Man's Connections to the Brookwood Victims

Crawford worked with both victims at a local restaurant. Tuscaloosa Violent Crimes Unit Captain Jack Kennedy stated that Crawford and Alvarez-Duenas had been friends but had fallen out. Authorities were still trying to establish a motive at the time.

Alvarez-Duenas was a father of three. His obituary described his devotion to his children and his work ethic.

Bates was originally from Chicago and was due to graduate in December, according to a fundraising page.

'Her determination, ambition, and incredible work ethic inspired everyone who knew her,' the description reads. 'She was the kind of person you could always count on, reliable, selfless, and always willing to help anyone in need without hesitation. She touched so many lives through her kindness, loyalty, and genuine love for others.'

Ring Footage Led Detectives to Alabama Man

Alvarez-Duenas had been watching a friend's home and dog while she was abroad. After noticing suspicious activity on her Ring cameras, the resident contacted her landlord, who alerted police.

Officers conducting a welfare check on 6 July entered the property on the 12900 block of Alabama Junction Road in Brookwood, according to a police press release.

They discovered Alvarez-Duenas dead in the entryway and Bates in a back bedroom closet. Both had been shot dead, as had the dog.

Detectives had already been searching for Crawford over a separate campus shooting at the University of Alabama in May when they recognised him from the Ring footage, police stated.

He also faced a charge of shooting into an occupied dwelling in that case. Police alleged that he fired several rounds while driving away, with the shots striking a building.

Local officers and the US Marshals Service later located him at a relative's apartment on Deerfield Drive in Northport. After initially refusing to come out of the apartment, he was taken into custody.

Tracing the Third Death in Alabama Man's Case

The investigation into the third death began in early November, when a witness told authorities that Crawford had allegedly admitted to killing another person, Kennedy stated.

Crawford allegedly told other people about the killing. Investigators compared witness accounts with digital evidence to trace Crawford's movements and locate the remains in woodland behind River Road Apartments on 8th Avenue NE.

The remains had been partly buried and deliberately concealed, Kennedy stated. Authorities believe the man was between 40 and 70 years old, most likely around 50.

Investigators believe the man may have driven a Chevrolet Cruze and frequented 10th Avenue Apartments at 1821 10th Ave. His identity remains unknown, and it is unclear whether he lived at that address.

excerpt: Robert Pattinson has been confirmed as the next James Bond, but Amazon MGM Studios has not disclosed his contract terms, including reports that he negotiated a three-film commitment and higher pay.
headline: Robert Pattinson's James Bond Deal Could Cover Three Films as Amazon Stays Silent on Contract Terms
html_content:
Robert Pattinson has officially landed James Bond, but the length of his tenure remains unconfirmed by Amazon MGM Studios. Reporting about his contract suggests the actor could play 007 across three films, while studio representatives have declined to discuss the terms.

Amazon announced Pattinson's casting on 16 November, ending speculation about Daniel Craig's successor. The announcement confirmed the actor and creative team for the next instalment, without disclosing his salary or a multi-film commitment.

The distinction leaves two separate questions for fans: who will play Bond has been settled, but how long Pattinson will remain in the role has not been publicly established by the studio.

A Reported Three-Film Commitment

Reporting published before the casting announcement described different contractual terms for actors competing to become the next Bond. Citing three sources familiar with the negotiations, the report said Josh O'Connor and Jack Lowden were required to commit to four films if selected. Pattinson reportedly negotiated a three-film commitment and higher pay, although no salary figure was disclosed.

These were described as agreements covering the initial film and options for subsequent instalments, negotiated during the casting process. The report did not provide a complete comparison of every candidate's terms.

A reported three-film arrangement should therefore not be presented as an announcement that three movies have been commissioned. It also does not establish that Pattinson must leave after a third appearance. Contractual options and a confirmed production slate are different things.

After his casting became official, Amazon MGM representatives declined to comment on the contract. The studio has neither publicly verified the reported number of films nor released the agreement's financial details.

Pattinson Calls Bond an 'Honour of a Lifetime'

Pattinson's first official comments focused on being selected rather than the negotiations behind his appointment. He described the role as 'the honour of a lifetime' and 'a dream come true.'

Denis Villeneuve will direct the next film from a screenplay by Steven Knight. Amy Pascal and David Heyman are producing, with Tanya Lapointe serving as executive producer.

In the announcement, Villeneuve thanked the actors involved in the selection process and welcomed Pattinson. Pascal and Heyman highlighted his versatility, humour and willingness to take creative risks as reasons for their confidence in him.

At 40, Pattinson becomes the seventh actor to play Bond in the official film series. Craig's final appearance was in No Time to Die, released in 2021. The next instalment is widely referred to as Bond 26, although its title has not been announced.

Bond Joins an Already Busy Career

The appointment adds another major franchise to Pattinson's workload. Amazon's announcement confirmed that he is in production on The Batman Part II and appears in Villeneuve's forthcoming Dune: Part Three.

His existing collaboration with Villeneuve gives the actor and director a working relationship before they begin their Bond film. However, the announcement did not explain how future 007 commitments would fit around his other projects.

Filming is expected to begin in 2027, but no production start date has been officially announced. For now, Pattinson's casting is confirmed; the reported three-film deal remains an account of private negotiations that Amazon MGM has chosen not to discuss publicly.

excerpt: Dezarae Sharp has spoken about messages from her former partner, Michael Comer, before their 11-month-old son was allegedly buried alive in South Carolina. The baby survived after being found in a buried dog crate.
headline: 'I Want Us to Be a Family': Mum Reveals Text From Ex Accused of Burying Their 11-Month-Old Baby Alive
html_content:
The mother of an 11-month-old boy found buried alive in South Carolina has described a message from her former partner in which he said he wanted them to be a family.

Dezarae Sharp said Michael Comer sent the text weeks before their son, Koah Sharp, disappeared on 9 November. The child was rescued the following afternoon, and Comer is accused of burying him alive. Sharp's account of their relationship and the messages was detailed in reporting published on 16 November.

Koah survived and was discharged from hospital on the night of his rescue. The Lexington County Sheriff's Department said his medical team expected him to make a full recovery.

The Message Before Koah Disappeared

Sharp said she had accused Comer of wanting to take their child away from her. His response, according to her account, was: 'I don't want to take him. I want us to be a family.'

She described another message in which he acknowledged becoming angry about their situation and again expressed a desire to reunite.

The couple had known each other since childhood and began dating in 2024, Sharp said. They separated following a domestic violence incident earlier this year. She later agreed that Koah could spend weekends with his father and paternal grandmother.

Despite the earlier difficulties, Sharp said she had not believed Comer would harm their son in the way authorities now allege.

A Caregiver Arrived To Find Them Gone

According to Sheriff Jay Koon, Koah was in his paternal grandmother's care before she left him with Comer while running an errand. Another caregiver was expected to arrive, but when that person reached the home, father and son were gone.

Deputies subsequently searched Comer's father's house on Parthenon Road in Batesburg-Leesville. They found open doors and baby belongings, but neither Comer nor Koah.

Investigators obtained security footage showing Comer without the child later that day. Officers arrested him that night after finding him hiding in an outbuilding, initially charging him with burglary. Koah was still missing.

Searchers Heard Koah Crying

More than 100 law enforcement and public safety personnel joined the search. On 10 November, searchers noticed freshly disturbed ground near Comer's father's home and heard the baby crying as they investigated.

Koah was found inside a buried dog crate and taken immediately for medical treatment.

Koon estimated that the child had been underground for approximately 24 hours, drawing on the timeline and footage showing Comer without him. That duration is an estimate, rather than a precisely established burial time.

The sheriff said the circumstances around the crate appeared to have allowed the infant enough air to survive. Authorities had not established a motive in the reporting reviewed. Sharp's account of the messages provides background to the relationship, but does not itself establish why the alleged attack occurred.

Father Denied Bond

Comer, 25, faces charges of attempted murder, unlawful conduct towards a child, custodial interference and burglary. He was denied bond at a hearing on 12 November. Prosecutors told the court that he had not helped investigators locate Koah. Those statements were prosecution allegations presented during the hearing, not findings following a trial.

His next court appearance was scheduled for 10 December, according to reporting from the hearing. The charges remain allegations, and Comer is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

excerpt: Kalshi is offering up to $135,000 for a researcher to stream a complete Grand Theft Auto VI playthrough, analyse its fictional economy and assess the game's wider impact.
headline: Kalshi Offers Up to $135,000 to Play GTA 6, Says LinkedIn Pulled 'Illegitimate' Dream Job Post
html_content:
Kalshi has advertised an unusual contract position that would see a successful applicant earn up to $135,000 (£102,100) by playing and analysing Rockstar Games' highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI.

The position, titled 'GTA VI Researcher', was published on 11 November and offers a fixed project fee of between $100,000 and $120,000 (£75,600–£90,700), alongside a further $15,000 (£11,350) completion payment.

Unlike a conventional gaming role, the successful candidate will be expected to stream their entire playthrough on Twitch or YouTube, starting at midnight on 19 November, the game's scheduled release date. They must continue until they complete the main story.

The role is remote, and Kalshi explicitly allows breaks, leaving the successful applicant to set their own schedule while playing.

The assignment also involves investigating Leonida, the fictional US state where the game takes place, and examining how its economy operates. Kalshi wants the researcher to identify the most effective money-making strategies, document their findings in spreadsheets and publish weekly reports.

The final deliverable will include an official 'State of the Leonida Economy' address. The company also wants an assessment of the game's impact outside the virtual world, including workplace absences, food delivery demand and potential productivity losses during launch week.

Kalshi Says LinkedIn Removed Job Advertisement

Kalshi said on 13 November that LinkedIn had removed the advertisement, flagging it as an 'illegitimate job post'.

Kalshi responded publicly on X, questioning why conventional professional services were considered legitimate employment opportunities while researching a major video game was apparently treated differently.

'JUST IN: LinkedIn just banned our GTA VI Researcher job posting for being "illegitimate." Strategy consulting is a real job, but playing GTA VI isn't? We will not stand for this blatant discrimination against gamers,' the company wrote.

Kalshi also tagged Elon Musk and called for the return of X's recruitment platform as an alternative.

However, the removal did not appear to end the recruitment drive. The vacancy remained available through Kalshi's own careers platform, where the company explicitly described it as a real job.

LinkedIn has not provided a detailed public explanation for the decision, meaning the precise circumstances behind the removal remain unclear.

Gaming Experience and Streaming Audience Among Requirements

Despite the unusual nature of the assignment, Kalshi has outlined specific qualifications for prospective candidates. Applicants must be at least 18 years old, have at least 10 years of gaming experience and possess three or more years of streaming experience.

They must also have an established audience and their own streaming equipment, internet connection and software. A background in economics or finance is not explicitly required, with the emphasis instead placed on understanding systems, identifying opportunities and analysing game mechanics.

By combining a six-figure contract with a high-profile streaming challenge, the company has attracted media coverage.

The position could therefore serve both as a genuine research project and a promotional exercise, introducing Kalshi to potential customers through gaming creators and their established communities.

With Grand Theft Auto VI scheduled to launch on 19 November 2026, excitement is reaching fever pitch as Rockstar Games prepares for one of the biggest releases in gaming history.

excerpt: A viral rumour claims a US emergency alert test on 17 November will trigger a 90-day blackout. FEMA, the FCC and fact-checkers found no evidence to support it.
headline: November 17 Blackout Panic Goes Global: What Really Happens When America's Emergency Alert Sounds?
html_content:
A viral claim that the world will go dark for 90 days from 17 November has sent social media into a spin. The rumour is linked to a real event, a nationwide test of the US Emergency Alert System (EAS), but fact-checkers and officials say there is no evidence that any blackout is expected.

People across the United States are due to hear the alert tone on Tuesday, while online users around the world continue searching for answers. Here is what the test involves, why the panic spread so fast, and what people actually need to know.

What Happens During the Emergency Alert Test?

The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) will run the test at about 2:20pm Eastern Time on 17 November, which is 7:20pm in the UK. The exercise is part of a routine nationwide check of the EAS.

Television and radio programmes will pause for roughly one minute while a message is broadcast in English and Spanish. According to the FCC, the announcement will make it clear that it is only a test and that no action is required from the public.

Unlike the nationwide exercise conducted in 2023, the 2026 test reportedly does not include phone alerts, so mobiles should stay silent. Instead, the alert will be distributed through FEMA's Integrated Public Alert and Warning System, known as IPAWS, which allows officials to push authenticated messages to broadcasters, cable operators and satellite providers.

People outside the US will not receive the alert.

How the '90-Day Blackout' Rumour Spread

Some posts on TikTok and X claim the test will be followed by 90 days of power and internet cuts, urging people to stockpile food and supplies. Fact-checking organisation PolitiFact found no evidence to support those claims and reported that a video appearing to show President Donald Trump announcing a blackout had been manipulated.

Several unrelated events appear to have fuelled the rumour. According to Snopes, a 2023 episode of The Simpsons showed a diary page dated 17 November during a Springfield blackout. Recent technology disruptions, including a Microsoft service outage on 12 November, appear to have contributed to online speculation.

France 24 reported cryptocurrency-focused accounts and misinterpretations of European emergency preparedness guidance helped amplify the rumour internationally.

Is a Blackout Actually Expected for 17 November?

No. Neither FEMA nor the FCC has mentioned any power cuts or internet shutdown. Officials have stated that the exercise is designed to assess emergency communications systems and does not involve electricity or internet infrastructure.

The test is also routine rather than unprecedented. FEMA is required by law to conduct a nationwide EAS test at least once every three years. Nationwide tests have been held since November 2011, and none has ever been linked to a power shutdown.

What You Should Do on 17 November

For most people, no action is required. Once the brief message ends, normal programming will resume and daily activities can continue as usual.

Officials and fact-checkers recommend checking dramatic claims against official sources such as FEMA and the FCC before sharing them online. It is also sensible to be cautious of videos and posts without clear sourcing.

Keeping a basic emergency kit at home is generally encouraged as part of ordinary preparedness. However, there is currently no evidence that the 17 November EAS test is linked to any planned blackout, power outage or internet shutdown.

excerpt: Melissa Dragon, a 54-year-old Massachusetts divorce lawyer, was found dead two days after she was reported missing. Authorities said foul play was not suspected as the medical examiner investigates.
headline: Massachusetts Divorce Lawyer Found Dead After Vanishing in Lexus SUV as Officials Withhold Further Details
html_content:
A Massachusetts divorce lawyer was found dead on Sunday, 15 November, two days after she was reported missing, authorities confirmed. Melissa Dragon, 54, was from Swampscott.

Essex County District Attorney Paul F. Tucker and Swampscott Police Chief Ruben Quesada announced Dragon's death in a joint statement. They thanked law enforcement partners and members of the public who helped with the search but said no further details would be released out of respect for her family.

The Massachusetts Office of the Chief Medical Examiner is investigating the cause and manner of Dragon's death. Authorities said foul play was not suspected.

A Two-Day Search Ends in Confirmation

Swampscott Police issued a missing-person alert seeking help to locate Dragon and her vehicle. The alert said she was last seen at approximately 10:30am on 13 November, travelling west on Lynnfield Street near Den Quarry Road in neighbouring Lynn.

Dragon was driving a blue 2015 Lexus RX 350 bearing Massachusetts registration 7DTH94. Police described her as having brown hair and brown eyes and wearing a black faux-fur coat, leopard-print leggings and grey boots.

The public appeal asked anyone who saw Dragon or the vehicle to contact police. Two days later, officials confirmed she had been found deceased. They did not identify where she was located or say whether the Lexus had also been recovered.

Investigation Into Death Remains Ongoing

Authorities have not provided details about the circumstances in which Dragon was found. Their statement said the medical examiner was determining the cause and manner of death and that no foul play was suspected.

Officials have not announced a cause of death. The absence of suspected foul play is not a final determination by the medical examiner, and no further investigative details have been made public.

The Massachusetts medical examiner's office says testing or a review of medical records and police reports may be needed when a cause of death is not immediately apparent after examination.

Legal Career and Memorial Fund

Dragon was the founding partner and chief litigator of Family Law Practitioners, P.C., a Woburn firm whose practice included divorce, child custody and child support matters. The firm's profile described her work as involving litigation and negotiation for clients facing family-law disputes.

Her professional profile lists a bachelor's degree from Emerson College in 1994 and a Juris Doctor from Suffolk University Law School in 1997. Martindale-Hubbell lists her as a member of Family Law Practitioners and records her admission to the Massachusetts bar in 1998.

Her experience included working as an administrative judicial clerk at the Massachusetts Department of Industrial Accidents and as a mediator in the Massachusetts Attorney General's Office, according to her profile.

Dragon was also reported to have been a founding partner of Child Advocacy Rights Education, an organisation in the Greater Boston area.

A GoFundMe campaign titled Melissa Sindeband Dragon Memorial Fund was organised by Robin Kaplan Price. The organiser's description said Dragon's closest friends had established the fundraiser to help her family with funeral costs, memorial arrangements and related expenses. As of 17 November, the campaign page showed $6,062 raised from 50 donations.

excerpt: Footage released by Le Média appears to show Gérard Depardieu touching a female extra during the 2011 filming of 'Turf,' according to an investigation by Mediapart.
headline: 'She Tried To Push His Hand Away': New Video Appears To Show Putin's French Actor Ally Gérard Depardieu Groping Female Extra
html_content:
New footage appears to show French actor Gérard Depardieu repeatedly touching a female extra during the 2011 filming of the comedy 'Turf' as she tries to push his hand away. The recording was released by French outlet Le Média, and its authenticity was verified by investigative publication Mediapart.

The woman, identified as Olivia, was 22 at the time. She told Mediapart that Depardieu touched her buttocks and crotch and put his hand down her top. His representatives did not respond to the publication's questions about the footage.

Depardieu received Russian citizenship from President Vladimir Putin in 2013 and publicly praised him, although he later criticised Putin's actions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The footage emerged days before the actor withdrew his appeal against a separate 2025 conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set.

🇫🇷🗣Gérard Depardieu agresse une figurante en plein tournage 😫 pic.twitter.com/8HohVWsdge

— Lâche L'affaire (@Lache_Laffaire1) November 12, 2026

Footage From the 'Turf' Film Set

The recording was made on 2 November 2011 at Auteuil racecourse in Paris, during filming involving about 150 extras. It shows Depardieu repeatedly touching Olivia's thigh, crotch and buttocks while she tries to move his hand away, according to a review of the footage.

She also alleged that Depardieu put his hand down her top and touched her breasts several times. Olivia said she attempted to remove his hand but that he continued touching her.

The footage had not previously been made public. Mediapart said it had examined the recording as part of its investigation into the incident.

Witnesses Describe Intervention on Set

Casting director Fany Touya-Calmon told the publication that she intervened after witnessing Depardieu's behaviour. She said she repositioned female extras and stayed close to the actor during later takes to prevent further contact.

Two members of her team and Olivia corroborated her account to the publication. Touya-Calmon also said she alerted the production manager and director Fabien Onteniente.

Onteniente shared that Olivia approached him in tears. He said he confronted Depardieu and told him to 'behave yourself.' The director recalled the actor looking 'sheepish' and behaving like 'a child who'd done something naughty.'

The production manager, Bruno Vatin, said in 2023 that he had no recollection of the incident. He suggested the chaotic nature of the shoot might have affected his memory.

Separate Sexual Assault Conviction Becomes Final

Depardieu, 77, was convicted in May 2025 of sexually assaulting two women during the 2021 filming of 'Les Volets Verts' ('The Green Shutters'). The victims were a 55-year-old set decorator and a 35-year-old assistant director. He received an 18-month suspended sentence and was ordered to register as a sex offender.

On 16 November 2026, Depardieu withdrew his appeal on the day the hearing was due to begin. The prosecution and the two women also withdrew their appeals, leaving the original conviction and sentence in force. The court ordered Depardieu to pay €1,000 (£834 or $1,100) towards the legal costs of the European Association Against Violence Against Women in the Workplace, which had been involved in the appeal proceedings.

In a statement, the actor said he had hidden behind 'provocation and bawdy humour' on film sets and offered 'deep and sincere apologies.' He added: 'I have been found guilty. I acknowledge and accept this conviction.'

Depardieu is also facing a separate case over allegations that he raped actor Charlotte Arnould at his Paris home in 2018. He denies the allegation and has appealed the decision sending him to trial. A ruling on that appeal is expected on 26 November 2026.
