excerpt: Trump dismissed concerns over US technology disruptions as the NSA managed a network interruption and separate outages hit aviation, banking and Microsoft services
headline: Trump Dismisses Chaos and Says 'It's Life' as America's Key Systems Face One Outage After Another
html_content:
President Donald Trump dismissed concerns about a series of technology disruptions affecting US aviation, banking services and Microsoft customers worldwide, telling reporters in Manila on 17 November: 'It's life.'

His remarks came as the National Security Agency (NSA) was dealing with a disruption affecting NSA Net, its classified internal communications network. The other incidents have been attributed to separate technical problems. No public evidence has established a connection between them and the NSA disruption.

Trump Dismisses Concerns Over Multiple Outages

Earlier in the exchange, Trump said the situation would be 'very much under control'. Asked whether he was concerned about the outages, he replied: 'No.' When a reporter mentioned the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and United Airlines, Trump said: 'It's life.' Asked about JPMorgan Chase, he repeated the phrase and added: 'When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine.'

Trump was also asked whether he was concerned about disruption to Thanksgiving travel. 'No, not at all. People are safe,' he said. A day earlier, he had rejected responsibility for the FAA ground stop. He praised Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and other officials for their response, while blaming ageing equipment and previous administrations for failing to modernise the air traffic control system.

NSA Net Disruption Forces Agency to Stagger Staff Arrivals

The disruption affected NSA Net, an internal network used for classified communications. Staff at the agency's Fort Meade headquarters in Maryland were given staggered arrival times to limit the number of people attempting to log in simultaneously. Backup facilities elsewhere in the United States were expected to take on some of the workload.

Recorded Future News reported that the network was not completely shut down but was experiencing intermittent service. Sources told CBS News that routine system patching was involved, while a US official described the disruption as a 'temporary degradation during scheduled maintenance'.

The precise circumstances had not been established publicly. Officials said mission-critical capabilities remained operational and that there was no evidence of a cyberattack.

Microsoft, FAA and Banks Report Separate Technical Failures

Microsoft's preliminary report into a global Microsoft 365 outage on 12 November identified three contributing factors: a latent defect in its networking gateway servers, a Teams failover that shifted traffic to a primary gateway also supporting Exchange Online and nearly 14% of that gateway's server capacity being unavailable.

The defect stemmed from a change whose deployment began in July. The combined pressures left affected servers unresponsive and triggered a wider network failure.

The FAA's nationwide ground stop on 13 November began at about 3.30pm Eastern Time and was lifted at 8.15pm. The agency said its legacy equipment became unstable after the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) network received about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.

Investigators identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, as possible sources. L3Harris, the FAA's network service provider, had been deploying a new router at the Arkansas site. The investigation into the root cause continued.

The FAA reported 12,462 flight cancellations that Friday, including 9,082 by major airlines, but cautioned that not all were directly caused by the ground stop. On 17 November, the Trump administration requested $50.1 billion (£38 billion) from Congress for air traffic control modernisation. The proposal includes funding for telecommunications infrastructure, airport facilities, consolidated air traffic control centres and towers.

JPMorgan Chase said a software bug involving its on-premises hardware slowed transaction processing on 16 November. The bank said customers' funds remained safe and that there was no evidence the problem was cyber-related, although some transactions were delayed.

United Airlines also reported a technology disruption that day. The airline told CNN that fewer than 150 flights were affected, with delays to departing services. Flights already in the air and United Express services were not disrupted.

The cause of the NSA Net disruption remained unclear. The NSA had not publicly identified what caused the interruption.

He praised Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and other officials for their response, while blaming ageing equipment and previous administrations for failing to modernise the air traffic control system. NSA Net Disruption Forces Agency to Stagger Staff Arrivals The disruption affected NSA Net, an internal network used for classified communications. Staff at the agency's Fort Meade headquarters in Maryland were given staggered arrival times to limit the number of people attempting to log in simultaneously. Backup facilities elsewhere in the United States were expected to take on some of the workload. Recorded Future News reported that the network was not completely shut down but was experiencing intermittent service. Sources told CBS News that routine system patching was involved, while a US official described the disruption as a 'temporary degradation during scheduled maintenance'. The precise circumstances had not been established publicly. Officials said mission-critical capabilities remained operational and that there was no evidence of a cyberattack. Microsoft, FAA and Banks Report Separate Technical Failures Microsoft's preliminary report into a global Microsoft 365 outage on 12 November identified three contributing factors: a latent defect in its networking gateway servers, a Teams failover that shifted traffic to a primary gateway also supporting Exchange Online and nearly 14% of that gateway's server capacity being unavailable. The defect stemmed from a change whose deployment began in July. The combined pressures left affected servers unresponsive and triggered a wider network failure. The FAA's nationwide ground stop on 13 November began at about 3.30pm Eastern Time and was lifted at 8.15pm. The agency said its legacy equipment became unstable after the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) network received about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. Investigators identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, as possible sources. L3Harris, the FAA's network service provider, had been deploying a new router at the Arkansas site. The investigation into the root cause continued. The FAA reported 12,462 flight cancellations that Friday, including 9,082 by major airlines, but cautioned that not all were directly caused by the ground stop. On 17 November, the Trump administration requested $50.1 billion (£38 billion) from Congress for air traffic control modernisation. The proposal includes funding for telecommunications infrastructure, airport facilities, consolidated air traffic control centres and towers. JPMorgan Chase said a software bug involving its on-premises hardware slowed transaction processing on 16 November. The bank said customers' funds remained safe and that there was no evidence the problem was cyber-related, although some transactions were delayed. United Airlines also reported a technology disruption that day. The airline told CNN that fewer than 150 flights were affected, with delays to departing services. Flights already in the air and United Express services were not disrupted. The cause of the NSA Net disruption remained unclear. The NSA had not publicly identified what caused the interruption.

excerpt: Tyla Wharmby was sentenced to life imprisonment after murdering 12-week-old Hunter Hodges in Kent and later changing his account to blame the baby's mother
headline: Man Who Murdered Girlfriend's Baby After Snapping Over His Crying Tried to Blame Grieving Mother for His Death
html_content:
A man who murdered his girlfriend's 12-week-old baby after erupting in anger over his crying later attempted to blame the grieving mother for the child's death.

Tyla Wharmby, 24, smashed Hunter Hodges' head against a hard surface during an attack in Ramsgate, Kent, on 15 July 2022, after becoming frustrated because the premature infant would not settle.

He was sentenced to life imprisonment at Canterbury Crown Court on 17 November 2026, with a minimum term of 21 years before he can be considered for parole.

Killer Changed His Story to Blame Mother

According to the sentencing remarks, Wharmby initially claimed he had been looking after Hunter before discovering that the baby's head was swollen.

However, when he realised doctors would identify the injuries as non-accidental, he changed his account and suggested that Hunter's mother, Shannon Hodges, had been responsible.

Mrs Justice Foster said he had 'callously' and 'untruthfully' changed his story to implicate Ms Hodges.

The judge said Hunter had suffered catastrophic injuries comparable to those sustained in a high-speed motor vehicle collision or a fall from a multi-storey building.

Kent Police said its investigation established that Wharmby had lied about the circumstances surrounding Hunter's death and deliberately inflicted the fatal injury shortly before emergency services were called.

The court also heard that Wharmby browsed online pornography shortly after inflicting the fatal injuries.

Baby Attacked After Crying

Mrs Justice Foster said Wharmby erupted in a sudden fit of anger because Hunter would not stop crying or settle.

Although the killing was not planned or premeditated, she described the violence inflicted on the baby as extreme.

'You smashed this baby against either the floor, the wall or a hard piece of furniture,' she told him.

Hunter was just 12 weeks old and, because he had been born prematurely, was closer in size to an average four-week-old baby.

The judge said Wharmby routinely fed Hunter overnight and regarded him as his own son. However, he had also inflicted serious injuries on the infant in the weeks before his death.

The court established that Wharmby had inflicted at least one earlier serious injury on Hunter through violent shaking between 1 June and 7 July 2022. He was also convicted of causing grievous bodily harm with intent in connection with the assault.

Mrs Justice Foster highlighted that Wharmby knew he struggled to control his temper. He had previously told a doctor about his worrying bouts of anger but had taken no steps to protect Hunter.

Parents Describe Lifelong Grief

Hunter's mother was woken shortly before 05:30 on 15 July 2022 when Wharmby brought the gravely ill baby into her room.

The baby's head appeared to have doubled in size, and he looked grey and floppy.

According to Kent Police, doctors discovered a fractured skull and severe swelling of his brain. Despite being transferred from the Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother Hospital in Margate to King's College Hospital in London, Hunter died that afternoon.

In a statement read to the court, Ms Hodges said her son had depended on adults to keep him safe.

'He was here, he was so loved and his life mattered,' she said.

She added that she should now have a four-year-old boy running around and laughing, but instead would spend her life wondering who Hunter might have become.

'I've been given a lifetime to grieve the loss of my son,' she said.

His father, Seamus Tuckell, recalled seeing his son's lifeless body covered in tubes in hospital.

'I cannot unsee those memories. It became clear it was not an accident,' he said.

Wharmby Sentenced to Life Imprisonment

Kent Police confirmed that Wharmby was found guilty of murder and causing grievous bodily harm with intent following a trial at Canterbury Crown Court.

He denied both charges but was convicted by majority jury verdicts on 29 October 2026.

Detective Inspector Adam Marshall, the senior investigating officer, described Wharmby as an 'incredibly dangerous man' who repeatedly refused opportunities to explain what happened to Hunter.

'Now that Wharmby's lies have been laid bare, he will rightly be spending many years behind bars,' DI Marshall said.

He added that the investigation had been distressing for officers and acknowledged the devastating impact of the case on Hunter's family.

excerpt: US Vice-President JD Vance said Americans did not need to build bunkers or stockpile food and water after separate outages affected Microsoft services, flights and banking customers.
headline: JD Vance Says Americans Don't Need Bunkers as He Warns 'You Have to Be Prepared for Everything' Amid Outages
html_content:
US Vice President JD Vance told Americans they did not need to build bunkers or stockpile food and water amid recent technology outages. Speaking on Fox News' The Ingraham Angle on Monday, 16 November, Vance said the administration did not see an imminent crisis, while stressing that the country still needed to prepare for emergencies.

The exchange followed disruptions involving Microsoft services, a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop and problems reported by online banking customers. The separate incidents prompted questions about their causes and whether households should prepare for something more serious.

Vance was responding to host Laura Ingraham, who asked whether Americans should take extra precautions following the recent disruptions. His answer drew a distinction between the government's responsibility to plan for emergencies and the personal measures some people were considering.

JD Vance Bunkers Comments Follow Questions From Friends

Vance said friends had contacted him to ask whether they should prepare to build a bunker or put aside food and water. He told Ingraham that his answer had been no.

'We don't see a crisis coming down, but you have to be prepared for everything,' he said.

"Should Americans be prepping for something here given what's just happened over the past two weeks?"

.@VP: "We do not see some crisis coming down, but you have to be prepared for everything." pic.twitter.com/na510SopEF

— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) November 17, 2026

The wording was reassuring, but it came with a qualification. Vance was not saying that serious disruptions were impossible. Instead, he said the government should be ready to handle the worst outcomes even while seeking to prevent them.

He also described military readiness and emergency planning as part of responsible government, rather than evidence that a crisis was approaching. His remarks did not announce a change to federal household preparedness guidance or identify a specific threat requiring Americans to take extraordinary precautions.

The timing helps explain the questions. Microsoft users had experienced service interruptions, while the FAA stopped departures nationwide on Friday, 13 November. Banking customers also reported problems accessing services.

The FAA later attributed its ground stop to instability in its telecommunications network. Its initial investigation identified excessive data traffic affecting legacy equipment and two potential locations involved in the disruption. The agency said it had no indication of a cyberattack or an outside malicious actor, although its investigation into the root cause continued.

JD Vance Bunkers Reassurance Contrasts With Cyberattack Fears

Not everyone was satisfied that the disruptions were unrelated. Republican Senator Josh Hawley told TMZ DC that he wanted answers about whether outages involving aviation, banks and technology could reflect a coordinated cyberattack.

Hawley questioned whether the incidents were coincidental, but acknowledged that he could be wrong. His concerns were questions rather than evidence that a coordinated attack had occurred.

The White House said on Tuesday, 17 November, that there was no evidence the wider series of disruptions resulted from a cyberattack. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also told Reuters that the outages affecting United Airlines, the FAA, Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase were not tied to cyberattacks. He suggested that newer technology being introduced on older computer systems could be overwhelming existing infrastructure.

These assurances do not amount to a complete technical explanation for every interruption. The FAA, for example, said its investigation into the telecommunications failure was continuing. However, the available findings do not establish that the separate incidents shared a common cause.

Vance's response was narrower than some of the questions being asked. He rejected the idea that Americans needed to rush into extraordinary preparations, while insisting that officials plan for possibilities they hope never materialise.

For travellers whose flights were halted and customers unable to access banking services, the consequences were immediate. Whether those individual failures reveal wider weaknesses remains a question for the agencies and companies responsible for explaining them.

excerpt: A leaked curved-glass sample may hint at Apple's possible 2027 anniversary iPhone design, but its origin, specifications and connection to the company remain unverified.
headline: iPhone 20 Pro Could Look Radically Different as Leaked Video Hints at a Bold New Curved Display
html_content:
Apple's iPhone 20 Pro could introduce a striking design change after a leaked video showed a curved glass sample believed to be linked to the company's 2027 anniversary models. The sample appears to curve along all four edges, potentially giving the phone's front a more seamless appearance. However, it is not a verified display panel or a finished iPhone, and Apple has not confirmed the design.

The clip was posted on X on 16 November by technology leaker Ice Universe, who called the anticipated redesign a 'milestone'. The product name 'iPhone 20 Pro' remains unconfirmed.

The Apple iPhone 20 Pro is going to feature a milestone design - let's take a look first pic.twitter.com/n8uNrZgh0S

— Ice Universe (@UniverseIce) November 16, 2026

Apple is approaching the 20th anniversary of the original iPhone, introduced in 2007. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported in August that Apple still planned a glass-centric redesign for 2027. He said the front and rear glass would curve towards the sides around a thin metal band. Apple has not confirmed those details.

What the Leaked iPhone 20 Pro Video Shows

The sample appears to have shallow curves on all four edges, rounded corners and a narrow black border. Its upper section has openings resembling those used for front camera and Face ID components. These details are consistent with earlier descriptions of the rumoured design, but they do not establish the final display or component layout.

MacRumors reported on 17 November that similar pieces had circulated online since early October. On 7 October, the Weibo account 体验more shared photographs of samples in two sizes, suggesting they resembled concepts based on leaked information. Ice Universe also posted a separate clip on 14 November, describing it as an approved '3D quad-curved cover glass' sample.

The latest footage shows a loose glass sample, not a working handset or proof of Apple approval. MacRumors suggested that the pieces were more likely early manufacturing tests by accessory makers working from rumours than components produced to Apple's actual specifications. Their precise origin remains unverified.

Ice Universe has also discussed shallow curves and optical effects that could make display borders less noticeable. MacRumors has described the wider design goal as an iPhone that resembles a single slab of glass. However, neither the sample nor earlier reports confirm how the final device will look.

How a Curved Display Could Affect Daily Use

A four-sided curve could change how the phone feels in the hand, although the sample cannot demonstrate its comfort or handling. In a translated Weibo post, Ice Universe wrote: 'The era of easy screen protector application is coming to an end. The era of a comfortable grip is approaching.'

A screen protector would need to match the final glass contours closely. If its dimensions differed, the edges could lift or leave gaps. PhoneArena has noted that protectors on earlier curved Android phones could peel away, contributing to manufacturers' move towards flat screens. Whether Apple's rumoured design would create similar problems remains unknown.

Weibo leaker Fixed Focus Digital claimed in August that the anniversary models would use the same glass manufacturing process developed for the iPhone Air, with modifications to produce more rounded components. This remains an unverified supply-chain claim.

The sample also appears to show an upper cut-out resembling the smaller Dynamic Island introduced on the iPhone 18 Pro. However, the glass does not establish the feature's final size or layout on a 2027 model.

Display analyst Ross Young, who has since retired, previously predicted that the smaller Dynamic Island could remain through 2027. The visible openings in the leaked sample are consistent with the possibility that the anniversary model will retain a front-facing cut-out rather than adopt a completely uninterrupted display. They do not confirm Apple's final decision.

Apple has not commented on the leaked footage or confirmed its anniversary iPhone design. Until the company announces a device, the model's name, appearance and specifications remain unconfirmed. The video offers a possible glimpse of Apple's design direction, not evidence of a finished iPhone.

excerpt: All 17 people aboard a Russian An-12 reportedly died after it caught fire near Kemerovo. Reports say the crew tried to steer it away from homes.
headline: Russian Military Plane Catches Fire Before Deadly Crash as Reports Say All on Board Were Killed
html_content:
The crew of a burning Russian An-12 military transport aircraft reportedly tried to steer it away from residential buildings before it crashed near Yagunovo in the Kemerovo region on Tuesday. Russian media reported that all 17 people aboard were killed.

The aircraft crashed on 17 November during a flight that Russian outlets said was travelling from Novosibirsk to Kansk. The incident was reported at about 9.30pm local time. Kemerovo Region Governor Ilya Seredyuk confirmed an aviation incident near Yagunovo but did not identify the aircraft or give a casualty figure. He later said the plane had been flying through the region. The reported route and death toll had not been officially confirmed.

Crew Reportedly Tried to Steer Burning Aircraft Away From Homes

REN TV, a Russian state-controlled broadcaster, reported that the crew tried to keep the burning aircraft away from residential buildings before impact. The claim was also carried by other outlets, but no official account has established the aircraft's flight path or confirmed the crew's actions.

Witnesses cited in Russian media reports said the aircraft was on fire before it descended rapidly and struck a field near Yagunovo. Local reports said there were no casualties or damage on the ground. The village is near Kemerovo, the regional capital, but authorities had not released a detailed account of the crash site or the aircraft's final movements.

Russian Media Put Death Toll at 17

REN TV and Izvestia, a Russian newspaper, reported that all 17 people aboard were killed. Izvestia attributed the figure to a source, while REN TV also reported that nobody survived. The governor's public statements did not confirm the number of people on the aircraft or the reported fatalities.

Early accounts differed. Telegram channels linked to Russian security services initially reported three deaths, while military bloggers put the number aboard at 13. Later reports raised the figure to 17. The discrepancies reflected the uncertainty in the first hours after the crash; no official casualty statement had reconciled the figures by Tuesday evening.

Russian Air Force's Antonov An-12 four-engine turboprop transport plane has crashed in Kemerovo Oblast located in central Russia on Tuesday evening.

All 17 personnel who were on board have reportedly perished.

According to BAZA, the investigators are currently examining three… pic.twitter.com/aMlq7kPcvk

— Status-6 (@Archer83Able) November 17, 2026

Governor Confirms Incident as Emergency Teams Respond

Seredyuk announced the aviation incident near Yagunovo in a Telegram post, saying emergency services were working at the scene and that he was heading there. He said regional authorities were providing assistance while the relevant agencies established the circumstances. An operational headquarters was later set up to coordinate the response.

In a subsequent video message, Seredyuk said the aircraft had been flying through the region when it crashed. He listed Emergency Situations Ministry personnel, police, the National Guard (Rosgvardiya) and disaster medicine teams among those at the site. His statements confirmed the incident and the emergency response, but did not identify the aircraft, confirm the reported death toll or establish the cause.

Cause of An-12 Crash Remains Unknown

Russian media reported that the aircraft caught fire while airborne. Baza, a Russian Telegram news channel, reported a possible aviation fuel leak, citing unnamed sources. The account has not been independently verified. No official finding has established what started the fire or whether it caused the aircraft to crash.

The aircraft was identified by Russian outlets as an Antonov An-12, a Soviet-designed, four-engine turboprop transport aircraft that first flew in 1957. It was developed to carry troops, military equipment and cargo and has been used in military transport operations. The reported Novosibirsk-to-Kansk route and an attempted emergency landing have not been independently confirmed. Authorities have yet to release findings on the aircraft's condition or the sequence of events leading to the crash.

It was developed to carry troops, military equipment and cargo and has been used in military transport operations. The reported Novosibirsk-to-Kansk route and an attempted emergency landing have not been independently confirmed. Authorities have yet to release findings on the aircraft's condition or the sequence of events leading to the crash.

excerpt: Leaked records examined by more than 230 journalists indicate Deutsche Bank flagged about $582m in suspicious Epstein-linked transactions and reveal previously undisclosed details about Trump's banking relationship.
headline: Deutsche Bank Leak Reveals $582M in Suspicious Epstein-Linked Transactions and New Trump Banking Details
html_content:
Deutsche Bank flagged $581.9 million (£437 million) in suspicious transactions linked to Jeffrey Epstein, according to leaked records examined by an international investigation published on Tuesday, 17 November 2026.

The findings also reveal previously undisclosed details about Trump's banking relationship with Deutsche Bank, including the accidental disclosure of financial information associated with his private banking accounts in 2017.

The investigation, called Inside Deutsche Bank, involved more than 230 journalists from 56 media outlets. They examined more than 15 million leaked files.

According to the Financial Times, an internal Deutsche Bank document showed that the bank filed 21 suspicious activity reports (SARs) covering around 3,200 transactions linked to Epstein or his companies between October 2013 and May 2019. The transactions were valued at $581.9 million (£437 million).

The figure is more than double the $250 million (£188 million) in suspicious Epstein-linked transactions that Deutsche Bank allegedly failed to report promptly, according to a report by Democratic Senator Ron Wyden in August 2026. The two figures reflect different sets of transactions and reporting, rather than necessarily representing separate sums.

Epstein's Deutsche Bank Transactions

The flagged transactions reportedly included payments to women, transfers involving shell companies and suspected misuse of charitable donations. They also included payments involving billionaire associates Leon Black and Glenn Dubin, whom bank records reportedly identified as apparent sources of funds.

Epstein became a Deutsche Bank client in August 2013, five years after his conviction for soliciting prostitution from a minor. The Financial Times reported that the bank ignored internal warnings before informing him in December 2018 that it intended to end their relationship.

South Africa's Financial Mail reported that the bank closed Epstein's two remaining accounts three days after his arrest in July 2019. A subsequent internal investigation identified at least 112 high-risk transactions.

The investigation also examined potential links between financial activity and sexual abuse at Epstein's Zorro Ranch in New Mexico, as well as suspected money laundering through his charity, Gratitude America.

An internal email described Ghislaine Maxwell as an alleged 'co-conspirator in Epstein's illegal activities'. Nevertheless, the bank reportedly allowed an arrangement involving one of Epstein's trusts, which listed Maxwell as a beneficiary, to proceed.

The relationship generated approximately $1 million (£750,000) annually for Deutsche Bank's wealth management business between 2015 and 2018. This was below the $2 million to $4 million (£1.5 million to £3 million) the bank had anticipated.

Trump's Deutsche Bank Ties

The Financial Times also reported that a bank employee accidentally sent a link containing financial information from 1,586 private banking accounts to an outside recipient's accountant in 2017. The information included accounts associated with Trump.

The recipient alerted the bank and deleted the file. Trump was not notified. Senior executives reportedly discussed whether he should be informed, while Christian Sewing, then head of the private bank and now Deutsche Bank's chief executive, described the incident as an 'awful mistake' in internal messages.

Dutch outlet Follow the Money identified suspicious financial transactions involving DT Marks Baku LLC, a Trump-owned company associated with the Trump International Hotel project in Azerbaijan.

Investigators traced a $141,261.82 transfer from Scottish shell company Faberlex LP, which had received funding from Azerbaijan's state-owned Baktelecom through Danske Bank's Estonian branch.

The initial transfer was returned following an account-number error, while an identical amount was subsequently sent to another offshore company, Datemile Alliance. The findings do not establish that Trump was aware of the transactions.

Follow the Money also identified suspicious transactions involving Trump-owned companies that Deutsche Bank's analysis linked to entities associated with Russian and Azerbaijani money-laundering networks.

The investigation reported that the bank did not disclose certain findings concerning the 2014 transactions to Congress when it was questioned about Trump's financial ties to Russia. However, the findings do not establish that Trump personally knew about or participated in any alleged wrongdoing.

The New York Times reported that Deutsche Bank maintained relationships with Russian billionaires Oleg Deripaska and Viktor Vekselberg despite internal warnings about money laundering and sanctions risks. Five of seven Russian oligarchs sanctioned by the Trump administration in 2018 had links to the lender.

Deutsche Bank said the matters dated back many years and pointed to improvements under Sewing's leadership, including €7 billion (£5.25 billion) invested in strengthening its internal controls between 2019 and 2025.

The leaked documents raise questions about the bank's handling of suspicious financial activity involving high-profile clients. However, they do not establish that Trump personally participated in money laundering or other wrongdoing.

excerpt: Former NVIDIA chief executive Jensen Huang says he would return if the board believes it would benefit the company, while directors reportedly continue searching for a permanent successor.
headline: 'Your Return Is Inevitable': Internet Reacts as Jensen Huang Breaks Silence Amid Chinese Spy Scandal
html_content:
Former NVIDIA chief executive Jensen Huang has said he would be honoured to return if the board decides his reinstatement would benefit the company. In a statement on Tuesday, 17 November, he said he would be willing to resume the role. Investor Erik Torenberg replied, 'Your return is inevitable', in a post on X.

Huang's statement was his first public response since he resigned on 12 November. He acknowledged serious mistakes in his personal life, said he regretted the problems caused to the board and pledged to co-operate with its independent investigation. NVIDIA appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and began searching for a permanent successor.

Excellent note. Your return is inevitable.

— Erik Torenberg (@eriktorenberg) November 17, 2026

The scrutiny involves Huang's reported relationship with Alice Huang, a former senior executive and key controller of Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed. Reuters reported that US intelligence agencies were examining her possible links to China's Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing. US Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department had not determined whether she was a spy. China has rejected the allegation. Reuters has also reported that it could not independently verify the espionage allegations.

Jensen Huang's Hope for Comeback Gather Support on X

Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick urged NVIDIA to bring its former chief executive back, writing, 'Let's bring Jensen back!!! LFG' in a post on X.

Let’s bring Jensen back!!! LFG https://t.co/TbSPwWoHBY

— travis kalanick (@travisk) November 17, 2026

Investor and All-In Podcast co-host Jason Calacanis also backed a return. He posted, 'Bring @JensenHuang back', adding a salute emoji in a separate X post.

Bring @JensenHuang back 🫡 https://t.co/aLqz6xKECk

— @jason (@Jason) November 17, 2026

Chainlink co-founder Sergey Nazarov had called for Huang's reinstatement on 15 November. 'Jensen Huang should be reinstated as the CEO of NVIDIA,' he wrote, praising Huang's impact on gaming, cryptocurrency and artificial intelligence. Nazarov also encouraged followers to sign a letter supporting his return in a post on X.

Jensen Huang should be reinstated as the CEO of NVIDIA. He has done an amazing job of building NVIDIA into a leading technology company, doing massive good in the world across many countries by supporting the growth of gaming, crypto and now AI on a global scale.

I have…

— Sergey Nazarov (@SergeyNazarov) November 15, 2026

The posts show support from individual public figures, rather than establishing wider agreement among NVIDIA employees or shareholders. Reuters separately reported that an online campaignhad gathered more than 180,000 signatures. However, the professional affiliations of signatories had not been independently verified.

NVIDIA Board Has Not Committed to Reinstatement

Public support has not changed the board's reported position. Reuters said on 16 November, citing three people familiar with the matter, that directors were not considering reinstating Huang. NVIDIA has not announced a change to its succession process.

A separate investigation concerns Megaspeed's business. The US Commerce Department said it opened an inquiry in 2024 into potential export-control violations after identifying suspicious activity involving possible semiconductor diversion. Investigators requested NVIDIA sales records in May 2025, and the chipmaker placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list in June 2025. US and Singaporean officials conducted an on-site end-use check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was then its chief executive. The Justice Department subsequently took the lead in the criminal investigation.

Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing and said Alice Huang left the company on 30 August 2025. It has described its business as lawful. Those export-control questions are distinct from the intelligence inquiry into her possible links to Beijing.

NVIDIA's board has said it has no reason to believe company secrets or US national security were compromised. On 17 November, it announced a new committee to oversee national security policies, export-control compliance and global trade risks, chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson. The committee will also include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri.

Huang has offered to return, but the board's search for a permanent CEO remains the formal process in place.

excerpt: Russian model Anastasia Drozdova was found stabbed to death in Moscow. Her former boyfriend allegedly posted an image from her Instagram before dying after a suspected suicide attempt.
headline: Russian Model Stabbed to Death by Ex-Boyfriend Who Allegedly Posted Her Body on Instagram With 'Paid the Price' Message
html_content:
A Russian model was stabbed to death by her reportedly abusive former boyfriend, who allegedly posted a photograph of her bloodied body on her Instagram account after the killing.

Anastasia Drozdova, 28, was found dead inside her rented apartment in Moscow on Saturday, 14 November 2026, following an alleged attack by Dmitry Zadvornykh, 38.

The suspect reportedly used her phone to upload the disturbing image alongside a chilling message before travelling to a shooting club, where he shot himself. He later died in hospital.

Ex-Boyfriend Posted Chilling Message

According to the New York Post, citing Russian broadcaster REN TV, Zadvornykh allegedly ambushed Drozdova at her apartment, stabbing her eight times before slashing her throat.

He then reportedly accessed her Instagram account and uploaded a photograph of her lifeless body to her Stories.

The image carried the message: 'You mocked the wrong person and paid the price. Goodbye.'

The US Sun, in a report published on 17 November, said Zadvornykh travelled approximately eight miles to a shooting club after the attack, where he attempted suicide. He sustained a critical gunshot wound and later died in hospital.

The Moscow branch of Russia's Investigative Committee opened a criminal case under Article 105 of the Russian Criminal Code, which covers murder.

Friends Reveal Alleged Harassment and Threats

The couple reportedly had an on-and-off relationship for several years, with friends claiming Drozdova had repeatedly tried to escape her former boyfriend.

The New York Post, citing Need To Know, reported that Drozdova had fled abroad several times, including to Turkey, before returning to Moscow.

'She ran away from him several times, including abroad,' a friend told Russian media.

'When she returned to Moscow, he would start messaging her again.'

In an interview with Russian outlet MSK1.RU published on 17 November, a close friend identified as Lera said Zadvornykh had repeatedly contacted Drozdova in the weeks before her death.

She recalled that he was constantly calling the 28-year-old, sending her flowers and attempting to arrange meetings.

'I asked her to move out of this apartment as soon as possible. I was very scared for her,' Lera told MSK1.RU.

Another acquaintance, Kristina, a beauty specialist who knew Drozdova during her time in Turkey, told the outlet that the suspect had allegedly threatened the model and attempted to hack her social media account in autumn 2025.

Kristina said Drozdova had been distressed following their separation and had occasionally mentioned the threats.

MSK1.RU also reported that Drozdova had been seeing another man, Adil, for approximately two months before her death. He told the publication that he had not known about the alleged threats from her former boyfriend.

Adil recalled seeing Drozdova for the last time on 12 November, when they went to the cinema. The following morning, he left for work. When she stopped responding to his calls and messages on Saturday, he became worried.

He rushed to her apartment after hearing about the killing but was unable to reach her.

Who Was Anastasia Drozdova?

According to MSK1.RU, Drozdova moved from Moscow to Turkey in 2021, where she developed a career in the beauty industry.

She initially offered eyebrow and eyelash treatments before expanding her work to training other women. She also reportedly worked as a fitness trainer and model, participating in fashion shoots.

The 28-year-old returned to Moscow in the summer of 2026 and had begun selling hair extensions, according to the Russian publication.

Zadvornykh worked as a men's laser hair removal technician. The New York Post, citing REN TV, also reported that he had a criminal record.

MSK1.RU spoke to one of Drozdova's former boyfriends, who described her as kind, supportive and determined to build an independent life.

Meanwhile, her mother, Lyudmila, told MSK1.RU that the family had not yet been allowed to collect her body because a forensic examination was required following her violent death.

Friends have reportedly organised a fundraising campaign to support her family.

Investigators are continuing their inquiry into the killing under Article 105 of Russia's Criminal Code.

excerpt: Equinor confirms an ongoing cyberattack on its IT systems, reporting no impact on production and no indications that data has been stolen.
headline: Equinor Hit by Cyberattack as Concerns Grow Over European Gas Supplies
html_content:
Equinor has confirmed an ongoing cyberattack targeting certain IT systems but says the incident has not affected its oil and gas operations or production.

The Norwegian energy company disclosed the attack on Tuesday, 17 November. It said resources had been mobilised to neutralise the attack and regain full integrity. Equinor reported no indications that data had been stolen and said relevant authorities were being informed. The company has not disclosed when the attack began, how access was gained or which systems were targeted.

Equinor Says Production Remains Unaffected

In a statement published on its website, Equinor said: 'Relevant resources have been mobilised to neutralise the attack and regain full integrity. There are no indications that data has been stolen. The attack has not affected Equinor's operations and production.' The company said it would provide further information when it became available.

Spokesperson Ellen Maria Skjelsbæk told the Norwegian news agency NTB that employees could experience disruptions to some services, particularly applications and internal IT systems. She said the company had not lost access to any of its systems and that staff did not need to take any specific action. The reported disruptions concern internal services, while the company says its production activities remain unaffected.

Norwegian Security Authorities Notified

Equinor has notified Norway's National Security Authority (NSM), the agency responsible for preventive national security and national cybersecurity coordination, and the Norwegian Ocean Industry Authority (Havtil), which supervises safety, security and emergency preparedness in the petroleum sector.

NSM said it was aware of the incident and in contact with Equinor. Communications adviser Mari Lerdal said the authority stood ready to assist if needed. Norway's Police Security Service (PST), the country's domestic security and intelligence agency, was also informed, according to public broadcaster NRK. Equinor has not identified any suspected perpetrators.

Norway Remains a Major Gas Supplier to Europe

Norway was the European Union's largest supplier of natural gas in 2025, accounting for 31% of the bloc's total gas imports and 54% of its pipeline gas imports, according to the European Commission. These figures underline Norway's importance to the EU gas market.

Equinor is one of Norway's major oil and gas producers. It also markets and sells the Norwegian state's share of oil and gas production from the continental shelf through the Norwegian State's Direct Financial Interests (SDFI), the government's direct ownership interests in offshore production licences.

The Norwegian state owns 67% of Equinor. The company has said its operations and production have not been affected, but has not published separate data on individual pipeline flows or deliveries to European customers.

Details of the Cyberattack Remain Unclear

Equinor has not disclosed how the attackers gained access, whether the incident involved ransomware or another form of intrusion, or which systems were affected. It has not said whether the incident was limited to corporate IT or involved operational technology used to control industrial processes.

The distinction matters because operational technology is used to monitor and control physical equipment, including systems involved in industrial production. Equinor has said the attack has not affected its operations or production, but has not provided a technical account of the systems involved. It has not given a timetable for resolving the incident and said further information would be shared when available.

excerpt: Apple acknowledged account access problems as complaints spread across its services, but a subscription fix did not signal an end to every issue.
headline: Apple Outage: Users Report iCloud Sign-In Errors as App Store and Apple Pay Complaints Emerge
html_content:
Apple users reported being unexpectedly signed out of their accounts on Tuesday, 17 November, with some unable to get back in after encountering verification failures. The sign-in difficulties raised concerns about access to iCloud photographs, files and contacts, alongside complaints involving payments, app downloads and device activation.

Euro Weekly News reported Apple Account sign-in failures and outlined their potential implications for customers relying on iCloud to access photographs, files and contacts. However, its report did not document individual customers being unable to open specific photographs or documents, or establish that data had been deleted or that iCloud Photos or iCloud Drive had suffered separate outages.

iCloud Users Encounter Errors After Sudden Sign-Outs

Customers described being logged out on iPhones and Macs, then receiving verification failures or other error messages when trying to sign back in. Some said they could not regain access, although the duration of individual lockouts and the total number of affected customers had not been established.

For people who rely on iCloud to reach personal material, an inability to authenticate could complicate access to connected services. The accounts did not specify whether the difficulties affected access through the Photos app, iCloud Drive or a web browser, or establish whether copies stored locally on devices remained available.

Apple Briefly Acknowledges Sign-In Problems

Apple's System Status page briefly acknowledged an Apple Account sign-in issue, warning that the service could be slow or unavailable. Its general status page subsequently showed no active problems, while Downdetector later recorded another increase in complaints involving Apple services and sign-ins.

Apple subsequently acknowledged that an internal software update had caused outages affecting several of its services. In a statement to USA TODAY, the company said many of its systems were back up and running, while it continued working to restore the remaining services. Apple also said the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack.

Subscription Purchase Issue Resolved Separately

Apple also acknowledged a problem with subscription purchases on Tuesday and marked it as resolved after about three hours. The update did not confirm that the separate account sign-in problems had ended.

The three-hour period applied to the subscription purchase issue, not the wider disruption, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. The report did not establish how long the other problems lasted or when affected customers could sign back in, download apps and make payments normally.

App Store and Apple Pay Draw Further Complaints

Beyond account access, customers described difficulty loading the App Store and downloading applications, while Apple Pay also featured in complaints. Other reports concerned Apple Music failing to connect, devices being unable to complete activation and problems involving Apple Support, extending the reported difficulties across several everyday tasks.

Those experiences were customer complaints rather than confirmation from Apple that every named service had suffered a complete outage. The San Francisco Chronicle did not establish the disruption's full geographical reach or whether customers experienced the same problems across different devices and accounts.

Developer Services Show Additional Disruption

Apple's separate developer status page showed multiple outages as of 10.30am on Tuesday, while developers also described problems signing in to App Store Connect, the platform used to manage applications. These developer notices were distinct from the general System Status updates concerning Apple Account access and did not establish a shared cause.

The disruption was subsequently attributed to an internal software update, Apple confirmed. Although many systems had recovered, the company said it was still working to restore the remaining services. Downdetector figures represent user-submitted reports rather than a verified count of affected customers.

excerpt: A US survey found 13% of adult Gen Z gamers plan to rearrange work or school for GTA VI, while an estimated 12.5 million gamers may change plans.
headline: GTA VI Launch: 13% of Gen Z Gamers Plan to Change Their Schedules Ahead of 19 November Release
html_content:
Generation Z gamers are the most likely to rearrange their work or school schedules for the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, with 13% saying they plan to make changes ahead of its release on 19 November, according to a new survey.

PCMag, a US technology publication, commissioned market research firm YouGov Plc to survey 2,024 American adults online between 23 and 27 October 2026. Of those surveyed, 1,154 qualified as gamers.

Overall, 8% of adult gamers said they intended to take paid leave or adjust their schedules to play the game. The findings suggest that an estimated 12.5 million US adult gamers could make such changes.

Gen Z Gamers Most Likely to Rearrange Their Schedules

Among the adult gamers surveyed, Generation Z recorded the highest proportion planning to change their schedules for the release, at 13%. As the survey covered adults aged 18 and over, its findings reflect only the adult portion of Generation Z.

Male gamers were also slightly more likely than female gamers to change their schedules, at 9% and 7%, respectively. Both figures refer to respondents who qualified as gamers, rather than the wider US adult population.

Survey Estimates 12.5 Million Gamers Could Change Their Plans

The overall 8% figure includes respondents planning to take paid leave, as well as those intending to change their working or school hours. The breakdown showed that 3% planned to take two or more days off, while another 3% intended to take one full day. A further 2% said they would take half a day off or adjust their hours.

The 12.5 million estimate was calculated using the US Census Bureau's 2025 adult population figure of approximately 269.8 million, an estimated 57.02% share of adults who play games and an adjusted survey figure of 8.15% for those planning schedule changes. It represents stated intentions extrapolated to the adult population, not confirmed leave bookings.

Most US Adults Do Not Plan to Play GTA VI at Launch

The survey found that 68% of all US adults did not intend to play Grand Theft Auto VI when it launches. This figure covers the full adult sample, including people who did not identify as gamers.

Among respondents who qualified as gamers, 14% said they planned to fit the game into their normal routines, while another 4% intended to reserve their evenings or weekends for playing. The figures distinguish casual play from respondents planning to change their schedules or take leave.

GTA VI Arrives 13 Years After Previous Mainline Release

Grand Theft Auto VI is the first new mainline entry in Rockstar Games' franchise since Grand Theft Auto V, which was released in September 2013. The developer has scheduled the sixth instalment for Thursday, 19 November 2026, more than 13 years after the previous game's release.

The new game returns to Vice City, a fictional city inspired by Miami, within the fictional state of Leonida. The story centres on Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos. Lucia is the franchise's first female lead protagonist in a mainline, story-driven Grand Theft Auto game.

Rockstar has confirmed versions for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Microsoft has also announced that the game will be available through Xbox Cloud Gaming on Xbox One from launch day, allowing players to stream it rather than play a native Xbox One version. No PC version has been confirmed for the 19 November release.

excerpt: A cane-carrying guest joins Chris Brown's concert routine, raising a question about who gets to define an audience member's experience.
headline: Chris Brown Grinds on an Elderly Fan With a Cane During SoFi Stadium Show, Prompting 'Downfall' Comment
html_content:
Chris Brown brought a fan carrying a red cane onstage at SoFi Stadium before serenading her and performing a grinding routine during 'Take You Down' on 15 November. The encounter drew contrasting reactions online, with one commenter calling it 'the downfall of Chris Brown' and others praising his guest.

The woman, identified as Ms Joyce, arrived wearing a long zebra-print fur coat, a black furry hat and sunglasses. Brown shared photographs of the pair together the following day, captioning his Instagram post 'LOVE HER'.

Chris Brown Brings Ms Joyce Into His Set

The performance took place during the third Los Angeles date of The R&B Tour, Brown's co-headlining run with Usher. Inviting a female fan onstage for 'Take You Down' is a regular part of Brown's set, rather than a format introduced specifically for this appearance.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by BROWN (@chrisbrownofficial)

Brown began by serenading Ms Joyce near a pole before laying her down on a nearby red couch. Complex describes the interaction as grinding in its headline, while Billboard separately reports that Brown laid her down and danced on her, providing further published support for description of the performance.

Ms Joyce Removes Her Coat During Performance

A more detailed account published by The Shade Room describes Ms Joyce removing her sunglasses during the serenade and taking off her coat after Brown removed his shirt. The report also describes her placing her hands on his back during the couch sequence.

Chris Brown brought a GRANDMA onstage during his performance of “Take You Down” at his Los Angeles concert and she had the time of her life 🤣 pic.twitter.com/l06Pi0V7sl

— Daily Loud (@DailyLoud) November 17, 2026

It includes a brief post-show exchange involving Ms Joyce and a younger woman who appeared to say she had given up her place for her. Ms Joyce said, 'You know what I mean, Jelly Bean?', although the exchange did not provide a detailed account of her experience.

Online Response Includes Criticism And Support

Among the supplied X comments, the account @TantumHon11590 wrote, 'The downfall of Chris Brown', followed by, 'Once a celebrated musician; Today an abashless debaucher'. Other accounts expressed disapproval more briefly, with @polomanszn posting 'Disgusting' and @KingMOBthe4th writing 'Rubbish'.

Supportive responses focused on Ms Joyce's participation, including @0xkarm's comment that 'grandma understood the assignment better than the whole crowd'. Another account, @legendaryh93901, wrote, 'Grandma came for a concert and left with a core memory she'll never forget!'

Celebrity Responses Follow Brown's Instagram Post

Brown's photographs also attracted responses from other entertainers, extending the discussion beyond the comments accompanying concert clips. Actress Taraji P. Henson wrote, 'God bless your heart babe. You gave her a night she will NEVER forget', while rapper Lupe Fiasco described the encounter as 'diabolical'.

Billboard reproduced those celebrity comments alongside its account of the performance and Brown's subsequent photographs. Their responses offered further individual interpretations of the encounter, rather than establishing how Ms Joyce herself regarded every aspect of the routine.

SoFi Stadium Show Features Bobby Brown

The wider concert included a guest appearance by Bobby Brown, who performed 'My Prerogative' and 'Rock Wit'cha'. Chris Brown and Usher reportedly closed the show with 'New Flame', following a programme that included guest performances and Brown's audience-participation segment.

SoFi Stadium's official listing identifies 15 November as the added third show for the co-headliners, corroborating the concert's date and venue. The listing concerns the event itself and does not provide a separate account of Ms Joyce's appearance or the choreography.

'Downfall' Comment Reflects One Viewer's Opinion

Ms Joyce's exact age has not been published, and the reports do not confirm that she is a grandmother. Several commenters nevertheless referred to her as 'grandma'.

The 'downfall' comment represented one viewer's opinion, while others praised her participation. Those responses alone do not establish a wider backlash or any impact on Brown's career.

excerpt: A series of cyber incidents, software bugs and maintenance failures disrupted US hospitals, airlines, banks, universities and online services in mid-November, with no common campaign identified.
headline: Cyberattacks and Outages in November: Here Are the Major US Disruptions Reported So Far
html_content:
Cyber incidents and technical outages disrupted US businesses in mid-November, affecting travel, banking, healthcare, aviation and online services. The incidents ranged from unauthorised access and malicious code to software defects and maintenance-related failures. Authorities and companies have not established a common cause linking them.

Cyber Incidents Affect Hospitals, Universities and Software Firms

Expedia Group said attackers accessed its systems through a compromised third-party technology provider. The company has not disclosed whether customer information was exposed or confirmed the extent of any potential data loss.

Vanderbilt University said OneDrive, SharePoint and Teams remained disabled on 17 November following a cyber incident. The university warned that restoring access could take several weeks, with the first milestone expected in early December.

ConnectWise investigated unauthorised activity involving ScreenConnect partner environments. Huntress detected its SCKit toolkit on 288 hosts across 48 organisations on 11 November. ConnectWise identified five third-party extensions potentially associated with the activity and disabled them across approximately 400 partner environments as a precaution. The presence of the extensions did not, by itself, establish that an environment had been compromised.

Bitrise took its developer platform offline on 13 November after detecting suspicious activity and confirming unauthorised access to an internal system. The company said the system did not store or process customer data and that it had found no evidence that customer data, secrets or source code had been exposed.

Monadnock Community Hospital confirmed on 16 November that a cyber incident had caused a server outage affecting its Peterborough hospital and locations in Jaffrey and Antrim. Third-party specialists were investigating what information, if any, had been affected.

Optimizely said an attacker exploited a Web Experimentation vulnerability to inject malicious code into customer projects. Report URI found 188 infected snippets across 178 organisations, including websites associated with the BBC, CNN and Zoom. The code could steal payment-card information and replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses. It traced about $7,040 (€6,392; £5,334) in cryptocurrency to attacker-linked wallets by 19:25 UTC on 16 November. The potential number of exposed payment cards remains unknown. Optimizely said it had fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects.

Technical Failures Disrupt Cloud Platforms, Airlines and Financial Services

Microsoft said a software defect exposed by changes in network traffic caused its 12-13 November global outage, affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot. The company traced the problem to a latent defect in networking gateway servers that caused them to become unresponsive under certain load conditions.

Anthropic reported several separate problems affecting Claude. These included elevated errors affecting its models and services on 16 November and difficulties joining calls through Claude Meetings beta on 16-17 November. Anthropic attributed the meeting issue to higher-than-expected demand. It said calls already in progress and other Claude features were unaffected.

AWS reported authentication, sign-up and connectivity problems in its US East (N. Virginia) region on 15 November. Its status dashboard listed 11 affected services, including IAM Identity Center, AWS Sign-Up, Amazon Connect and CloudWatch. The problems were subsequently resolved.

The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop on 13 November after excessive data traffic destabilised legacy telecommunications equipment during router replacement work. The agency said its network received approximately 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. Air traffic resumed at 8:15 p.m. ET after the system stabilised.

Workday placed its WD1 production tenants into maintenance on 13 November after an issue involving its disaster-recovery environment left production data in an inconsistent state. Florida Atlantic University confirmed that its Workday service was restored on 14 November.

United Airlines experienced a technology outage on 16 November that delayed departing flights for about 100 minutes. A pilots' union memo said applications used for crew communications and final aircraft weight information were affected. United said flights already airborne and United Express operations were unaffected. The airline reported no indication of a cybersecurity incident.

JPMorgan Chase attributed transaction delays on 16 November to a software bug in its on-premises hardware systems. The bank said customers could still access their accounts and funds and that there was no evidence the problem was cyber-related. Plaid also reported intermittent errors involving Chase transactions.

Apple attributed several service disruptions on 17 November to an internal update. Customers reported problems involving iCloud, Apple Pay, Apple Support and other services. The company said many systems had been restored and that the incident was not caused by a cyberattack.

The National Security Agency reported temporary network degradation during scheduled maintenance on 17 November. It said some internal systems were affected but that mission-critical capabilities remained fully operational.

OpenAI's status history recorded separate incidents involving image-generation services, Workspace Agent runs, website publishing, ChatGPT and advertising billing, and API cost data between 12 and 17 November. These were service-specific technical problems rather than evidence of a wider security breach.

excerpt: Apple said an internal update caused widespread outages affecting iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay and other services, while denying that a cyberattack was responsible.
headline: Apple Denies Cyberattack After Internal Update Causes Worldwide Service Outages
html_content:
Apple has blamed an internal update for widespread disruptions affecting several of its services worldwide, including iCloud, the App Store and Apple Pay, on Tuesday, 17 November 2026.

The outage left users struggling to sign in to their accounts, download applications and access various Apple platforms. The company said the disruptions were not caused by a cyberattack, adding that many systems had already returned online while it worked to restore the remaining affected services.

Apple Confirms Internal Update Triggered Outages

An Apple spokesperson told TIME that an internal update had caused the service disruptions, adding that many of the company's systems had already been restored.

'Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,' the spokesperson told TIME. 'We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.'

According to Variety and other reports, Apple's System Status page listed problems affecting several services, including iCloud Account and Sign In, AppleCare on Device, Apple Business, Apple School Manager, Schoolwork and iCloud web applications. Users also reported difficulties accessing the App Store, Apple Pay and other platforms.

The disruptions affected both individual customers and organisations relying on Apple's digital services.

Sign-In Problems Extend to Apple Devices and Developer Platforms

According to 9to5Mac, some iPhone and Mac users were unexpectedly signed out of their accounts and encountered verification failures and unknown error messages when attempting to sign back in.

Meanwhile, MacRumors reported that Apple's separate developer status page listed disruptions involving Accounts, App Store Connect, Apple Music API, Apple Music Connect and Apple Podcasts Connect.

The problems prevented some developers from accessing App Store Connect, the platform used to manage applications and submit updates to Apple's marketplace.

Downdetector also recorded a surge in user reports involving iCloud, Apple Support and Apple Pay.

Apple Works to Restore Affected Services

Apple's System Status page changed throughout Tuesday as the company worked to resolve the disruptions.

Mashable reported that Apple Music and iCloud Mail, which had experienced problems earlier in the day, were subsequently marked as resolved. Apple Pay was also reported to be available.

However, other services continued to experience problems, including iCloud account access, AppleCare on Device and certain business and education platforms.

Apple did not immediately provide further technical details about the internal update or specify when all remaining services would be fully restored.

Customers were advised to monitor the company's official System Status page for updates.

Outages Follow Series of Technical Disruptions

The Apple incident came amid several technical disruptions affecting major companies and essential services in the United States in recent days.

Microsoft experienced a significant outage affecting Outlook and other Microsoft 365 services the previous week. The company attributed the disruption to a technical issue involving its network infrastructure, rather than a cyberattack, according to Variety.

On Friday, 13 November, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop after excessive data traffic destabilised parts of its telecommunications network, affecting communications and radar systems used by air traffic controllers.

The FAA said its legacy equipment became unstable when data flooded its network. The ground stop lasted more than four hours, and the FAA said its initial investigation had identified a problem involving router functionality. Its investigation continued.

Several major US banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and U.S. Bank, also saw increased customer reports of service problems on Monday, 16 November, according to Downdetector. JPMorgan Chase confirmed that a technical issue had affected some transactions, while Bank of America said its systems had operated normally throughout the day.

excerpt: A British tourist accused of smashing a Jesus statue in Lithuania has received an unexpected invitation from a priest who wants to forgive him.
headline: British Tourist Accused of Smashing Jesus Statue Gets Invitation From the Priest Who Wants to Forgive Him
html_content:
A British tourist accused of destroying a statue of Jesus Christ outside a church in Lithuania has received an unexpected invitation from the priest who initially helped publicise the incident. Despite the suspect facing a possible three-year prison sentence, Father Elijas Anatolijus Markauskas says he wants to welcome the man back, give him an opportunity to apologise and spare him further punishment.

The invitation follows an incident at the Shrine of Divine Mercy in Vilnius earlier this month. Speaking to Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT on 17 November, the priest expressed concern that the international attention surrounding the case could damage the suspect's future.

Lithuanian Priest Offers Forgiveness to British Tourist

Markauskas, vice-rector of the Shrine of Divine Mercy, initially appealed for help identifying the person responsible after footage of the incident circulated online.

However, he has since expressed sympathy for the suspect. 'Looking at his face, I can see that he is not an evil person,' he told LRT in remarks translated from Lithuanian. The priest said he would welcome the man if he returned to the church and offered an apology. He also expressed hope that the authorities would refrain from imposing punishment.

Markauskas believes the statue may have broken during reckless behaviour rather than a deliberate attempt to destroy it. His interpretation, however, does not establish the suspect's intentions.

As of 17 November, there was no confirmation that the tourist had contacted the church or accepted the invitation.

What Happened to the Jesus Statue in Vilnius?

According to Lithuanian police, the incident occurred between the evening of 11 November and the early hours of 12 November in the church courtyard on Dominikonų Street.

Footage showed a man removing a gold-coloured figure of Jesus from a wooden cross and carrying it into the street. The sculpture subsequently broke apart, leaving pieces scattered across the pavement.

Investigators identified and questioned a British citizen born in 1989. British media have identified the suspect as Aaron Goodfellow, 37, although Lithuanian authorities have not publicly confirmed his name.

Prosecutor Edvinas Navickas told Lithuanian broadcaster TV3 that the man had travelled to the country as a tourist and may have been under the influence of alcohol.

Shocking CCTV footage has captured the moment a man drops and smashes a golden statue of Jesus Christ after allegedly stealing it. The statue is believed to have been taken from the nearby 15th-century Shrine of Divine Mercy Church in Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania. The footage reportedly shows two men, suspected to be drunk British tourists, laughing as one approaches the other carrying the statue. Moments later, the precious religious image falls and shatters. Such disrespect towards a sacred religious object is deeply disturbing and unacceptable.

— Rev .Vitus (@Vitus_osst) November 14, 2026

British Tourist Could Face Three Years in Prison

Lithuanian prosecutors confirmed to Delfi that the investigation is proceeding under Article 312(2) of the country's Criminal Code, concerning damage at places of public reverence. Possible penalties include community service, a fine, restrictions on liberty, arrest or imprisonment for up to three years.

Police said the suspect was cooperating with investigators and that his identity document had been confiscated. The priest's willingness to forgive him does not automatically end the criminal investigation.

Britons Apologise as Church Plans Replacement Statue

Markauskas also told LRT that the church had received apologies from people in Britain following the incident. According to reports, businesses in Italy and Poland have offered to help fund a replacement sculpture, with the church hoping to install one by Easter.

The shrine, home to the original Divine Mercy painting, is closely associated with Catholic teachings about compassion and forgiveness.

Meanwhile, the priest has expressed concern about misleading images and false claims about the suspect's background circulating online, urging people against turning the incident into hostility towards other communities.

excerpt: Senator Roger Wicker has rejected Donald Trump's proposal to replace electromagnetic catapults on Ford-class aircraft carriers with steam systems, warning of major costs and delays.
headline: Trump Faces GOP Backlash Over Steam Catapult Order as Senator Calls Plan 'Non-Starter'
html_content:
US President Donald Trump is facing growing opposition from Republican lawmakers over his order to replace electromagnetic catapults with traditional steam-powered systems on America's newest aircraft carriers, with a senior senator warning that the proposal could cost billions and delay naval modernisation.

Senator Roger Wicker, the Republican chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, openly rejected the proposal during a confirmation hearing for Navy Secretary nominee Hung Cao on Tuesday.

'Returning to steam is a non-starter, and everybody needs to understand that,' Wicker told Cao, signalling growing resistance within Trump's own party to the directive.

Why Trump Wants Steam Catapults

The Ford-class carriers use the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS), which relies on electromagnetic energy rather than steam pressure to propel aircraft from the flight deck.

The technology is installed aboard USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN-78), USS John F. Kennedy (CVN-79) and USS Enterprise (CVN-80). The future USS Doris Miller (CVN-81) is also being built around the system.

Trump has repeatedly criticised EMALS, arguing that the technology is unnecessarily complicated and has contributed to delays and rising costs in the Navy's shipbuilding programme.

In August, he issued a National Security Presidential Memorandum directing the Navy to prepare a plan to convert the future Doris Miller from electromagnetic catapults to traditional steam-powered systems. The directive also called for a return to hydraulic weapons elevators.

The President has argued that the Navy should prioritise 'proven, reliable, and affordable technologies and ship designs' rather than relying on systems he considers overly complex.

At the same time, critics say replacing EMALS would mean abandoning technology around which the Ford-class carriers were designed, potentially creating additional engineering challenges and reducing operational capabilities.

Republicans Warn of Billions in Conversion Costs

Republican lawmakers on the Senate Appropriations Committee have also raised concerns about the financial and operational implications of the proposed conversion.

The committee's 2027 defence appropriations bill, released on Monday, would require the Navy to submit a report comparing the effectiveness of electromagnetic and traditional steam-powered catapult systems.

'The Committee is concerned that such a major redesign would result in many billions of dollars in additional costs and many years in programme schedule delays,' Republican lawmakers wrote in an accompanying explanatory statement.

Preliminary estimates put the design work needed to reintroduce steam catapults at approximately $10 billion (£7.6 billion), according to reports.

Democrats Also Question Trump's Aircraft Carrier Plan

Senator Tim Kaine, a Democrat from Virginia, told Cao that sailors aboard USS Gerald R. Ford had spoken positively about the electromagnetic launch system during his recent visit.

'Just because the president directed it, I do hope you'll consider the experience of those who've been operating these launches on the Ford,' Kaine said. He warned that returning to steam could result in higher costs and 'diminished capacity'.

On the other hand, Cao argued that electromagnetic catapults and elevators had contributed to delays affecting the Ford-class programme.

Congress Scrutinises Trump's Steam Catapult Directive

The growing resistance comes as Trump seeks congressional approval for a proposed $1.5 trillion (£1.14 trillion) defence budget before the end of the year.

The Senate appropriations bill does not itself cancel the President's directive, but its requirement for a Navy assessment signals that lawmakers want greater scrutiny before the service commits to an expensive redesign.

With Democrats set to take control of both chambers of Congress on 3 January, the debate over defence spending and naval modernisation could become increasingly contentious.
